desc: In Eclipse iceoryx-rs, versions 0.0.11 to 0.0.13 and 0.1.0 as well as on the latest main branch. `SampleReceiver::<T>::take()` and `Sample::<T>::deref()` are safe functions that hand the caller a `&T` pointing at a chunk written by another iceoryx process, but the subscriber path neither requires `T: ShmSend` nor verifies that the received chunk is at least `size_of::<T>()` bytes / `align_of::<T>()`-aligned. A peer process that publishes an undersized chunk, or any chunk at all when the subscriber chose a pointer-bearing `T`, drives a `#![forbid(unsafe_code)]` subscriber into out-of-bounds reads of adjacent shared-memory chunks or dereference of a publisher-controlled pointer. Resolution: It will not be fixed since this is a known limitation in iceoryx as it is the users responsibility to specify the same data type on sender and receiver side. [iceoryx2](https://github.com/eclipse-iceoryx/iceoryx2) is the successor of iceoryx-rs where the API is designed to prevent this by default. It is strongly recommended to migrate to iceoryx2 which is actively maintained and receives security support. The iceoryx-rs package has officially reached End-of-life and will not receive any features, bugfixes or security fixes.

This data may be stored in the browser history and in server or proxy logs, or transmitted via the HTTP Referer header, depending on the configuration and browsing flow. Its inclusion in the URL could allow for the unauthorized disclosure of information to third parties with access to those logs or recipients.

FlowIntel contains an authorization flaw in its duplicate alert ingestion logic. When a duplicate alert is received and its content is updated, the ownership and visibility scope fields (owner user and owner organization) were not refreshed to reflect the connector's current scope. As a result, an alert that was originally created under a broader visibility scope retained that broader scope even after the connector's scope was narrowed or changed. This means that users or organizations that should no longer have visibility into a given alert could continue to access it, because the stale ownership fields were never updated during the duplicate-update path. The issue affected all duplicate updates, including those involving alerts in terminal review states and those recovered from uniqueness conflicts. Security impact: - Unauthorized disclosure of security alert content to users or organizations outside the intended visibility scope. - Stale access persists indefinitely until the alert is independently re-scoped or deleted. Affected version: <4.1.0.

desc: The web installer of JTL-Shop executes its state-changing installation tasks without checking whether the shop is already installed, and was not removed or locked after the installation. An unauthenticated remote attacker who can reach the installer directory can supply their own database credentials, create administrator and synchronisation accounts and overwrite the shop configuration. This can lead to a full takeover of the shop, including code execution on the server.

The Slimbox plugin for WordPress is vulnerable to Stored Cross-Site Scripting via the 'comment (anchor title within comment HTML)' parameter in all versions up to, and including, 1.0.8 due to insufficient input sanitization and output escaping. This makes it possible for unauthenticated attackers to inject arbitrary web scripts in pages that will execute whenever a user accesses an injected page. WordPress core comment KSES permits unauthenticated commenters to post anchor elements with href and title attributes, so an entity-encoded payload stored in the title attribute survives sanitization verbatim; the browser then decodes the entities when populating the DOM .title property, and the Slimbox library's jQuery .html() caption sink renders it as executable HTML.

The Fancy Lightbox plugin for WordPress is vulnerable to Stored Cross-Site Scripting via the 'comment' parameter in all versions up to, and including, 1.0.0 due to insufficient input sanitization and output escaping. This makes it possible for unauthenticated attackers to inject arbitrary web scripts in pages that will execute whenever a user accesses an injected page. Successful exploitation without administrator interaction requires that the attacker first have one comment approved so that a subsequent payload comment is auto-published; the injected script only executes when a user clicks the malicious image link inside the comment. Successful exploitation additionally requires an action by an administrator — the attacker cannot trigger the vulnerability on their own.

The Slimbox Plugin plugin for WordPress is vulnerable to Stored DOM-Based Cross-Site Scripting via the 'el.title (HTML-decoded title attribute of a stored <a rel^=lightbox> element)' parameter in all versions up to, and including, 1.3 due to insufficient input sanitization and output escaping. This makes it possible for authenticated attackers, with subscriber-level access and above, to inject arbitrary web scripts in pages that will execute whenever a user accesses an injected page. Exploitation requires a companion plugin such as bbPress that permits low-privileged users to store anchor elements with arbitrary title and rel attributes, as WordPress core comment handling does not preserve rel on anchor tags by default.

The WP-Slimbox2 Plugin plugin for WordPress is vulnerable to Stored Cross-Site Scripting via the 'comment' parameter in all versions up to, and including, 1.1.3.1 due to insufficient input sanitization and output escaping. This makes it possible for unauthenticated attackers to inject arbitrary web scripts in pages that will execute whenever a user accesses an injected page. Successful exploitation requires a logged-in user, typically an administrator, to click the attacker's image link in the comment; however, because unmoderated comments appear in the WordPress moderation queue where administrators routinely interact with them, the moderation gate does not meaningfully prevent exploitation. Successful exploitation causes the attacker's own account to receive the complete Administrator role.

The checkout of JTL-Shop stores the delivery address ID submitted by the customer in the session and adopts it into the order without verifying that the address belongs to the ordering customer. A remote attacker with access to the checkout, including a guest, can thereby attach the delivery address of another customer to their own order. Name and address of the other customer, and depending on the shop configuration further contact data, then appear in the order confirmation and customer account. As the IDs are sequential, addresses can be enumerated. Goods may also be shipped to the wrong address.

desc: The administration page "Offene Bestellungen" (open orders) of the JTL PayPal Checkout plugin for JTL-Shop outputs the customer name of pending orders without output encoding. A registered customer (free self-registration) can submit an HTML-entity-encoded name, which is decoded to markup when the billing address of an order is written. If the PayPal payment is left unfinished, the order is listed on the page and the name is rendered as markup in the browser of an administrator who opens the page. The script code runs with the privileges of that administrator and can, for example, create a new administrator account. Guest orders are not affected, because the name is encoded again.

desc: @fastify/middie is the middleware engine that adds Express and Connect style middleware support to Fastify. In versions up to and including 9.3.6, middie does not honor the router's caseSensitive setting and matches path-scoped middleware mount paths with a case-insensitive regular expression that does not fold non-ASCII characters, while Fastify's router, when caseSensitive is set to false, lowercases the request path with a Unicode-aware conversion that maps the KELVIN SIGN character (U+212A) to the ASCII letter k. A request that spells a k in a protected mount path as the percent-encoded KELVIN SIGN is therefore routed to the protected handler while the middleware mounted on that path, such as authentication, authorization, or rate limiting, never matches and is skipped, letting an unauthenticated client reach the handler. Only applications that set caseSensitive to false and protect a mount path containing the letter k are affected. The issue is fixed in @fastify/middie 9.3.7, and users should upgrade to 9.3.7 or later. As a workaround, enforce authorization in a Fastify hook such as preHandler that runs after routing, or keep routing case-sensitive, which is the default.
tags: Pré-authentification à distance; Contrôle d'accès défaillant

@fastify/middie is the middleware engine that adds Express and Connect style middleware support to Fastify. In versions 8.3.0 through 9.3.6, the internal helper that normalizes a path-scoped middleware's mount path only handles string inputs, but the use method also accepts an array of mount paths and passes it through unchanged, so the normalization silently does nothing. As a result, a trailing slash on an array element survives into the generated route-matching regular expression, and an element that is exactly the root path, meaning a catch-all mount, is dropped entirely. Requests to subroutes of the affected mount paths then skip the path-scoped middleware, such as authentication, authorization, or rate limiting, while Fastify's router still dispatches them to the handler, allowing an unauthenticated client to reach protected routes. Applications are affected when they mount middleware on an array of paths in which an element ends with a slash, including one introduced by a plugin prefix that ends with a slash, or is exactly the root path. The issue is fixed in @fastify/middie 9.3.7, and users should upgrade to 9.3.7 or later. As a workaround, enforce authorization in a Fastify hook such as preHandler that runs after routing, and avoid array mount paths with a trailing slash element for security relevant middleware.

@fastify/middie is the middleware engine that adds Express and Connect style middleware support to Fastify. In versions up to and including 9.3.6, middie builds the match regular expression for each path-scoped middleware from its mount path without collapsing duplicate slashes, even when the application enables the ignoreDuplicateSlashes router option. Under that option Fastify's router collapses duplicate slashes in both the registered route and the request path, so a mount path containing a doubled slash is served by the router at its single-slash form while the middleware's compiled match still requires the doubled slash and never matches. A path-scoped middleware such as authentication, authorization, or rate limiting is therefore skipped while the router dispatches the request to the protected handler, without any authentication required. Applications are affected when they enable ignoreDuplicateSlashes and a middleware mount path reaches middie with a duplicate slash, most commonly when a plugin prefix that ends with a slash is joined to a mount path that starts with one. The issue is fixed in @fastify/middie 9.3.7, and users should upgrade to 9.3.7 or later. As a workaround, enforce authorization in a Fastify hook such as preHandler that runs after routing, and avoid mount paths and plugin prefixes that introduce duplicate slashes.

No data is disclosed and no code is executed.

desc: The Strava datasource plugin's resource handler POST /strava-api forwards a client-supplied endpoint string, and its query parameters, to the Strava API (https://www.strava.com/api/v3/<endpoint>) without validation. When the datasource is not in OAuth pass-through mode, the request is made with the access token stored on the datasource, not the caller's identity. Grafana authorises plugin resource calls only on the datasources:query permission, which Viewers have by default. Any such caller could therefore request any Strava API path the connected account's OAuth grant allows, for example athlete/clubs or routes/{id}, and read the response. The plugin's frontend (stravaApi.ts) only needs a fixed set of paths: athlete, athlete/activities, activities/{id}, activities/{id}/streams and segments/{id}. Requests to Strava are GET only, so the issue is read-only. Affected: plugin versions 1.2.0 through 1.7.2. The fix restricts endpoint to those five patterns and is pending release. The check runs before the access token is resolved, so a rejected request never causes a token refresh or any call to Strava. Paths with .. segments are rejected as well.

flowintel contains a CSV injection vulnerability in its audit log CSV export functionality. Attacker-influenced text recorded in audit logs could be interpreted as spreadsheet formulas when an administrator opened the exported CSV file in a spreadsheet application. The vulnerable behavior allowed an attacker who could influence audit log content (for example by generating network traffic that is captured and logged) to embed formula-like strings (such as =CMD() or =HYPERLINK()) into audit entries. When the resulting CSV export was opened in a spreadsheet application, these strings could be executed as formulas, potentially leading to data exfiltration, data manipulation, or execution of further malicious actions within the spreadsheet context. Preconditions: - An attacker must be able to influence content that is recorded in flowintel audit logs. - An administrator or user must export the audit logs to CSV and open the file in a spreadsheet application that interprets formulas. Security impact: - Potential information disclosure from the spreadsheet or linked resources. - Potential integrity impact on data within the spreadsheet application. - No direct compromise of the flowintel application itself. Affected version: <4.1.0

MISP contains an authorization bypass affecting the event protection mechanism. In MISP, a protected event is designed to be modifiable only through the events/edit endpoint with a valid cryptographic signature. However, the protection check was enforced solely on that single route. All other write endpoints that operate on an event—attributes (add, edit, delete), objects (delete), events (populate, publish, unprotect, upload_sample, upload_analysis_file), tags (attach, detach), event reports (edit, delete), galaxy clusters (attach, detach), and cryptographic keys (add, delete)—lacked the equivalent check. As a result, an authenticated user holding the sync permission (perm_sync) who is neither a site administrator nor an internal sync user (perm_sync_internal), and who belongs to the same organization as the event's creator (orgc_id), could modify, delete, or add data to a protected event without providing a valid signature. This included the ability to unprotect the event entirely, publish it to other instances, and add cryptographic signing keys that would subsequently permit signed edits, effectively nullifying the protection mechanism. The vulnerability requires an authenticated sync user account within the event's creator organization. No user interaction or special network conditions are required; standard API calls to the affected endpoints are sufficient. The security impact is a loss of integrity over protected threat-intelligence events: an attacker can inject, alter, or remove attributes, objects, tags, reports, and galaxy cluster associations, and can remove the protection flag or add signing keys to enable persistent unauthorized modification.

MISP contains an authorization and scope flaw in the ObjectReference model's captureReference method. When a user saves an event (via REST API, sync, or feeds), any object reference included in the payload is looked up by its UUID across the entire MISP instance rather than being scoped to the event being saved. An authenticated user with permission to add or edit events can therefore include the UUID of an object reference belonging to a different event—including events in other organizations that the user cannot view—and cause the system to overwrite that foreign reference's relationship_type, comment, deleted flag, and timestamp with attacker-supplied values. The affected reference is neither deleted nor recreated in the attacker's event; its fields are silently rewritten in place. This constitutes a cross-tenant integrity violation: data integrity of object references in events the attacker has no read or write access to is compromised. The vulnerability is reachable through any event save path (REST add/edit, inter-instance sync, feed ingestion) and requires only a valid authenticated session with event modification privileges and knowledge or discovery of a target reference UUID.

Session serializer mismatch can lead to remote code execution. Session upload progress, when enabled, can store attacker-controlled data in a session key using the php_binary or php_serialize session serializer. If the same session is later read with the php serializer, because session.serialize_handler is changed at runtime or differs between applications sharing a session store, bytes inside the key can be passed to the unserializer. A remote attacker able to submit a multipart upload can inject objects, which may lead to code execution when the reading application contains a suitable gadget chain, or to session corruption or denial of service. This issue affects PHP versions before 8.2.36, 8.3.* before 8.3.37, 8.4.* before 8.4.28 and 8.5.* before 8.5.13.

desc: In Eclipse Ditto versions 1.1.0 to 3.9.8, when pre-authentication is enabled, the gateway service accepts the pre-authenticated subject not only from the `x-ditto-pre-authenticated` HTTP header set by a trusted reverse proxy, but also from an undocumented `x-ditto-pre-authenticated` URL query parameter that a client can set. A reverse proxy that only overwrites the header therefore does not stop clients from supplying their own subject. With the default configuration of the Ditto Helm chart (`global.jwtOnly: false`, which implicitly enables pre-authentication), the bundled nginx skips HTTP Basic authentication for any request with an `Authorization: Bearer` header and forwards it without the pre-authentication header. An unauthenticated remote attacker can send an invalid Bearer token together with the query parameter to authenticate as any chosen policy subject. Pre-authentication succeeds before the JWT is validated, so the attacker can read and modify Things and Policies with that subject's permissions. As a mitigation, disable pre-authentication in the gateway (`ENABLE_PRE_AUTHENTICATION=false`) or, when using the Helm chart, configure `global.jwtOnly: true`.

Partially overwritten session files can lead to remote code execution. The files session save handler, which is the default, writes updated session data into the existing session file without first clearing it. If a write is interrupted, the file can contain the beginning of the new session followed by the end of the old one, and bytes of an ordinary string can later be unserialized as objects. An attacker who can influence the session data, for example through session upload progress, and interrupt a write at a suitable point may inject objects, which can lead to code execution when the application contains a suitable gadget chain. Session data can also be corrupted. This issue affects PHP versions before 8.2.36, 8.3.* before 8.3.37, 8.4.* before 8.4.28 and 8.5.* before 8.5.13.

Denial of service through folded HTTP response headers. The HTTP stream wrapper joins each continuation line of a folded response header to the accumulated value by allocating a new string and copying the whole value, so a response with many short continuation lines takes disproportionate CPU time to parse. An attacker who controls an HTTP or HTTPS response fetched through file_get_contents(), fopen() or other stream functions, by making the application request a chosen URL or by influencing a server it already contacts, can keep PHP workers busy. Repeated or concurrent requests can cause a denial of service. This issue affects PHP versions from 8.1.32 through 8.1.34, from 8.2.28 before 8.2.36, from 8.3.18 before 8.3.37, from 8.4.5 before 8.4.28 and 8.5.* before 8.5.13.

desc: Mixed-case HTTPS and FTPS URLs can expose data in plaintext. The HTTP and FTP stream wrappers recognise URL schemes case-insensitively, but enable TLS only when the scheme contains a lowercase "s" at a fixed position. A URL such as HTTPS:// or FTPS:// passed to file_get_contents(), fopen() or other stream functions, or received as an HTTP redirect target, is therefore handled over unencrypted HTTP or FTP. An attacker able to observe the network traffic can read data the application expected TLS to protect, including credentials, request bodies and transferred files. This issue affects PHP versions before 8.2.36, 8.3.* before 8.3.37, 8.4.* before 8.4.28 and 8.5.* before 8.5.13.

PHAR OpenSSL signature bypass via algorithm downgrade. The Phar extension selects the signature verification method from the signature type stored in the archive, and only the OpenSSL types consult the separate .pubkey file holding the trusted public key. An attacker who can modify an OpenSSL-signed Phar archive, but not its public key file, can switch the signature type to a keyless hash such as SHA-256 with a recomputed digest, so the altered archive passes verification even with phar.require_hash enabled. An application that loads the archive may then execute attacker-controlled PHP code. Native, tar-based and zip-based phars are affected. This issue affects PHP versions before 8.2.36, 8.3.* before 8.3.37, 8.4.* before 8.4.28 and 8.5.* before 8.5.13.

desc: Use-after-free via repopulation of last_fatal_error_backtrace global after shutdown. A fatal error raised while modified INI settings are restored during request shutdown can repopulate the stored fatal error backtrace after the executor has been cleaned up. The request memory is then freed, and a diagnostic emitted before executor initialization in a later request handled by the same PHP-FPM or mod_php worker can access the stale backtrace. The shutdown error requires per-path configuration of max_memory_limit, or of zlib.output_compression together with output_handler (which .user.ini can also set). The early diagnostic requires Apache per-directory configuration or, for PHP-FPM, a PHP_VALUE or PHP_ADMIN_VALUE parameter sent by the front end. This can cause memory corruption and worker crashes, and may allow remote code execution. This issue affects PHP versions 8.5.* before 8.5.13.
tags: Pré-authentification à distance; Corruption mémoire; RCE; Déni de service; Zero-click

desc: PHP-FPM request smuggling through an unread HTTP request body. PHP does not discard the unread part of an HTTP request body at request shutdown when the application has opened php://input without reading it to the end. When the front end reuses backend connections, which is not the default in nginx or Apache (for example nginx with fastcgi_keep_conn on, or Apache mod_proxy_fcgi with enablereuse=on), PHP-FPM can parse the leftover bytes as a new FastCGI request. An unauthenticated remote attacker can use a single crafted multipart/form-data request to forge a backend request with chosen parameters such as SCRIPT_FILENAME, REMOTE_ADDR and PHP_ADMIN_VALUE, which can lead to execution of attacker-controlled PHP code. With LSAPI, subsequent requests on the connection can be disrupted. This issue affects PHP versions before 8.2.36, 8.3.* before 8.3.37, 8.4.* before 8.4.28 and 8.5.* before 8.5.13.

PHP-FPM epoll use-after-free can lead to local privilege escalation. When catch_workers_output is enabled and the epoll event backend is used, the PHP-FPM master can close a worker's output pipe in fpm_child_close() without removing the associated event, and the delayed cleanup can free the worker record while its epoll registration is still active. A later event is then dispatched through a pointer into freed memory. A local attacker who can execute PHP code in an FPM worker can crash the master or execute code with its privileges, commonly root. catch_workers_output is disabled by default but enabled in the official PHP-FPM Docker images. This issue affects PHP versions from 8.1.20 through 8.1.34, from 8.2.7 before 8.2.36, 8.3.* before 8.3.37, 8.4.* before 8.4.28 and 8.5.* before 8.5.13.
tags: Corruption mémoire; Élévation de privilèges; Déni de service

desc: PHP-FPM status endpoint XSS via unescaped user and script fields. The PHP-FPM full status output includes the request method, authentication user and script filename of each worker without escaping them for the HTML, XML or JSON format. When the status endpoint is enabled, an unauthenticated remote attacker can store markup in a worker's scoreboard entry with an ordinary request, for example through the username of an HTTP Basic authentication header that the web server forwards to PHP-FPM, or through the script filename where the attacker can influence it. When a user views the full status page as HTML, the injected JavaScript runs in the origin of that page. The attacker does not need access to the status endpoint. Malformed XML or JSON output can also disrupt monitoring tools. This issue affects PHP versions before 8.2.36, 8.3.* before 8.3.37, 8.4.* before 8.4.28 and 8.5.* before 8.5.13.

Incorrect RFC 3986 URI serialization for oversized input. The Uri\Rfc3986\Uri class does not correctly handle the output-size limit and errors of the uriparser library when converting a URI back to a string. For a URI whose string representation reaches approximately 2 GiB, toString(), toRawString() and other serializing operations can return a truncated or invalid string instead of an error. An application that accepts attacker-controlled URI data of that size, has enough memory to process it and trusts the result may make incorrect validation or routing decisions, and the large allocations can exhaust memory. parse_url() and Uri\WhatWg\Url are not affected. This issue affects PHP versions 8.5.* before 8.5.13.

desc: Use-after-free in magic method backtraces can lead to remote code execution. When collecting the arguments of a method call handled by __call() or __callStatic() for a backtrace, PHP can read stale values that may refer to freed memory. If a fatal error such as exceeding memory_limit occurs while an application enters such a call, with fatal_error_backtraces enabled (the default) and zend.exception_ignore_args disabled, a remote attacker who controls enough request data to influence memory allocation may cause memory corruption, crash the PHP worker or, with knowledge of memory addresses, execute arbitrary code. php.ini-production enables zend.exception_ignore_args, which prevents this. This issue affects PHP versions 8.5.* before 8.5.13.

desc: Use-after-free after interrupted session shutdown. The session extension records the filename of the executing script when a session starts. If a fatal error occurs in an application callback while the session variables are destroyed at shutdown, such as stream_close() of a user-defined stream wrapper, the pointer is retained after the request memory is freed, and a later request handled by the same worker can free the stale string. An attacker who can trigger such a failing cleanup may crash the worker or corrupt memory; code execution has not been demonstrated. This requires the filename to be allocated in request memory, for example when the script is not cached by OPcache. This issue affects PHP versions 8.3.* before 8.3.37, 8.4.* before 8.4.28 and 8.5.* before 8.5.13.
tags: Pré-authentification à distance; Corruption mémoire; Déni de service; Zero-click

desc: Timezone cache use-after-free can lead to remote code execution. In non-thread-safe builds, a diagnostic written to a file-based error_log during module startup, for example for an invalid date.timezone value or a session configuration warning, causes the timezone cache to be allocated in startup memory that is freed while a reference to it is kept. A diagnostic raised early in the first request of a worker, such as the max_input_vars warning, then accesses the freed cache. On such a deployment an unauthenticated remote attacker can crash PHP-FPM, Apache mod_php or CGI workers with a crafted request. Arbitrary code execution may be possible and has been demonstrated with known memory addresses. This issue affects PHP versions before 8.2.36, 8.3.* before 8.3.37, 8.4.* before 8.4.28 and 8.5.* before 8.5.13.
tags: Pré-authentification à distance; Corruption mémoire; RCE; Déni de service; Zero-click

desc: Double free during DOM XML serialization. The XML serializer of Dom\XMLDocument and Dom\HTMLDocument can share ownership of a generated namespace prefix between the namespace-prefix maps of an element and a descendant, so the prefix is used after being freed and then freed a second time. The document does not need to be malformed. An application that parses attacker-controlled XML or HTML with these classes and serializes it with saveXml() can be crashed, and repeated requests can cause denial of service. Code execution has not been demonstrated. This issue affects PHP versions 8.4.* before 8.4.28 and 8.5.* before 8.5.13.
tags: Pré-authentification à distance; Corruption mémoire; Déni de service; Zero-click

desc: SOAP use-after-free when processing DTD entity references. The SOAP extension frees the document type definition (DTD) of a parsed XML document while attribute values can still refer to entities it owns, and can then read freed memory. Removing the DTD also bypasses the SOAP server's rejection of documents that contain one. An unauthenticated remote attacker who can send a crafted request to a SOAP endpoint, or who controls a WSDL or schema document loaded by the application, can crash the PHP process and cause denial of service. Memory disclosure and code execution have not been confirmed. This issue affects PHP versions before 8.2.36, 8.3.* before 8.3.37, 8.4.* before 8.4.28 and 8.5.* before 8.5.13.
tags: Pré-authentification à distance; Corruption mémoire; Déni de service; Zero-click

desc: PHP-CGI out-of-bounds read and write during PATH_INFO correction. The PHP CGI binary (php-cgi), in CGI and FastCGI mode with cgi.fix_pathinfo enabled (the default), can perform an out-of-bounds read and write when the path removed from SCRIPT_FILENAME or PATH_TRANSLATED is longer than the supplied PATH_INFO, or when PATH_INFO is empty. This requires a web server mapping that passes such inconsistent values, or a FastCGI listener reachable by untrusted clients. An unauthenticated remote attacker can crash the process, may obtain process memory if the application exposes PATH_INFO or PATH_TRANSLATED, and may corrupt memory. PHP-FPM and the Apache module are not affected. This issue affects PHP versions before 8.2.36, 8.3.* before 8.3.37, 8.4.* before 8.4.28 and 8.5.* before 8.5.13.
tags: Pré-authentification à distance; Corruption mémoire; Déni de service; Zero-click

desc: In Eclipse Ditto versions 2.0.0 to 3.8.14 and 3.9.0 to 3.9.8, the authorization check for JSON merge patch commands on Things (HTTP `PATCH` / Ditto Protocol `merge`) does not check permissions for fields deleted or set to an empty object by the patch: fields with a `null` value or an empty object value (`{}`) are skipped by the check, and Ditto's regex-based key deletion with the documented `{{ ~<regex>~ }}` syntax is not recognized as a deletion. An authenticated user with WRITE permission on any part of a Thing can therefore delete other attributes, features and the definition of that Thing, or overwrite or create fields as empty objects, including parts the policy revokes or never grants WRITE on. -->

In Eclipse Ditto versions 2.4.0 to 3.9.8, Thing fields a requester is not allowed to read can be disclosed through the `condition` and `live-channel-condition` headers, which are evaluated against the full Thing: the READ check of `live-channel-condition` is skipped when a `condition` header is also present on Thing query commands (3.0.0 to 3.9.8); both headers are evaluated without any authorization on WoT Thing Description requests (`Accept: application/td+json`) when WoT TD permission filtering is not active (by default in 3.0.0 to 3.8.14, in 2.4.x with WoT integration enabled, and in 3.9.x with filtering disabled); the `condition` of live messages and live events is evaluated without a READ check, and of claim messages without any permission (3.1.0 to 3.9.8); and the twin response of a Thing query with a non-matching `live-channel-condition` is returned without filtering it by the policy (3.0.0 to 3.9.8). This allows an authenticated user to read Thing fields they are not allowed to read, in some cases without any permission on the Thing.

In Eclipse Ditto versions before 3.8.15 and 3.9.0 to 3.9.8, the policy enforcers do not let a revoke win over a grant in two kinds of permission checks. Checks of several permissions at once compare the highest grant weight with the highest revoke weight across all requested permissions instead of per permission, so the "check permissions" API (`POST /api/2/checkPermissions`, available since 3.7.0) can report a set of permissions as granted although one of them is revoked. Partial permission checks, which authorize retrieving Things and Policies and determine the receivers of events, count a grant on a sub-resource although the same permission is revoked on that sub-resource for another subject of the same authorization context (or, with the memory-optimized policy evaluator, for the same subject). A requester can thereby learn about the existence of Things and Policies and receive metadata without any readable content, and an application relying on the check permissions result may grant access the policy denies. The content of retrieved Things and Policies is still filtered correctly, and modifications are not affected.

In Eclipse Ditto versions 3.9.0 to 3.9.8, the resolved policy view (`GET /api/2/policies/{policyId}?policy-view=resolved`) does not restrict merged policy content to what the caller may read in the policy it originates from. Imported and namespace-root entries are returned in full as soon as the caller may read any part of them in the source policy, entries of transitive imports and of the imports of namespace-root policies are only checked against the intermediate policy, and content copied into an entry by `references`, also from another entry of the same policy, is not checked against the referenced entry. An authenticated caller with READ on a policy can therefore read subjects, resources and granted/revoked permissions of policy entries that are hidden from them, including by explicit revokes, when reading the originating policy directly.

In Eclipse Ditto versions before 3.9.9, Thing events delivered via WebSocket, Server-Sent Events and connections disclose field values which the policy does not allow the subscriber to read. A READ revoke for one subject of the subscriber's authorization context is not applied when another of its subjects is granted READ. For subscribers with partial READ access, subscription RQL filters, the SSE `_context`, `thing-json` placeholders and extra fields are evaluated on the unfiltered event. This allows an authenticated subscriber with at least partial READ access to a Thing to obtain the values of fields it may not read when events for that Thing are emitted.

### Summary ui With `strip_ansi=True`, Pydantic AI Harness's `ToolOutputLimits` capability removes ANSI escape sequences from tool output with a pattern that takes time quadratic in the length of a line. A tool result of a few hundred kilobytes, crafted with many unterminated escape sequences, can occupy the event loop for tens of seconds to minutes, delaying every other request and agent run in the process. ### Details This affects applications that set `strip_ansi=True` on `ToolOutputLimits` (named `OverflowingToolOutput` before 0.13.0) and run tools whose output an attacker can influence, such as shell commands, file reads, fetched pages or MCP servers. Stripping runs on the event loop before the capability reduces the output, so its own size limits do not bound it. The assumed attacker can place text in content a tool returns. ### Mitigation Upgrade `pydantic-ai-harness` to 0.70.0 or later. Until then, leave `strip_ansi` at its default, `False`. On Pydantic AI v1, the harness cannot be upgraded past 0.4.0. Upgrade to Pydantic AI v2 and `pydantic-ai-harness` 0.70.0, or leave `strip_ansi` off.
tags: Pré-authentification à distance; Déni de service

desc: OFFIS DCMTK 3.5.4 through 3.7.1 contains an integer overflow in DJCodecEncoder::encodeTrueLossless size checks that allows attackers to trigger a heap out-of-bounds read. Attackers can supply a crafted DICOM file with large Columns, Rows and SamplesPerPixel values that, when compressed with true-lossless JPEG, crashes the application.

OFFIS DCMTK 3.7.1 contains a heap buffer overflow vulnerability in togglePlanarConfiguration8 and togglePlanarConfiguration16 in djcodece.cc, which compute row offsets using rows instead of columns. Attackers can supply a crafted color-by-plane DICOM image with more rows than columns that is compressed with the true-lossless JPEG codec to corrupt heap memory, causing crashes and potentially code execution.

modified eCommerce Shopsoftware through 3.3.0 contains a stored cross-site scripting vulnerability that allows authenticated administrators to inject scripts via the unsanitized products_model field. Attackers with product editing permission can store JavaScript that executes in browsers of other administrators, storefront visitors, and customers viewing carts and order history.

Tiptap @tiptap/core 2.0.0-alpha.0 before 3.30.4 contains a cross-site scripting vulnerability that allows attackers to inject DOM attributes via a __proto__ key passed to mergeAttributes(). Attackers can supply untrusted JSON attribute data whose __proto__ replaces the merged object's prototype, causing DOMSerializer.renderSpec to render injected event handlers that execute JavaScript.

Tiptap @tiptap/core 3.7.0 before 3.30.5 contains a regular expression denial of service vulnerability in parseAttributes and parseShortcodeAttributes that allows attackers to exhaust CPU through quadratic backtracking. Attackers can supply Markdown with long crafted attribute strings parsed by createBlockMarkdownSpec, createAtomBlockMarkdownSpec or createInlineMarkdownSpec to stall browser pages or server processes.

desc: Cozy Cloud cozy-stack 1.6.62 before 1.6.69 contains an authorization bypass vulnerability in the shared-drive move handler that allows authenticated users to access other instances' files. Attackers owning a shared drive can name another instance's domain and any directory ID as the move source to copy and delete the victim's file tree.

WatchAlert 2.0.0 through 3.9.20 contains an insecure direct object reference vulnerability in the /api/w8t/datasource/dataSourceGet endpoint that lets authenticated users read other tenants' datasources because lookups omit tenant_id filtering. Tenant members with datasource view permission can request another tenant's datasource ID to obtain basic auth passwords, AWS and Alibaba Cloud keys, and Kubernetes kubeconfigs.

HotGo 2.18.6 through 2.19.0 contains an information disclosure vulnerability that allows authenticated backend users to read other administrators' private letters because the messageIds helper omits the receiver filter. Low-privilege users can call GET /admin/notice/pullMessages, which is exempt from role permission checks via exceptAuth, to retrieve titles, contents and senders of private letters.

MISP contains an authorization bypass in its server-to-server proposal synchronization mechanism. Two related flaws were identified: 1. The events/pushProposals endpoint located the target event by UUID without enforcing any access-control check. A sync user with perm_sync could push shadow-attribute proposals to any event on the local instance, including events with restricted distribution (e.g., distribution level 0, visible only to the owning organisation). The stored proposal also carried the sender-supplied event_uuid and event_org_id rather than the local event's actual identity, corrupting the data model. 2. When accepting an edit proposal (old_id != 0), the code resolved the target live attribute by UUID alone (Attribute.uuid = shadow.uuid) without scoping the lookup to the proposal's own event. A malicious sync user could therefore craft a proposal whose uuid matched an attribute in a different event; upon acceptance, the wrong attribute would be modified or deleted. The same unscoped lookup existed in the ShadowAttribute::acceptProposal path. Preconditions: an authenticated user with sync permission (perm_sync) on a MISP instance that participates in server-to-server synchronisation. The attacker must know or enumerate the UUID of a target event or attribute. Security impact: unauthorised read access to restricted events, unauthorised insertion of proposals onto events the user cannot see, and unauthorised modification or deletion of attributes belonging to other events. This compromises the confidentiality and integrity of threat-intelligence data across organisational boundaries within a MISP deployment.

MISP contains an authorization flaw in the sharing group capture logic. When a sharing group is re-captured with a newer modified timestamp and an updated roster, the application unconditionally overwrote the type, nationality, sector, and contacts fields of every organisation listed in the roster, including the host organisation. This behaviour was reachable by any user holding the perm_sync role, and additionally by any external server pulled from or any feed fetched, because those operations execute with the privileges of the site administrator who initiated them. As a result, a low-privileged sync user or a malicious/compromised external feed or pull source could silently corrupt organisation records on the receiving MISP instance without any site-admin or internal-sync authorization. The vulnerability does not disclose data or affect availability; the impact is limited to integrity of organisation metadata (type, nationality, sector, contacts). The fix restricts organisation detail updates to internal sync operations (pulls over links flagged as internal, or senders holding perm_sync_internal) and site administrators; all other sync, pull, and feed operations may only match existing organisations by UUID or create new ones, without modifying their stored details.

flowintel allows users with editor-level access to author case and task fields, including aggregated tags. When these records are exported as CSV, the field values are written verbatim into the output file. Because no sanitisation is applied to user-supplied text before CSV serialisation, an attacker can store values that begin with spreadsheet formula triggers (such as =, +, -, @, or their fullwidth Unicode equivalents, or leading control/whitespace characters). When a victim opens the exported CSV in a spreadsheet application (e.g. Microsoft Excel, LibreOffice Calc), the stored text is interpreted and executed as a live formula rather than displayed as literal text. This can lead to unintended data manipulation within the spreadsheet, potential data exfiltration via formula functions, or execution of downstream commands depending on the spreadsheet application and its configuration. The vulnerability requires the victim to actively open the CSV file in a spreadsheet application; the flowintel application itself is not directly compromised. Affected: <4.1.0
In JetBrains Rider before 2026.3 code execution was possible via MSBuild configuration files in parent directories
In JetBrains ReSharper before 2026.3 the What's New feature did not verify server certificates
In JetBrains ReSharper before 2026.3 server host names were not verified during certificate validation
In JetBrains IntelliJ IDEA before 2026.3 the GitHub plugin exposed GitHub access tokens via its public API

MISP contains an authorization flaw in the handling of remote pull and feed operations. When a non-internal pull or a feed processes incoming data and encounters an existing sharing group, the application did not verify that the remote server's organization was actually a member of that sharing group before allowing the group's metadata to be updated. The captureRemote mechanism previously stored only a boolean flag indicating whether the link was internal, and the authorization check in captureSGExisting relied solely on that flag. For non-internal pulls and feeds, the check was insufficient: a remote server whose organization was not a member of the target sharing group could still cause the group record to be modified (for example, altering the local flag, the modified timestamp, or other group properties). A feed, which has no associated server organization at all, could likewise trigger an update to an existing sharing group's metadata. The security impact is an integrity violation: an authenticated remote entity with sync or feed privileges can alter sharing group attributes that govern how data is distributed among organizations, potentially changing the local flag or other access-relevant properties of groups it does not belong to. The vulnerability requires an authenticated user with the ability to initiate a pull or feed (a sync user or feed administrator) and a target sharing group that exists on the local instance. No unauthenticated access or user interaction is required.

MISP contains an authorization and input-validation flaw in its event push mechanism. When a user with push permissions initiates a push of events to a remote MISP instance, the system fails to enforce two critical checks: (1) it does not verify that an event is published before including it in the push, allowing unpublished (i.e., not yet publicly shared) events to be transmitted to the remote server; and (2) it does not verify that the pushing user has read access to the event, causing events the user cannot fetch to be sent as empty event shells, thereby disclosing the existence and metadata of events the user is not authorized to view. Additionally, the remote server's reply selecting which offered events to accept is used without validating that the selected identifiers actually correspond to events in the offered set, potentially allowing the remote to reference events outside the intended scope. The vulnerability requires an authenticated user with push permissions on the source MISP instance and a configured push target. The security impact is unauthorized disclosure of confidential threat-intelligence data (unpublished events and events restricted by user permissions) to a remote MISP instance that should not receive them.

Goproxy before 1.9.4 contains a weak key generation vulnerability in NewCounterEncryptorRandFromKey that derives RSA and Ed25519 leaf certificate private keys from public data due to misuse of hash.Sum. Attackers with the CA certificate and one observed leaf certificate can regenerate that host's leaf private key and impersonate the host to clients trusting the proxy CA.

MISP contains a vulnerability in the cryptographic signature verification of protected events. When a MISP instance signs a protected event for synchronization, it strips all whitespace from the JSON body before computing the PGP signature (preg_replace("/\s+/", "", $data)). The receiving instance performs the same whitespace-stripping before verification. Because the signature covers only the whitespace-free representation, a network relay positioned between two MISP instances can insert whitespace characters into JSON object keys (effectively renaming fields) or into identifier values such as UUIDs, timestamps, and distribution fields without invalidating the signature. The receiving instance accepts the modified event as authentic. The vulnerability affects the protected event synchronization path: event creation (EventsController::add), event editing (EventsController::edit), event viewing (EventsController::view1), and server-to-server pull synchronization (ServerSyncTool, Server model). An attacker with a network position to intercept and modify traffic between MISP instances can alter the semantic content of protected events while the PGP signature still validates, undermining the integrity guarantees that protected events are designed to provide. The fix introduces two complementary mechanisms. First, a post-verification scan rejects any received body that contains whitespace in JSON keys (except under Galaxy cluster 'meta' keys) or in identifier-like values (uuid, id, timestamp, distribution, date). Second, a new exact-byte signature scheme (x-pgp-signature-v2) signs the body as transmitted, without whitespace normalization. MISP 3.0 and later peers exchange this exact-byte signature; older peers retain the legacy whitespace-stripped signature. A signature_version field is embedded in protected events so that a 3.0 receiver refuses a body carrying that marker if only the legacy signature is present. Both mechanisms together close the whitespace-injection vector while preserving backward compatibility with pre-3.0 instances.

MISP, a threat intelligence sharing platform, contains a vulnerability in its cryptographic key management for protected (PGP-signed) events. Two related defects allow a revoked PGP key to remain effective for signing and validating protected events. First, the validateProtectedEvent() method in the CryptographicKey model iterates over the event's stored cryptographic keys to verify a PGP signature but does not check the revoked flag on each key. A key explicitly marked as revoked is still used to validate signatures, meaning an entity whose key has been revoked can continue to sign protected events and have them accepted by the MISP instance. Second, the captureCryptographicKeyUpdate() method, responsible for synchronizing the key list when a sync user edits a protected event, contained a query bug (find('first') instead of find('all')) that caused only the first stored key to be considered. As a result, revocations of additional keys were never persisted, keys absent from the pushed list were not removed, and entries lacking an explicit fingerprint were mismatched and incorrectly deleted. Additionally, the revocation logic did not enforce the invariant that a revocation, once stored, is never lifted by subsequent pushes. A third minor issue: a signed protected event submitted without any cryptographic keys triggered an unhandled 500 error rather than a proper rejection response. Preconditions: the attacker must be an authenticated sync user with permission to add or edit protected events on the MISP instance. The impact is that revoked keys retain signing authority, key revocations propagated by sync partners are silently dropped, and the integrity of the protected-event trust chain is compromised. In a multi-instance MISP deployment, events signed by revoked keys can propagate to other instances, extending the integrity impact across the sync network.

SOAP information disclosure through malformed array dimensions. The SOAP extension reads an uninitialized array position when decoding an encoded array whose arraySize attribute is empty, whitespace-only or non-numeric, or when such dimensions come from a WSDL definition. Four bytes of unrelated heap data can then be used as an integer key in the decoded array. An unauthenticated remote client can trigger this with a crafted request to a SoapServer endpoint, and a malicious SOAP server with a response to SoapClient. Heap memory is disclosed only if the application returns or otherwise exposes the decoded array. This issue affects PHP versions before 8.2.36, 8.3.* before 8.3.37, 8.4.* before 8.4.28 and 8.5.* before 8.5.13.

desc: MRemoteNG establishes encrypted but unauthenticated channel with Microsoft SQL Server backend. Client accepts any certificate the server presents, including a self-signed certificate supplied by an attacker. An attacker positioned between the client and the SQL server (for example via ARP/DNS spoofing) can transparently pintercept the connection (man-in-the-middle) and read all traffic, including the encrypted connection-password table read and the database login. Vendor did not provide the range of vulnerable versions. Only version 1.76.20 was tested and confirmed vulnerable. Other versions may also be vulnerable.

MRemoteNG uses single MD5 hash with no salt and no iterations for key-derivation. An attacker who obtains the encrypted data can brute-force a weak or moderate passphrase offline at extreme speed and then decrypt every stored connection password. When the default passphrase is in use, no cracking is needed at all; the key is derived from a publicly known value. Vendor did not provide the range of vulnerable versions. Only version 1.76.20 was tested and confirmed vulnerable. Other versions may also be vulnerable.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved: rust_binder: wake epoll on self-work queued to poll thread When a thread pushes work to its own todo list, InnerThread::push_work() returns PushWorkRes::OkNotifyPoll if the thread uses epoll, but four call sites in thread.rs discard this return value. As a result, a non-blocking BC_* write that enqueues work onto the calling thread's todo list without also reading will not wake epoll. Check the return value and call self.process.notify_poll(false) when PushWorkRes::OkNotifyPoll is returned. This is similar to commit 97830f3c3088 ("binder: signal epoll threads of self-work"), but in C Binder pending thread work also prevented subsequent process work from waking epoll, causing a permanent hang, which is not the case in Rust Binder. This means that in practice, it merely delays notifications rather than completely failing to send them.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved: ksmbd: rebind completed CREATE replays without draining the old channel A completed DurableHandleReqV2 CREATE can be replayed through another channel while its original channel is exiting. The existing replay path returns the open but leaves its connection and oplock references pointing at the old channel. Its open count also stays on that channel, and a later CLOSE through the surviving channel decrements the wrong counter. After checking the owner, lease key and persistent flag, verify that an active open is still published in the requesting session's file table. Do this even when no oplock was granted, and before processing a consumed replay. Do not read a borrowed opinfo session pointer for this check. Keep a healthy original binding. If the original channel is exiting or releasing, move the open and its own oplock references to the requesting channel. Serialize this with CLOSE using the session file-table lock, and with detach, reconnect and notification snapshots using m_lock. The earlier lock index and lease-table changes make their lifetimes independent of this connection change. No old-channel r_count wait is needed, including when an unrelated request remains active there. Account final close against fp->conn in one place, balance durable detach and reconnect, and transfer the count with a replay binding change. A final global lookup put may run after CLOSE has removed the volatile id; unlink the open from the inode list on that final close as well. A live completed CREATE replay may follow a break that lowered the durable open's batch oplock. Apply the batch eligibility check only to detached reconnects, while retaining the owner, lease key and persistent flag checks for active replays.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved: ksmbd: fix invalid pointer dereference when get_inode_acl() fails When get_inode_acl() fails, it returns an ERR_PTR(), but ksmbd_acls_fattr() stored that pointer in smb_fattr without checking for errors. Later callers then passed the error pointer to security descriptor helpers or posix_acl_release(), resulting in an invalid pointer dereference. This was reproduced on an XFS-backed share when xfs_get_acl() returned ERR_PTR(-ENOMEM). Querying the SMB ACL from a CIFS client triggered the crash: BUG: unable to handle page fault for address: fffffffffffffff8 RIP: smb_acl_sec_desc_scratch_len+0x58/0x90 [ksmbd] Call Trace: smb2_query_info+0x40d/0x17c0 [ksmbd] handle_ksmbd_work+0x1ca/0x770 [ksmbd] Fix this by checking the return values from get_inode_acl() in ksmbd_acls_fattr(). Treat -EOPNOTSUPP as indicating that no ACL is available, and propagate all other errors to the callers. Update smb2_open() and smb2_get_info_sec() to handle these errors.

desc: In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved: ksmbd: fix out-of-bounds read when padding the final compound response Compound response handling pads the last response of a compound to an 8-byte boundary by growing the final iov and the RFC1002 length. smb2_allocate_rsp_buf() allocates exactly response_sz. A command can fill the response buffer to within 7 bytes of its end, for example a QUERY_INFO whose output is bounded only by the space left. The padding can then run past the allocation, and ksmbd_tcp_writev() reads those bytes when it sends the response. BUG: KASAN: slab-out-of-bounds in _copy_from_iter+0x744/0x10e0 Call Trace: _copy_from_iter+0x744/0x10e0 tcp_sendmsg_locked+0x2290/0x3f80 ksmbd_tcp_writev+0x10c7/0x1ab0 [ksmbd] Allocate room for the padding when the request is a compound, as smb2_read() and smb2_read_pipe() do for their payloads. response_sz is unchanged, so commands still fill only up to it, and kvzalloc() zeroes the padding.

desc: In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved: HID: hid-lenovo-go-s: Add suspend function and gate access under bool. Currently a device can suspend while delayed work is pending or executing. Cancel delayed work if it was pending and restart it if it hasn't run yet. Gate access to show/store functions behind a bool to prevent access prior to cfg_setup() being completed.

desc: In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved: HID: hid-lenovo-go-s: Prevent deadlock if device removed during setup hid_gos_cfg_remove() calls a mutex before canceling delayed work. That delayed work function calls mcu_property_out(), which holds the same mutex. Prevent deadlock my removing the mutex prior to stopping the work. Additionally, since cancel_delayed_work has the potential to re-arm, switch to disable_delayed_work.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved: HID: roccat: kovaplus: reject short button reports The raw event callback runs before HID core validates and zero-pads the report. It passes the buffer to helpers which inspect data[0] and read a complete struct kovaplus_mouse_report_button for button reports. A truncated report can therefore cause an out-of-bounds read. Require enough data for the button report before calling either helper. Commit 47669bec44fe ("HID: asus: refactor the two workqueues and init sequence") added the same kind of raw-event length validation to hid-asus.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved: HID: picoLCD: check for fb_deferred_io_init() error fb_deferred_io_init() allocates deferred I/O state, populating info->fbdefio_state, or leaving it NULL if an error occurs. Currently picolcd_init_framebuffer() ignores its return value. Therefore if an error arises in fb_deferred_io_init() (for instance, due to an allocation failure) info->fbdefio_state is left NULL. When the file is subsequently opened, fb_open() will dereference a NULL pointer (calling fb_deferred_io_open()). Fix this by checking for the error. Also correct cleanup ordering - defio is initialised after the sysfs file, so cleanup defio first.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved: HID: mcp2221: always initialize and cancel init_work The writable gpio_mode_enforce parameter can change between probe and remove. If it changes from false to true after probe, remove skips cancellation of init_work. Pending or running work can then access devm-managed driver state after teardown. Changing it from true to false can make remove cancel an uninitialized delayed work item. Initialize init_work whenever IIO is reachable and cancel it unconditionally on remove. Keep the parameter check only for scheduling the initialization. The false-to-true cancellation gap was previously reported by Sashiko. We also encountered this issue during our static-analysis research.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved: HID: mcp2200: validate READ_ALL response length The HID core invokes raw_event callbacks before validating the report length. mcp2200_raw_event() casts a READ_ALL response to struct mcp_read_all_resp and reads fields through offset ten without checking that the response contains the structure. A one-byte READ_ALL response reproduced the issue under KASAN: BUG: KASAN: slab-out-of-bounds in mcp2200_raw_event+0x24b/0x3a0 Read of size 1 by task hidtrigger/89 Call Trace: mcp2200_raw_event+0x24b/0x3a0 kasan_report+0x139/0x170 Reject an incomplete READ_ALL response with a protocol error before reading its fields. The common completion path then wakes the command waiter with the error instead of leaving it to time out. Commit 47669bec44fe ("HID: asus: refactor the two workqueues and init sequence") added the same kind of raw_event length validation to hid-asus.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved: HID: cp2112: validate response report lengths The HID core invokes raw_event callbacks before validating the report length. cp2112_raw_event() reads every field of a transfer status response without checking size. For a data response, it reads the length at offset two and copies that many bytes from offset three, again without ensuring that the input report contains them. Require a complete transfer status structure. For data responses, first require the header and then ensure the clamped payload length fits in the received report before copying it. Commit 47669bec44fe ("HID: asus: refactor the two workqueues and init sequence") added the same kind of raw_event length validation to hid-asus.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved: HID: core: Fix out-of-bounds left shift by 32 in s32ton() Syzbot reported an out-of-bounds shift (32-bit integer shifted left by 32) in the s32ton() routine in the HID core. This routine converts a signed 32-bit integer to a signed n-bit integer, and it caps the value of n at 32. But when n == 32 there's no need to do anything; it can simply return the input value. This will avoid calculating (1 << n) when n is 32, which was the cause of the invalid shift.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved: HID: amd_sfh: Use report type from request node Use report type from request node while sending feature and input reports to HID core. The cli_data report type array is never assigned and feature reports are sent as input reports.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved: KVM: PPC: Book3S HV: Add preempt_disable() around virtual-mode HPTE bit-lock users kvmppc_hv_find_lock_hpte() requires virtual-mode callers to run with preemption disabled, because it can return with HPTE_V_HVLOCK still held until the caller later unlocks the HPTE. Existing virtual-mode callers in book3s_64_mmu_hv.c already follow that rule. Two virtual-mode call paths do not: 1. kvmppc_handle_exit_hv() calls kvmppc_hpte_hv_fault() for hash-mode data-side and instruction-side faults after guest exit, with preemption already enabled. kvmppc_hpte_hv_fault() calls kvmppc_hv_find_lock_hpte() directly. 2. kvmppc_pseries_do_hcall() executes virtual-mode handlers for HPT hcalls via kvmppc_pseries_do_hpt_hcall() with preemption enabled. The handlers for H_ENTER, H_REMOVE, H_READ, H_CLEAR_MOD, H_CLEAR_REF, H_PROTECT, and H_BULK_REMOVE spin on try_lock_hpte() or lock_rmap(), and H_ENTER also reaches kvmppc_do_h_enter(), which uses arch_spin_lock() on kvm->mmu_lock. That raw lock choice is intentional because kvmppc_do_h_enter() is also used by real-mode callers, so the correct fix is to establish the proper preemption context at the virtual-mode caller boundary. If a vCPU thread is preempted while holding HPTE_V_HVLOCK, any other thread on the same CPU trying to acquire the same bit-lock can spin indefinitely. The same applies to lock_rmap() users and to the H_ENTER path while holding the raw mmu_lock. Fix this by adding preempt_disable()/preempt_enable() pairs around the two kvmppc_hpte_hv_fault() call sites in kvmppc_handle_exit_hv(), and around the kvmppc_pseries_do_hpt_hcall() invocation in kvmppc_pseries_do_hcall(). Targeting only the HPT hcall helper avoids wrapping non-HPT hcalls (such as H_RTAS, H_CONFER, H_REGISTER_VPA) that perform page faults, blocking memory allocations, or context switches.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved: KVM: guest_memfd: Establish memslot<=>guest_memfd bindings *after* memslot is ready Wait to bind a memslot to a guest_memfd instance until *after* the memslot is fully prepared, as creating the binding in guest_memfd will effectively expose the memslot to readers. As pointed out by Sashiko, binding the memslot before it's ready to be exposed to the rest of the world can break various memslot assumption and rules. E.g. x86 could observe a NULL rmap pointer if a PUNCH_HOLE hit the guest_memfd after the binding was created, but before KVM made it through kvm_prepare_memory_region().

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved: KVM: guest_memfd: take the invalidate lock when unbinding a dying file kvm_gmem_unbind() takes mapping->invalidate_lock only if the get_file_active() succeeds. When the guest_memfd file is dying, its reference count is already zero so get_file_active fails and the binding is removed without holding the invalidate lock. kvm_gmem_invalidate_{start,end}() checks f->bindings independently to decide whether to begin or end KVM MMU invalidation. So, the bindings must therefore remain stable between the two calls. Otherwise, unbind can remove a binding after start increments mmu_invalidate_in_progress, but before end finds the binding and decrements it. Example, unbind race with memory failure: CPU 0: memory failure CPU 1: memslot delete ---------------------------------- --------------------------- (guest_memfd file is dying) kvm_gmem_error_folio() kvm_gmem_invalidate_start() finds binding mmu_invalidate_in_progress++ kvm_gmem_unbind() get_file_active() fails removes binding kvm_gmem_invalidate_end() no binding found counter stays elevated mmu_invalidate_retry() then returns 1 forever, so guest page faults retry without ever installing a mapping and the guest hangs. Remove the distinction between live and dying files in the unbind path. Always use slot->gmem.file and take the invalidate lock when it's non-NULL. Normal unbind callers hold slots_lock, which prevents release from clearing the pointer or freeing the file state until unbind completes. Final VM teardown can only see a NULL pointer because guest_memfd pins the KVM until release has cleared all bindings.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved: KVM: TDX: Enable Bus Lock VM exit Enable Bus Lock VM exit functionality for TDX guests. Bus Lock VM exit is an existing feature supported by KVM. Userspace can enable Bus Lock VM exit through KVM_BUS_LOCK_DETECTION_EXIT when it's reported as supported. However, KVM reports the support of this CAP just based on the hardware capability but doesn't differentiate between VMX and TDX. This leads to the issue that userspace can enable this cap for TDX guests without getting an error, but the feature is not actually enabled because KVM doesn't call the TDX module API to program the relevant TD VMCS fields. Enable Bus Lock VM exit for TDX guests by programming the BUS_LOCK_DETECTION control in the TD VMCS and by adding the exit handler. Note, there is no enumeration bit for this feature by TDX module because all TDX modules support it and allow to set the TD VMCS as long as the hardware supports the feature.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved: KVM: TDX: Enable Notify VM exit Enable Notify VM exit functionality for TDX guests. Notify VM exit is an existing feature supported by KVM. Userspace can enable Notify VM exit through KVM_CAP_X86_NOTIFY_VMEXIT when it's reported as supported. However, KVM reports the support of this CAP just based on the hardware capability but doesn't differentiate between VMX and TDX. This leads to the issue that userspace can enable this cap for TDX guests without getting an error, but the feature is not actually enabled because KVM doesn't call the TDX module API to program the relevant TD VMCS fields. Enable Notify VM exit for TDX guests by: - Invoking TDX module API calls to set NOTIFY_VM_EXITING and Notify Window in TD VMCS. It's done in tdx_vcpu_init() where other TD VMCS bits are set. Since TDX vCPU cannot be reset, it only needs to be configured once when initializing the TDX vCPU. - Adding corresponding exit handler for TDX Notify VM Exit. Notify VM exit can happen when executing the IRET instruction. If the IRET unblocks the NMI blocking state, bit 12 of the exit qualification is set. In this case, the VMM needs to restore the "blocked by NMI" state when it decides to re-enter the guest. For TDX, KVM cannot manage the GUEST_INTERRUPTIBILITY_INFO and it's TDX module's responsibility to handle it. Extract the common part without NMI blocking handling into a helper in common.h so that it can be shared between VMX and TDX. Note, KVM uses "pre-production" terminology for the feature formally called Notify VM-Exit. All public versions of the SDM refer to the feature as Instruction Timeout. This will be remedied in the near future, for now, use KVM's terminology for consistency. Note, #2, there is no enumeration bit for Notify VM exit by TDX module because all TDX modules support it, and allow to set the corresponding TD VMCS fields as long as the hardware supports the feature.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved: KVM: x86: Zero reserved synic flags when delivering message to avoid stack leak Ensure all reserved flags are zeroed when setting the msg_pending flag as part of SynIC message delivery, as setting only msg_pending can leak seven bits of kernel stack data to the guest. E.g. gcc typically uses a bitwise-OR to set the msg_pending flag, without initializing the on-stack variable. Precisely zero the flags, e.g. as opposed to zeroing the entire structure, to make it somewhat more obvious that the flags *need* to be zeroed. E.g. it would be quite easy to misread the initial read of guest memory and think that zeroing the entire structure is completely superfluous.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved: KVM: x86: Take SRCU in kvm_zap_gfn_range() kvm_zap_gfn_range() walks memslots and rmaps and may drop mmu_lock to reschedule. Callers that do not already hold kvm->srcu (or slots_lock) can race with memslot deletion: synchronize_srcu_expedited() does not wait, kvm_free_memslot() frees the old slot and its rmap, and the zap resumes on freed memory. The VFIO noncoherent-DMA path hits this by zapping the entire GPA space without SRCU. KASAN reported: BUG: KASAN: vmalloc-out-of-bounds in slot_rmap_walk_next+0x82/0x1c0 Read of size 8 at addr ffffc900005c1008 Call Trace: slot_rmap_walk_next+0x82/0x1c0 __kvm_rmap_zap_gfn_range+0x17a/0x280 kvm_zap_gfn_range+0x2a6/0x6a0 kvm_vfio_set_attr+0x576/0x770 kvm_device_ioctl+0x1ff/0x3b0 Take SRCU inside kvm_zap_gfn_range() so every caller is covered. Nesting with an existing kvm->srcu critical section is fine; the helper uses a local index. Drop the now-redundant SRCU pair from __kvm_set_or_clear_apicv_inhibit().

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved: KVM: x86: Request event processing for exception VM-Exits Request event processing whenever kvm_queue_exception_vmexit() queues an exception VM-Exit. Most callers reach the helper through kvm_multiple_exception(), which already sets KVM_REQ_EVENT, but nested asynchronous page faults call it directly. Without another event request, vcpu_enter_guest() skips kvm_check_and_inject_events() and re-enters L2. A subsequent VM-Exit can clear the pending exception while reconstructing vectoring state, losing the synthetic #PF VM-Exit. The APF reason remains PAGE_NOT_PRESENT and a later regular #PF can consume the stale value. Setting KVM_REQ_EVENT in the common helper ensures that L1 receives the queued VM-Exit before KVM re-enters L2.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved: KVM: x86/xen: Enforce 4-byte alignment of vcpu_info registration Xen's map_guest_area() enforces that vcpu_info is aligned to sizeof(xen_ulong_t). KVM has no such check, allowing a guest to register vcpu_info at an arbitrary byte alignment. Enforce unconditional 4-byte alignment regardless of the current shinfo mode. This is sufficient because subsequent commits ensure that all locked atomic operations on vcpu_info fields use at most 32-bit accesses. Return -ENXIO on failure, matching Xen's map_guest_area() behaviour for unaligned requests. Originally observed in review of an unrelated patch: https://lore.kernel.org/all/20260604193554.1BA311F00893@smtp.kernel.org/

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved: KVM: x86/mmu: Bug the VM if KVM attempts to walk more levels than the MMU has Extend the "EFER.LMA && !CR4.PAE" check, which exists largely to guard against KVM configuring a paging32 MMU with more than 2 levels of paging, with a very explicit check for exactly that: that KVM isn't trying to walk more levels of paging than the MMU template provides. I.e. harden KVM against all bugs that would cause KVM to generates accesses beyond the bounds of guest_walker's arrays, regardless of how KVM ended up with the misconfigured MMU. Note, don't use w->cpu_role.base.level directly as the paging64 template only provides two levels of page tables for PAE paging on 32-bit hosts, and handles the third level by manually emulating the PDPTR access.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved: KVM: nSVM: Ignore EFER.LMA if EFER.LME=0 when preparing L2 state Force EFER.LMA=0 if EFER.LME=0 when preparing L2 state for VMRUN, i.e. mimic real hardware's behavior of ignoring EFER.LMA if EFER.LME=0. VMRUN unfortunately allows the nonsensical combination, i.e. doesn't fail, but KVM itself has an invariant EFER.LMA can be set et if and only if EFER.LME is set. Breaking that invariant can lead to a variety of issue, particularly in MMU code that keys off EFER.LMA when determining whether to emulate/virtualization 4/5-level paging versus PAE paging.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved: KVM: nSVM: Reject KVM_SET_NESTED_STATE if L1 has EFER.LMA=1 && EFER.LME=0 Reject KVM_SET_NESTED_STATE if the incoming L1 host state has what is effectively an impossible EFER combination of LMA=1 but LME=0, i.e. if the state says long mode is active but not enabled. Unlike VMX, SVM doesn't have an explicit consistent check for the illegal combination; presumably hardware simply ignores EFER.LMA if EFER.LME=0. Unfortunately, KVM doesn't ignore EFER.LMA in this case and consumes the illegal state when constructing the shadow MMU for L2. E.g. if userspace also clears CR4.PAE, then kvm_calc_cpu_role() will compute a role with 4 or 5 levels of paging, but shadow_mmu_init_context() will wire up the MMU to use the paging32 template, which maxes out its levels at 2. Note, the "real badness" is effectively the same as what happened with the nVMX bug fixed by commit 112e66017bff ("KVM: nVMX: add missing consistency checks for CR0 and CR4"). Unfortunately, the sanity check added by commit 72e2fb24a0b0 ("KVM: x86/mmu: Bug the VM if a vCPU ends up in long mode without PAE enabled") doesn't work for this case, since L2 state is active at the time of the page fault, but it's L1 that has the bad state.
