desc: In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved: ovl: do not copy up a dentry that was removed A change to a removed file through an open descriptor replaces whatever has its old name in the upper layer. Copy up must only create a name in the upper directory, never replace one. After an unlink, an rmdir or a rename over a lower dentry, a dentry that an open file keeps alive still has its old parent and name, but in the upper directory that name is now a whiteout or a new object. ovl_copy_up_workdir() renames the copy over it, which brings back the removed object and destroys whatever took its name. An unprivileged user opened a lower FIFO and unlinked it, root created a file at that name, and fchmod on the old descriptor replaced the file of root with the FIFO. Fix this by looking up the target name of the rename in ovl_copy_up_workdir() with LOOKUP_EXCL, so that copy up fails with -EEXIST if the name is taken, as copy up with O_TMPFILE already does when it links the copy to the name. [amir: use LOOKUP_EXCL instead of relying on d_unhashed()]

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved: ovl: check that the parents of volatile/dirty are dirs An unprivileged user crashes the kernel by mounting overlayfs with the volatile option. A dentry that serves as the parent of a lookup must be a directory. ovl_create_volatile_dirty() walks work/incompat/volatile/dirty by name, and ovl_lookup_or_create() returns an existing entry whatever its type. A file or a symlink that another task creates during the mount becomes the parent of the next lookup, which calls a NULL ->lookup. An unprivileged user mounted overlayfs with "volatile" in a user namespace while a second process created a symlink named work/incompat, and the mount task oopsed on a NULL ->lookup call. Fix this by returning -ENOTDIR from ovl_lookup_or_create() when the caller asked for a directory and the existing entry is a non-dir.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved: ovl: always encode the origin fh when index is enabled On an overlay with index=on,nfs_export=on, copy up of a directory crashes the kernel once an LSM has started to deny CAP_DAC_READ_SEARCH to the mounter, the task that mounted the overlay. The mount and the LSM policy change require root. After that, any user who can write to a directory that exists only in a lower layer triggers the oops by doing so. Before a file or directory that exists only in a lower layer is changed for the first time, overlayfs copies it to the writable upper layer. This is called copy up. On copy up, ovl_get_origin_fh() encodes the file handle of the lower inode, called the origin. It returns NULL if ovl_can_decode_fh() says that the lower filesystem cannot decode handles. Whether the callers can handle NULL depends on the index option: - Without an index, NULL is fine: the callers store an empty origin xattr. - With index enabled, overlayfs keeps entries for copied up inodes in an internal index directory. The name of an index entry is derived from the handle, so ovl_get_origin_fh() must return a handle or an error. The mount only enables the index if ovl_can_decode_fh() succeeds for all layers, but the result can change later. The function checks the export operations of the filesystem and capable(CAP_DAC_READ_SEARCH). Copy up runs with the mounter's credentials, and an LSM can start to deny the capability to those credentials after the mount. ovl_get_origin_fh() then returns NULL with index enabled. This goes wrong in two callers: - With nfs_export=on, copy up of a directory creates an index entry for the directory. ovl_create_index() passes the NULL handle to ovl_get_index_name_fh(), which dereferences it. - If the result changes while mount(2) is still running, ovl_get_indexdir() passes a NULL from ovl_get_origin_fh() to ovl_verify_set_fh() in the same way. Before the commit in the Fixes tag, these two callers encoded the handle themselves, without consulting ovl_can_decode_fh(). Reproduced with a BPF LSM program that started to deny the capability after the mount. An unprivileged touch in a directory that had not been copied up yet oopsed in ovl_get_index_name_fh(). With this patch the touch succeeds and the directory gets its index entry. Fix this by calling ovl_can_decode_fh() in ovl_get_origin_fh() only when index is disabled.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved: ovl: use the pinned upper dir in ovl_fix_origin() Renames made directly on the upper filesystem during a lookup crash the kernel. A dentry that is passed to vfs_setxattr() must be pinned. ovl_fix_origin() passes upper->d_parent to ovl_set_impure() without a reference, and the lookup holds no lock of the upper directory. A rename on the upper filesystem changes d_parent, and only the child pins the new parent, so a second rename and an rmdir free it. With delays in ovl_fix_origin() and ovl_set_impure(), renaming the upper directory twice and removing the intermediate parent during the lookup of a merge directory without an origin xattr gave a KASAN use-after-free in vfs_setxattr(). Fix this by passing the upper dentry that the overlay parent holds. [amir: add helper ovl_set_impure_dir()]

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved: ovl: take a snapshot of the name for copy up The copy up of a directory reads a freed dentry name when a lookup moves the directory at the same time. A pointer to the name of a dentry is only valid while something stops a move of the dentry. ovl_do_copy_up() keeps a plain copy of c->dentry->d_name in c->destname, and ovl_copy_up_start() only keeps ovl_rename() away. When a lookup finds the same directory under another name after a change to the lower layer, d_splice_alias() moves the dentry and frees its external name. With a delay in ovl_do_copy_up(), a chmod of a lower-only directory with a 60 byte name raced with a rename of that directory in the lower layer and a stat of the new name, and KASAN reported a use-after-free in lookup_noperm_common(). Fix this by using take_dentry_name_snapshot() for c->destname.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved: ovl: set OVL_WHITEOUTS before publishing the upper dir Listing a directory while it is copied up causes a use-after-free of the readdir cache. A merge directory must never be iterated as a real upper directory: that mode frees the cache in OVL_I(inode)->cache without looking at its refcount, while files opened in merged mode still use it. ovl_copy_up_workdir() publishes the upper dentry before it sets OVL_WHITEOUTS, and ovl_dir_open() samples both without a lock, so an open between the two stores finds the upper directory and takes it for a real one. With a delay between the two stores, an unprivileged process that listed a directory during its copy-up saw only "." and "..", and its next getdents freed the readdir cache of another descriptor. Fix this by setting OVL_WHITEOUTS before ovl_inode_update(), so that ovl_dir_reset() agrees with ovl_dir_open(), and by testing OVL_TYPE_MERGE() of the path type in ovl_dir_open(), so that an open that observes the upper dentry never iterates a merge dir as a real dir, regardless of the order in which it observes the flag. [amir: test OVL_TYPE_MERGE() instead of smp_rmb() in ovl_dir_open()]

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved: ovl: hold a reference on the parent in readdir Listing a directory on an overlay uses a freed dentry and crashes the kernel when a lookup moves the directory at the same time. Code that can sleep may only use d_parent without a reference while something stops a move of the dentry. ovl_iterate_real(), ovl_need_adjust_d_ino() and ovl_cache_update() use the d_parent of the listed directory and hold only the lock of that directory. When a lookup finds the directory under another parent after a change to a layer, d_splice_alias() moves it without that lock and drops its reference on the old parent. With a delay in ovl_iterate_real(), getdents64 on an overlay directory raced a rename in the lower layer and a lookup that moved its dentry, and after an rmdir of the old parent KASAN reported a use-after-free in security_inode_getattr(). Fix this by using dget_parent() in the three functions. [amir: fix comments in ovl_need_adjust_d_ino()]

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved: smb: client: hold server info until cifsd exits The last session reference can be dropped while the cifsd demultiplex thread is still running clean_demultiplex_info(). That thread frees TCP_Server_Info there, racing with cifs_put_tcp_session() as it releases the server crypto state. syzbot reported a KASAN use-after-free in cifs_crypto_secmech_release(). Keep an object reference for the cifsd thread. Defer final crypto, session-key, network namespace, string, and structure cleanup until both the last session reference and the thread reference are dropped. Drop the thread reference after clean_demultiplex_info() has finished using the server. Build-tested with ARCH=arm64 and W=1 for fs/smb/client/connect.o. The KASAN reproducer was not run on the patched kernel.

desc: In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved: smb: client: fix OOB last_entry pointer from unbounded LastNameOffset CIFSFindFirst() and CIFSFindNext() locate the last entry of a TRANS2_FIND_FIRST2 or TRANS2_FIND_NEXT2 response by adding the LastNameOffset of the response parameters to the start of the data area, and store the result in psrch_inf->last_entry. MS-CIFS 2.2.6.2.2 defines that offset as the offset of the entry's file name; the client follows the reading of NT and Samba servers, which point it at the entry. LastNameOffset is only checked against CIFSMaxBufSize, which says nothing about the response actually received: validate_t2() lets the data area start up to 1024 bytes into the buffer, and SendReceive() copies at most CIFSMaxBufSize + MAX_CIFS_HDR_SIZE bytes of a response, 16468 by default, into a cifs_request allocation of CIFSMaxBufSize + MAX_SMB2_HDR_SIZE bytes, 16588 by default. The pointer itself can therefore be placed anywhere from the end of the received data to 820 bytes past the end of the allocation. The read through that pointer is far larger than its displacement. find_cifs_entry() hands last_entry to cifs_save_resume_key() after every FindNext and after the FindFirst of a search rewind, and cifs_fill_dirent() takes the length of the name from the entry itself: a __le32 FileNameLength for most levels, a __u8 for SMB_FIND_FILE_INFO_STANDARD, and for SMB_FIND_FILE_UNIX the result of a scan for the terminating NUL over up to PATH_MAX + 1 UTF-16 units. The name is recorded as the resume name of the search, and the next CIFSFindNext() rejects only a recorded length of PATH_MAX or more before copying the name into the ResumeFileName of its request and sending it with the resume key taken from the same entry: up to 4 KiB of memory from past the end of the allocation leaks to the server, and for SMB_FIND_FILE_UNIX the NUL scan runs about twice as far before the length is even known. The entry does not have to lie outside the response for that either: a maximal response ends about 120 bytes before the end of the allocation, so an entry in its last bytes with a name just under PATH_MAX has nearly all of that name copied from past the allocation. It needs nothing unusual from the client: a FindNext response that reports no entries and does not end the search makes find_cifs_entry() send the next FindNext at once, carrying whatever was parsed at LastNameOffset, and a search rewind can do the same after its FindFirst. SMB1 is not negotiated by default: this takes a malicious or compromised server, a mount of it with an explicit vers=1.0, which CONFIG_CIFS_ALLOW_INSECURE_LEGACY (default y) permits, and a directory listing on that mount. In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved: ocfs2: snapshot dentry names in file and setattr traces Patch series "ocfs2: stabilize dentry names in file and setattr traces", v4. Snapshot names at all six users of ocfs2__file_ops and at the separate setattr event. Patch 1 handles the five ordinary file-operation callers and setattr. Patch 2 handles release separately to preserve its locked open-count sample and take the snapshot outside that critical section. The release explanation distinguishes its existing RCU lifetime coverage from name/length consistency. It does not claim that the ordinary callers' external-name UAF interleaving crosses the held inode spinlock. The release source change is unchanged from v3. Patch 1 also removes the read callback's redundant NULL-inode check. The two patches apply independently and leave trace formats unchanged. This patch (of 2): The open, fsync, read, write and splice-read trace calls pass the live dentry name and length to the shared ocfs2__file_ops event class. ocfs2_setattr() passes the same unprotected arguments to its own event. Both events size and copy a __string field separately. A reference to the dentry does not pin the external storage backing an individual name. With an event enabled, a caller can be preempted after loading the name pointer. A long-to-short rename can then replace the name and reclaim its old external allocation before the trace callback sizes or copies it, provided no other snapshot retains that allocation. The setattr inode lock does not exclude every rename: a same-directory rename of a source directory need not take that directory's inode lock. It can therefore change the dentry name while setattr records its event. Inline names and separately loaded lengths can also change during trace record sizing and copying. Take a dentry name snapshot around each of these six trace calls and pass both the string and length from the snapshot. Check event enablement before taking a snapshot. Keep the event classes and formats unchanged. Also remove the redundant NULL-inode check in the read callback. file_inode() returns the open file's inode, which is already used by the trace call above the check. The historical report below is from the read path. In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved: ocfs2: pin refcount trees before dropping the lookup lock A refcount tree returned to ocfs2_lock_refcount_tree() must stay alive until that caller releases its operation reference. However, ocfs2_get_refcount_tree() returns the cached pointer after dropping osb_lock, and the caller only takes its kref afterwards. The registry reference does not protect this gap from concurrent removal. This can happen when another node frees a refcount root and reuses its block with a different generation while this mount retains the old cached tree. Two local operations on different inodes sharing the new root, such as data CoW and an external xattr update, can then look up the same stale tree. Their inode locks are independent, and both the REFCOUNT DLM lock and rf_sem are acquired after the first operation reference. The following ordering is possible, with no other operation references: Data CoW Xattr update -------- ------------ Look up the old tree under osb_lock, then drop osb_lock Look up the same tree and take a kref Acquire the tree locks and read the new on-disk generation Erase the old tree under osb_lock Unlock and drop the operation kref Drop the registry kref, freeing tree Take a kref through the freed tree pointer The final kref_get() accesses freed rf_getcnt storage, and subsequent accesses in ocfs2_lock_refcount_tree() also use the freed allocation. Take the operation reference in ocfs2_get_refcount_tree() before releasing osb_lock, including when an insertion loses to another lookup. Removal must acquire the same lock, so it cannot drop the registry reference before the lookup has pinned the tree. Keep the existing unlock and error path puts. The two callers that already hold the refcount tree lock keep their borrowed lookup behavior and do not acquire an extra reference. In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved: ocfs2: fix chunk number of the first chunk in a local quota file Mounting a crafted OCFS2 image can corrupt kernel memory. When the local quota file header of such an image claims zero chunks, the first quota entry allocated during the mount gets a chunk number taken from a kernel pointer, and releasing that entry clears a bit far outside the chunk bitmap. The write will corrupt the data stored at that address, and the corruption may lead to a system crash or damage unrelated data. Mounting requires CAP_SYS_ADMIN, so it takes an untrusted image, such as removable media or a loop mount of a file from elsewhere. Since the chunk number comes from a kernel pointer, the address of the bit that gets cleared differs from boot to boot, and the issue has been reported under several titles: - BUG: unable to handle kernel paging request in ocfs2_local_release_dquot - KASAN: use-after-free Write in ocfs2_local_release_dquot - KASAN: slab-out-of-bounds Write in ocfs2_local_release_dquot - KASAN: slab-use-after-free Write in ocfs2_local_release_dquot - KFENCE: use-after-free write in ocfs2_local_release_dquot Note that none of these is a use-after-free in the quota code: the chunk and its buffer head are alive. The bit that gets cleared lies far outside the bitmap. KASAN and KFENCE name each report based on the object occupying that address, which explains why the same issue is reported under so many different titles. In the report I sent, the address fell in a free page, which KASAN labels use-after-free. There are known reproducers. Both a syzkaller and a C reproducer are available from the Google Drive link [1] in my report thread. The issue was found by our modified syzkaller, not a theoretical thing found by an LLM. I have not seen it outside fuzzing, so it is not affecting me in the real world. The local quota file in OCFS2 is divided into chunks, and each chunk begins with a header block holding a bitmap of the quota entries that chunk has handed out. Chunks are numbered from zero, and that number is used to convert the file offset of an entry back into a bit position in the bitmap. ocfs2_local_quota_add_chunk() appends a new chunk to the in-memory list and numbers it one past the chunk that was last: list_add_tail(&chunk->qc_chunk, &oinfo->dqi_chunk); chunk->qc_num = list_entry(chunk->qc_chunk.prev, struct ocfs2_quota_chunk, qc_chunk)->qc_num + 1; The predecessor is looked up after the new chunk is added to the list, so if the list was empty, the prev pointer is the list head itself. The head is the dqi_chunk member of struct ocfs2_mem_dqinfo and is not a chunk, so reading qc_num through it lands 16 bytes past the start of the head, on the dqi_gqinode pointer that follows it. The first chunk of the file is then numbered with the lower half of a kernel pointer instead of 0. The list is empty when the local quota file header claims the file has no chunks. ocfs2_local_read_info() takes dqi_chunks from that header without validating it, so an image with dqi_chunks == 0 takes this path when the first quota entry is allocated. ocfs2_create_local_dquot() turns the bad number into a file offset with ol_dqblk_off(), which shifts a 32-bit block number left by the block size bits, so the top bits of such a large block number are lost. ocfs2_local_release_dquot() turns the offset back into a bit index with ol_dqblk_chunk_off(), using the full chunk number, so the lost bits push that index far outside the bitmap, and clearing it corrupts unrelated memory. Compute the chunk number before putting the chunk on the list, and use 0 when the list is empty.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved: ocfs2: cancel quota sync work before freeing quota info OCFS2 quota info owns dqi_sync_work and must outlive both its timer and qsync_work_fn(). ocfs2_local_free_info() frees that owner without cancelling the work, relying on the quota suspend/disable wrappers. Loading quotas on a read-only to read-write remount can successfully queue the work in ocfs2_global_read_info() and then fail while attaching a dquot to an existing inode in add_dquot_ref(). The quota core unwinds that failure directly through dquot_disable(), bypassing the OCFS2 wrapper: Remount task (s_umount write) Timer/workqueue ocfs2_global_read_info() schedules dqi_sync_work add_dquot_ref() returns an error dquot_disable() ocfs2_local_free_info() frees oinfo delayed-work timer expires qsync_work_fn() reads oinfo The timer core can then write to the freed embedded timer, or qsync_work_fn() can read oinfo->dqi_gqinode before its s_umount trylock. The outer ocfs2_disable_quotas() cleanup skips the failed type because dquot_disable() has already cleared its loaded state. Cancel dqi_sync_work synchronously at the start of ocfs2_local_free_info(), before dropping the global inode or freeing any owner state. The work is initialized whenever read_file_info() succeeds. dquot_disable() holds s_umount for write, so the callback skips its quota scan via down_read_trylock() and can finish without waiting for teardown. The synchronous cancel also handles its self-rearm. In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved: ocfs2/dlm: hold the lookup reference across convert AST enqueue dlm_convert_lock_handler() drops the reference it took when it found the lock on res->granted at its leave label, one statement before it calls dlm_queue_ast(). dlm_free_dead_locks() takes res->spinlock and drops the list and base references, so a peer death landing in that gap leaves the handler's own put as the one that frees the lock, and __dlm_queue_ast() then reads lock->lockres from freed memory. The handler is registered next to dlm_create_lock_handler(), so a convert message buffered on a dying peer's socket arrives on the same o2net receive work that o2net_disconnect_node() does not wait for. The two can interleave as follows, with the reference counts as they are before this fix: Socket data-ready Node-down thread Receive worker ----------------- ---------------- -------------- o2net_data_ready() select sc under callback read lock o2net_disconnect_node() queue shutdown begin flush; new color queue sc_rx_work in the new color release callback lock shutdown socket flush returns read buffered convert_lock dlm_convert_lock_handler() find lock on res->granted dlm_lock_get() refs = 3 lock res->spinlock __dlmconvert_master() call_ast = 1 unlock res->spinlock DLM node-down cleanup lock res->spinlock dlm_free_dead_locks() unlink lock put list ref refs = 2 put base ref refs = 1 unlock res->spinlock dlm_lock_put() refs = 0 free lock dlm_queue_ast() __dlm_queue_ast() read lock->lockres (use-after-free) __dlmconvert_master() only moves the lock between lists, so the count entering the gap is base, list and lookup. Drop the lookup reference after the AST is queued instead of before it and the race ends with the one __dlm_queue_ast() took, which dlm_flush_asts() releases later with ast_pending cleared and ast_list unlinked. No extra get is needed, and the normal case ends with the same count as before. dlmconvert_master() has the same shape but is only reached from dlmlock() for a lock this node owns, which dlm_free_dead_locks() never matches.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved: ocfs2/dlm: hold a lock reference across grant AST enqueue A newly granted remote lock must remain alive until its grant AST is queued. dlmlock_master() publishes the lock on res->granted with its base and queue references, then drops res->spinlock before calling dlm_queue_ast(). The resource's reserved AST count does not retain the lock itself. This can fail when a peer dies with an immediately grantable CREATE buffered on its socket. O2NET's node-down callback flushes receive work before DLM cleanup, but the flush only waits for work queued on entry. A data-ready callback that already selected the socket container can queue new receive work after the flush advances its work color. Socket shutdown does not discard bytes already queued for TCP receive. The late receive work and DLM node-down cleanup can interleave as follows (the lock reference operations shown are before this fix): Socket data-ready Node-down thread Receive worker ----------------- ---------------- -------------- o2net_data_ready() select sc under callback read lock o2net_disconnect_node() queue shutdown begin flush; new color queue sc_rx_work in the new color release callback lock shutdown socket flush returns read buffered CREATE dlmlock_master() lock res->spinlock add lock to granted unlock res->spinlock DLM node-down cleanup lock res->spinlock dlm_free_dead_locks() unlink lock put queue/base refs free lock unlock res->spinlock dlm_queue_ast() __dlm_queue_ast() read lock->lockres (use-after-free) DLM cleanup holds res->spinlock while dlm_free_dead_locks() drops the queue and base references. The CREATE handler no longer holds that spinlock when __dlm_queue_ast() reads the lock, before taking its AST list reference. Take a temporary lock reference under res->spinlock when a grant AST will be queued, and drop it after dlm_queue_ast(). This keeps the lock alive across cleanup until the AST path has taken its own reference, without reversing the existing AST/resource lock order. In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved: ocfs2/heartbeat: unlink live slots when their node is missing o2hb_shutdown_slot() returns immediately when its node is no longer in the configfs registry. A slot can still be linked in o2hb_live_slots when that lookup fails. Region teardown or startup-error cleanup then frees the slot array without removing its embedded list member. With the same peer live in another region, the next list update can follow a predecessor into the freed array. Reusing the node number can also make a later insertion encounter that stale member. Always remove the slot under o2hb_live_lock, even when node lookup fails. Preserve aggregate membership accounting and the last-region DOWN callback: the existing callback interface explicitly permits a NULL node for DOWN events. Only drop the node reference when lookup returned one. This closes both normal release and startup-abort paths without changing the publication or callback locking protocol. Also require a configured node before admitting a new live slot in o2hb_check_slot(). The early live-bitmap check is not held through admission: the last live slot in another region can be removed in between. Without a node, admission can then queue an UP event with a NULL argument and hit the event helper's BUG_ON. Existing live slots can still leave and generate NULL-node DOWN events. A controlled probe-instrumented test reproduced this while stopping one of two regions after removing the peer from configfs. In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved: media: rc: Fix use after free in bpf progs Since commit dccc0c3ddf8f ("media: rc: fix race between unregister and urb/irq callbacks"), rcdev->raw is no longer set to NULL after device unregister. raw->progs could point to stale data.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved: media: rc: After rc_unregister_device() timers can be re-armed If rc_keydown() is called after rc_register_device(), then the timers can be re-armed. Delete them again for a final time.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved: media: rc: Use after free in ir_raw_event_handle() If rc_unregister_device() is called while IR is being processed, then ir_raw_event_handle() could call wake_up_process(dev->raw->thread) after kthread_stop(dev->raw->thread). Avoid use after free by using get_task_struct().

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved: media: rc: mce_kbd: Fix inconsistent locking of keylock data->keylock is taken with spin_lock() in ir_mce_kbd_decode(), which runs in the raw IR decode kthread with local interrupts enabled, but with spin_lock_irqsave() in mce_kbd_rx_timeout(), the rx_timeout timer callback, which runs in softirq context. If the decode kthread is holding keylock via spin_lock() when a timer interrupt fires on the same CPU and the softirq runs mce_kbd_rx_timeout(), the softirq spins forever waiting for a lock that only the now-preempted kthread can release, while the kthread cannot run again until the softirq gives up the CPU. This deadlocks the CPU.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved: media: rc: Ensure registered is cleared in error path If rc_register_device() fails, ensure that registered is not set to true. If lirc_register() succeeded, then userspace could have an open file descriptor open. This leads to a use-after-free. lirc_unregister() must be called with registered = false, else there is a possibility that an fd is open and polling, which would never return POLLERR unless registered is false. Note that registered must be changed under dev->lock, many functions read registered under lock (e.g. lirc_ioctl).

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved: media: rc: Ensure that rc_unregister_device() does not free input device During or after rc_unregister_device(), IR may still be reported which results in a input event being reported. This could result in a null pointer deref in rc_keydown() or a use-after-free of the input device if the pointer was read before it is set to NULL.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved: nvmet-auth: serialize access to DH-HMAC-CHAP state to fix UAF A REPLY AUTH_SEND command can derive a dhchap_skey key while a concurrent AUTH_RECEIVE command observing this REPLY state executes the failure path and frees that key. The REPLY command then continues and writes into freed memory, causing a use-after-free. KASAN reports it as: BUG: KASAN: slab-use-after-free in __sha256_final Write of size 4 at addr ffff88800359c540 ... nvmet_auth_sq_free (drivers/nvme/target/auth.c:237) nvmet_execute_auth_receive (drivers/nvme/target/fabrics-cmd-auth.c:621) Add a mutex to each submission queue to serialize authentication commands and timeout handling. Unlock the mutex before completing requests and ignore outdated timeout callbacks. Limit timeout delays to prevent immediate expiry on 32-bit kernels.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved: nvmem: core: Fix OOB read for bit offsets of more than one byte When the bit offset is BITS_PER_BYTE or larger the read position is advanced by `bytes_offset`. This is not taken into account in the per-byte read loop which still reads `cell->bytes` resulting in an out of bounds read of `bytes_offset` bytes. The information read OOB does not leak directly as the erroneously read bits are cleared. Detected by KASAN while looking for a use-after-free in simplefb.c.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved: pps: generators: don't use the driver's info after unregister A file that was opened before pps_gen_unregister_source() keeps pps_gen, and with it the pointer to the driver's pps_gen_source_info. PPS_GEN_SETENABLE and PPS_GEN_USESYSTEMCLOCK keep using that pointer after the driver has gone: - pps_gen_tio allocates its info with devm_kzalloc(), so after an unbind both ioctls read freed memory, and SETENABLE calls the driver's enable() with its freed private data. - pps_gen-dummy does not set info->owner, so it can be unloaded while the file is open, and the ioctls then read the unloaded module's data and call its code. TIO can't probe in a VM, as it needs ART. A test driver that registers its info in devm memory like TIO does, unbound while /dev/pps-gen0 is open, gives: BUG: KASAN: slab-use-after-free in pps_gen_cdev_ioctl+0x4c1/0x580 Read of size 1 at addr ffff88800e647f38 by task ppsgen64/145 ... Freed by task 146: kfree+0x25a/0x6d0 release_nodes+0xd1/0x140 devres_release_all+0x10e/0x1a0 device_unbind_cleanup+0x71/0x250 device_release_driver_internal+0x41b/0x570 unbind_store+0xd9/0x100 and unloading pps_gen-dummy while its file is open oopses: BUG: unable to handle page fault for address: ffffffffa0203040 Oops: Oops: 0000 [#1] SMP KASAN NOPTI RIP: 0010:pps_gen_cdev_ioctl+0x372/0x580 Protect info in the ioctl handler with a mutex, and clear it under the mutex on unregister, so that unregister waits for the ioctls using it and later ones fail with -ENODEV. PPS_KC_BIND does the same for a removed PPS device since commit 3649f9a6b897 ("pps: don't allow PPS_KC_BIND on removed devices"). The sysfs attributes need nothing new: they are removed, and their callbacks drained, before info is cleared.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved: power: supply: sbs-battery: disable polling before supply teardown The managed poll-work cancellation is registered before the power supply, so cleanup unregisters the supply before draining polling. A pending or running poller can then call power_supply_changed() on the released supply. Commit 8d59cf3887fb ("power: supply: sbs-battery: Fix use-after-free in power_supply_changed()") moved the IRQ request after supply registration, but did not change the poll-work cancellation order. Add a later managed action that disables and drains polling before supply teardown. Its retained disabled state prevents external-power callbacks from rearming the poll work after it has been drained. Keep the original autocancel to initialize work before supply callbacks can run and to cover failed supply registration. The teardown ordering issue was found by static analysis.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved: power: supply: pf1550: drain IRQ work before unregistering supplies The VBUS work calls power_supply_changed(), but its managed cancellation is registered before the supplies. Cleanup can therefore unregister a supply while IRQ-triggered work is still pending. Commit 838767f50747 ("power: supply: pf1550: Fix use-after-free in power_supply_changed()") moved IRQ requests after supply registration, but left work cancellation before the supplies. That change protects the direct IRQ callbacks, while this fix drains the work they queue. Register the three work items after both supplies and before the IRQs. Cleanup then frees the IRQ producers, drains the work, and unregisters the supplies. The teardown ordering issue was found by static analysis.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved: phy: core: Fix race-condition between _of_phy_get() and try_module_get() Sashiko asked during a patch review if the existing usage pattern had a race condition; specifically in of_phy_get() if it was possible between returning from _of_phy_get() and running try_module_get() that a module might be unbound leading to use-after-free. Looking at the code this appears to be so, there is no linkage between the phy and module under a synchronisation primitive. Using the phy_provider_mutex in phy_get() will ensure there is a link between the returned phy pointer and the module_get() bumping the module reference count. Amend phy_get(), of_phy_get() and devm_of_phy_get_by_index() to fix the same usage pattern. phy_provider_unregister() must take the phy_provider_mutex so amending phy_get()/of_phy_get() to take that same mutex guarantees there is no use-after-free.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved: spi: spi-pci1xxxx: quiesce DMA engines on transfer timeout If a DMA-mapped transfer times out waiting for DMA_TERM and neither DMA abort interrupt arrived, pci1xxxx_spi_transfer_with_dma() returns through the error label while both DMA engines are still enabled, the done/abort interrupt status is still armed and the transfer state (p->xfer, p->tx_sgl, p->rx_sgl) is still registered. The ISRs keep firing afterwards: they reprogram the DMA engines from p->tx_sgl / p->rx_sgl and signal completion through p->xfer and p->spi_xfer_done, all of which the SPI core is free to unmap or reuse once transfer_one() has returned, which is a use-after-free. A late done interrupt can also start the next transfer queued behind the failed one. Stop both DMA engines, drain the pending done/abort interrupt status and synchronize the DMA IRQs before dropping the in-progress state and the transfer pointers, and re-enable the engines afterwards so that subsequent transfers keep working. The engines are only turned back on once both were confirmed to have stopped: re-enabling an engine that failed to stop would cancel the pending stop request and let it keep running into buffers the SPI core is about to unmap or free, which is exactly the window this patch closes. An engine that failed to stop is left disabled, as the abort paths already do. The DMA interrupt status and mask registers are shared between the two SPI instances, so the cleanup drains only this instance's done/abort status bits instead of masking the interrupt lines, which would also suppress the peer instance's completion interrupts. Also make the DMA ISRs ignore interrupts while no transfer is in progress so that a stray MSI after the cleanup can no longer act on the cleared state. No PCI1XXXX hardware was available for testing and QEMU has no model of this PCIe part, so the timeout path was exercised with a userspace replica of the timeout branch and the DMA ISRs, with the register and interrupt accesses mocked: on the unfixed code both a wedged engine that clears after the timeout and a late done interrupt touch the freed transfer state, while with this fix applied neither does and an engine that failed to stop is left disabled. The module was also loaded and unloaded in a QEMU x86_64 guest running a kernel with this fix applied.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved: ufs: use u64 for directory size in ufs_last_byte ufs1_read_inode() and ufs2_read_inode() copy the untrusted 64-bit on-disk size into inode->i_size. ufs_last_byte() then truncates that value to an unsigned int before calculating the valid extent of a directory folio. A directory size of exactly 4 GiB is truncated to zero. In ufs_find_entry(), subtracting the requested record length from that zero forms an endpoint almost 4 GiB beyond the mapped folio. A crafted UFS2 image produces: BUG: KASAN: use-after-free in ufs_find_entry+0x583/0x6e0 [ufs] Read of size 1 ... ufs_find_entry ufs_inode_by_name ufs_lookup __lookup_slow path_lookupat The KASAN classification reflects that the adjacent physical page was free; the source-level operation is an out-of-folio read. A controlled UFS1 test with CONFIG_UFS_FS_WRITE enabled also made ufs_find_entry() return a directory entry from an adjacent anonymous page. unlink() then passed that pointer to ufs_delete_entry(), which cleared the adjacent page's 3 2-bit d_ino. This write result reproduced three out of three times. UFS normally requires a privileged mount path. A relevant boundary is a privileged automounter or image-processing service handling an attacker-supplied filesystem. The write primitive additionally requires UFS1 to be mounted read-write with CONFIG_UFS_FS_WRITE enabled; the read is reachable with read-only UFS2. Keep the intermediate size arithmetic at 64 bits so non-final pages are bounded at PAGE_SIZE. With this change, the same controlled tests reach the real on-disk directory entry and produce no adjacent-page write or KASAN report. A reproducer and full validation logs are available on request. The vulnerable helper is present in v7.2-rc3, v7.1, v6.18.38, v6.12.95, v6.6.111, and upstream master at 1229e2e57a5c. Runtime reproduction and fix validation were performed in an x86-64 QEMU guest running v7.2-rc3 with generic KASAN.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved: usb: gadget: fix refcount underflow in gadgetfs_bind() error path gadgetfs_bind() calls get_dev() only on the success path, but gadgetfs_unbind() called from the enomem error label unconditionally calls put_dev(). When bind fails (e.g. ENOMEM), put_dev() fires without a matching get_dev(), leaving the refcount unbalanced. A subsequent close of the ep0 file descriptor calls dev_release() -> put_dev() which hits zero and frees the object; then gadgetfs_kill_sb() calls put_dev(the_device) again on the already-freed pointer, triggering a refcount underflow and use-after-free. Fix by calling get_dev() at the start of gadgetfs_bind(), before any error path that invokes gadgetfs_unbind(), so the reference is always balanced regardless of whether bind succeeds or fails.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved: vfio/nvgrace-gpu: Use a core-only open_device in fallback mode When the ACPI memory properties are missing or the C2C link is down, the device is exposed through nvgrace_gpu_pci_core_ops. That table opens through nvgrace_gpu_open_device() but closes through vfio_pci_core_close_device(), so open and close are not symmetric. nvgrace_gpu_open_device() registers nvdev->usemem for poison handling unconditionally. In fallback mode usemem.memlength is zero, and register_pfn_address_space() inserts a node covering [0, ULONG_MAX]. Nothing removes it: a second open fails with -EBUSY, and once the device is unbound the node outlives the nvdev that contains it. The next open after a rebind reports: BUG: KASAN: slab-use-after-free in interval_tree_iter_first+0x209/0x310 Read of size 8 at addr ffff88800894aa30 by task nvgrace_repro/203 Call Trace: <TASK> dump_stack_lvl+0x5d/0x80 print_report+0x153/0x4c6 kasan_report+0xe4/0x1a0 interval_tree_iter_first+0x209/0x310 register_pfn_address_space+0x97/0x100 nvgrace_gpu_open_device+0x21c/0x730 vfio_df_open+0x213/0x520 vfio_df_ioctl_bind_iommufd+0x3e8/0x6e0 vfio_device_fops_unl_ioctl+0x782/0x1570 __x64_sys_ioctl+0x13c/0x1c0 do_syscall_64+0x106/0x630 entry_SYSCALL_64_after_hwframe+0x77/0x7f </TASK> Allocated by task 188: ... _vfio_alloc_device+0x3a/0x500 nvgrace_gpu_probe+0xcb/0x660 local_pci_probe+0xcf/0x170 ... Freed by task 188: ... kfree+0x20d/0x600 device_release+0xcf/0x250 kobject_put+0x152/0x2f0 pci_device_remove+0xb0/0x1c0 device_release_driver_internal+0x38d/0x540 unbind_store+0xde/0x100 ... Give the fallback table its own open_device that only calls vfio_pci_core_enable() and vfio_pci_core_finish_enable(), the counterpart of vfio_pci_core_close_device(). Fallback mode then never touches the nvgrace memory regions, as Alex suggested. This should be safe because the fallback table uses the vfio-pci core read, write and mmap handlers, so nothing there uses the state nvgrace_gpu_open_device() sets up. The one visible difference is that a fallback open no longer fails when BAR0 cannot be mapped, which matches vfio-pci.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved: wifi: mt76: mt7996: unlink TWT flow if the MCU rejects the agreement mt7996_mac_add_twt_setup() links a new flow into dev->twt_list before asking the MCU to add the agreement, but exits without unlinking the flow if the request fails. The flow-ID and table masks are only committed after MCU success, so the still-linked flow is invisible to the mask-gated teardown paths. If the station retries the setup, the same slot is cleared and its embedded list node reinitialized while it is still linked, corrupting dev->twt_list. If the station disassociates instead, teardown skips the flow and station storage can be freed while the node remains linked. A later scheduling or debugfs twt_stats walk can then dereference the freed flow, resulting in a use-after-free. Unlink the flow when the MCU rejects the agreement. This restores the list to its pre-request state while leaving the unchanged mask and agreement accounting untouched.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved: wifi: ath9k: delete channel-context timers on deinit ath9k_deinit_channel_context() cancels chanctx_work but does not delete the offchannel and sched timers set up by ath9k_init_channel_context(). If either timer fires after deinit (e.g. during driver unload or suspend), it accesses sc->sc_ah which may already be freed by ath9k_hw_deinit(), causing a use-after-free. Delete both timers with timer_shutdown_sync() before cancelling the work item.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved: xen-blkfront: unbind irq before tearing down ring and shadow requests In blkif_free_ring(), the driver tears down the ring's persistent grants, shadow request arrays, and shared ring structure (xenbus_teardown_ring), and only calls unbind_from_irqhandler() at the very end. While blkif_free_ring() is freeing persistent grants and clearing the shadow array, the event channel interrupt (blkif_interrupt) is still registered and active. If an interrupt arrives from the backend during this teardown window, blkif_interrupt() reads rinfo->ring.sring and, via blkif_completion(), accesses rinfo->shadow[id].grants_used and rinfo->shadow[id].sg. blkif_free_ring() tears these structures down without holding rinfo->ring_lock, and the handler only checks info->connected at entry, so this is a real race resulting in a use-after-free or NULL pointer dereference. Fix this by moving unbind_from_irqhandler() to the beginning of blkif_free_ring(). Calling unbind_from_irqhandler() first frees the IRQ and synchronizes with any in-flight interrupt handlers on other CPUs before ring memory and shadow request structures are deallocated, matching the teardown order in drivers/net/xen-netfront.c.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved: staging: rtl8723bs: fix protected RX frame validation in decrypt path The RX software decrypt path mishandles crafted protected frames from a malicious AP in two ways: 1) decryptor() never checks that a protected frame is long enough to hold the 802.11 header plus the per-cipher trailer. All of rtw_wep_decrypt(), rtw_tkip_decrypt() and rtw_aes_decrypt() compute length = hdr.len - hdrlen - iv_len; and act on the result, and recvframe_chkmic() similarly computes datalen = hdr.len - hdrlen - iv_len - icv_len - 8; for TKIP (the 8-byte Michael MIC is not accounted for in icv_len). A frame shorter than hdrlen + iv_len + icv_len (+ 8 for TKIP) underflows these unsigned subtractions, turning into a ~4 GiB iteration count in aes_decipher()/arc4_crypt()/rtw_seccalctkipmic() or a ~4 GiB crc32_le() length, causing out-of-bounds reads/writes of up to ~4 GiB starting from the rx skb. Reject such frames in decryptor() before touching the IV; this covers all three ciphers and the TKIP MIC check, and also keeps the unconditional iv[3] access within the frame. 2) validate_80211w_mgmt() keeps using the frame - two memcpys through the stale rx_data pointer and a pkt_len update - before checking whether decryptor() returned NULL. On decrypt failure (e.g. a unicast protected deauth/disassoc/action frame with a bad MIC, which this path always software-decrypts) the skb has already been freed, so this is a use-after-free read/write, and the caller's error path frees the frame a second time, drifting free_recvframe_cnt. Bail out immediately when decryptor() fails, freeing the temporary mgmt_DATA buffer first. Discovered by Atuin - Automated Vulnerability Discovery Engine.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved: serial: core: shut down initialized port on removal When a serial port configured as a console is opened and subsequently closed, tty_port_shutdown() skips invoking port->ops->shutdown() because port->console is true. As a result, tty_port_initialized() remains true and the port's interrupt handler stays registered in the irq subsystem. If the underlying device is later unbound or removed (e.g. via sysfs driver unbind or device hot-unplug), serial_core_remove_one_port() unregisters the console, frees uport->name via kfree(), and tears down the port without shutting it down or freeing its IRQ. Consequently, the irqaction descriptor remains registered in genirq with action->name pointing to freed memory. This triggers a use-after-free read whenever genirq accesses action->name, such as when reading /proc/interrupts: BUG: KASAN: slab-use-after-free in string+0x476/0x570 Call Trace: string+0x476/0x570 vsnprintf+0x422/0x1300 seq_printf+0x... show_interrupts+... Fix this by acquiring port->mutex in serial_core_remove_one_port() after console unregistration, clearing port->console under the mutex to prevent data races with concurrent tty_port_shutdown(), and invoking uart_shutdown(NULL, state) if the port remains initialized. This ensures that port->ops->shutdown() is called and the IRQ is freed before kfree(uport->name).

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved: scsi: dc395x: sync the waiting_timer before freeing the host The waiting_timer callback re-arms itself and takes the host lock. adapter_uninit() currently stops it with timer_delete(), which does not wait for a callback already running on another CPU. The final scsi_host_put() that frees the host (and the host lock the callback dereferences) runs right after adapter_uninit(), so a concurrent or just re-armed callback can fire after the free, leaving a potential use-after-free window. Replace timer_delete() with timer_shutdown_sync() at the top of adapter_uninit(), before the host-lock section: the timer is dequeued, a running callback is waited for and rearming is blocked before the chip is halted, so it cannot fire at all once the adapter has ceased to function. Waiting outside the lock avoids the self-deadlock that would result from syncing a callback blocked on the lock we still hold. No shutdown is needed for selto_timer because it has no reachable armer or callback. This issue was found by an in-house static analysis tool.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved: net: sched: prevent scheduling deactivated qdiscs TAPRIO can schedule a deactivated qdisc after some_qdisc_is_busy() has reported it idle. Commit 47e8dbb6e763 ("net/sched: do not reset queues in graft operations") made graft deactivation skip queue reset, leaving TAPRIO's timer armed. A late callback schedules NET_TX softirq work, whose dequeue path can race the unlocked child-queue reset in taprio_reset(). The same skb can be queued for deferred freeing by RTNL and dequeued for transmission. In the reproducer, the TAP reader frees it before __rtnl_unlock() reads its next pointer. KASAN reports a slab-use-after-free in __rtnl_unlock+0xa3/0xd0, with a read of size 8 from the freed skb. Reject deactivated qdiscs in __netif_schedule(). Callers' RCU protection lets the existing grace period join earlier scheduling calls before the busy check. Restart nonempty transmit queues on reactivation so suppressed scheduling does not strand packets.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved: mtd: virt-concat: unlink discarded items before freeing mtd_virt_concat_destroy_items() frees each item without removing it from concat_node_list. list_for_each_entry_safe() protects the current traversal, but concat_node_list still points to the freed items afterward. The function also unwinds errors from mtd_virt_concat_node_create(). A later initialization can traverse a freed item in mtd_is_part_concat(), causing a use-after-free. Unlink each item before freeing it.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved: mshv_vtl: detach poll waiter on POLLFREE MSHV_SET_POLL_FILE keeps a poll wait entry after the ioctl returns. A file reference does not always pin the registered waitqueue: signalfd_poll() uses current->sighand->signalfd_wqh, whose lifetime is tied to the task. signalfd_cleanup() sends POLLFREE before the sighand is freed. The MSHV callback currently leaves its entry linked, so __wake_up_pollfree() warns and a later replacement calls remove_wait_queue() through a stale wqh pointer. A source-equivalent KASAN run reproduced: BUG: KASAN: slab-use-after-free in _raw_spin_lock_irqsave _raw_spin_lock_irqsave remove_wait_queue harness_ioctl [mshv_pollfree_harness] The object belonged to sighand_cache and had been released through slab_free_after_rcu_debug() after __cleanup_sighand(). On POLLFREE, unlink the entry under the provider waitqueue lock. Preserve the existing CPU cancellation before publishing a NULL wqh, since a NULL load lets a racing replacement reuse the persistent poll state. Use a matching acquire load under RCU when removing a normal registration. The callback takes no mutex and does not sleep, so the existing mutex-to-waitqueue-lock order is unchanged. An LLM assisted the source audit, fix development, and validation of this issue.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved: mptcp: hold MP_JOIN msk ref when cloning reqsk TCP request migration clones pending request sockets with inet_reqsk_clone(). For MPTCP MP_JOIN requests this byte-copies subflow_req->msk, but the clone does not own a reference. The original and cloned requests can consequently drop the same msk reference, leaving one request with a dangling pointer. This manifests as a KASAN slab-use-after-free in subflow_req_destructor(): BUG: KASAN: slab-use-after-free in subflow_req_destructor (net/mptcp/subflow.c:45) Write of size 4 at addr ff1100010e008d40 by task swapper/0/0 CPU: 0 UID: 0 PID: 0 Comm: swapper/0 Not tainted 7.2.0-rc5-00353-gc27e36054537 #10 PREEMPT(full) Call Trace: subflow_req_destructor (net/mptcp/subflow.c:45) subflow_v4_req_destructor (net/mptcp/subflow.c:694) __reqsk_free (net/ipv4/inet_connection_sock.c:906) reqsk_timer_handler (include/net/request_sock.h:137 net/ipv4/inet_connection_sock.c:1147) Allocated by task 10014: sk_prot_alloc (net/core/sock.c:2246) sk_clone (net/core/sock.c:2488) mptcp_sk_clone_init (include/net/sock.h:1848 net/mptcp/protocol.c:3564) subflow_syn_recv_sock (net/mptcp/subflow.c:883) tcp_check_req (net/ipv4/tcp_minisocks.c:934) Freed by task 0: slab_free_after_rcu_debug (include/linux/kasan.h:235 mm/slub.c:2677 mm/slub.c:6439) rcu_core (kernel/rcu/tree.c:2645 kernel/rcu/tree.c:2897) Last potentially related work creation: kmem_cache_free (mm/slub.c:2638 mm/slub.c:6377 mm/slub.c:6504) __sk_destruct (net/core/sock.c:2289 net/core/sock.c:2391) sk_destruct (net/core/sock.c:2419) __sk_free (net/core/sock.c:2430) sk_free (net/core/sock.c:2441) mptcp_close (include/net/sock.h:2020 net/mptcp/protocol.c:3399) inet_release (net/ipv4/af_inet.c:442) The buggy address belongs to the cache MPTCP of size 2968 The buggy address is 128 bytes inside a freed 2968-byte region A non-NULL subflow_req->msk means that the request owns one reference. The third ACK can concurrently transfer the original request reference to the child and release it, so taking an unconditional hold on the copied pointer is unsafe. MPTCP sockets use SLAB_TYPESAFE_BY_RCU and all current inet_reqsk_clone() callers run in an RCU read-side critical section. Document and lockdep-check that calling-context requirement. Read the pointer from the original request and acquire a reference only if it is still live. Use refcount_inc_not_zero_acquire() so the subsequent ownership validation cannot be reordered before the try-get, then re-read the original request to verify that it still owns the same msk. If either check fails, clear the clone pointer; otherwise its normal destructor balances the new reference. Mark the ownership-transfer store with WRITE_ONCE() to match the lockless reads. The following patch completes the clone fixup for MP_CAPABLE token ownership. Both patches carry the same Fixes tag and are required for stable backports.
