In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved: nvmet: fix use-after-free of the old registrant in nvmet_pr_preempt() nvmet_pr_preempt() handles a preempt sent by the reservation holder by changing the reservation type with nvmet_pr_update_reg_attr(), unless the reservation is of an All Registrants type. For the holder that helper does not modify the registrant in place: it puts a copy on the registrant list, points pr->holder to the copy and passes the old registrant to kfree_rcu(). If the reservation type changed, nvmet_pr_preempt() then hands &reg->hostid of that old registrant to nvmet_pr_resv_released(). Unless the reservation released notification is masked, that function takes subsys->lock and compares the host id against every controller of the subsystem. The caller only holds pr->pr_sem and is not in an RCU read-side critical section, so nothing keeps the old registrant alive while it is read. The result is a read of 16 freed bytes that decides which controllers get the notification. Found by code inspection. kfree_rcu() defers the free, so it usually happens after the read; when the pending free is forced to run before the read, KASAN reports the host id as freed memory. Pass the host id of the controller that sent the command instead. The registrant was looked up by that host id, and the controller outlives the request.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved: platform/x86: asus-wmi: fix use-after-free unregistering kbd_led led kbd_led_update_all() registers asus->kbd_led with devm_led_classdev_register() on the platform device, but kbd_led is embedded in struct asus_wmi, which asus_wmi_remove() frees at its end. The driver core calls .remove() before devres_release_all(), so the deferred devres release runs led_classdev_unregister() on memory that has already been freed. Whether that faults depends on whether the slab has been reused in between, which makes the crash on module unload intermittent and silently corrupts the led classdev state in the remaining runs. Unregister the led classdev explicitly in asus_wmi_led_exit(), after the led workqueue has been destroyed: kbd_led_work can then neither run nor be queued anymore, since asus_ref.asus is NULL too, so kbd_led_registered is stable and the classdev can be released while the memory embedding it is still alive. devm_led_classdev_unregister() also drops the devres entry, leaving nothing to run at unbind cleanup time; it warns when no devres entry exists, hence the kbd_led_registered check.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved: PM: EM: Fix use-after-free of perf domain in netlink doit handlers The doit handlers dropped em_pd_list_mutex before dereferencing the perf domain, so a concurrent device unregister could free it while the reply was being built. Encode the reply from em_perf_domain_for_id() callbacks, which run under the mutex, and allocate the skb outside of it, like the dumpit path already does. This issue was found by an in-house static analysis tool.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved: pps: generators: fix use-after-free when closing a removed device The cdev of a PPS generator is embedded in struct pps_gen_device, but nothing ties the lifetime of that structure to the cdev: pps_gen is freed by the release function of its device, and an open file holds a device reference only until pps_gen_cdev_release() drops it. When the generator is unregistered while /dev/pps-genN is open, that put_device() drops the last reference and frees pps_gen, and __fput() then calls cdev_put() on the freed cdev: BUG: KASAN: slab-use-after-free in cdev_put+0x53/0x60 Read of size 8 at addr ffff88801383e138 by task ppsgen64/149 Call Trace: cdev_put+0x53/0x60 __fput+0x745/0xad0 fput_close_sync+0xd9/0x1b0 __x64_sys_close+0x86/0xf0 ... Freed by task 149: kfree+0x25a/0x6d0 device_release+0xca/0x3c0 kobject_put+0x169/0x320 pps_gen_cdev_release+0x51/0x80 __fput+0x36a/0xad0 pps.c had the same bug, fixed in commit c79a39dc8d06 ("pps: Fix a use-after-free"). Fix it the usual way: embed the struct device in pps_gen_device and register both with cdev_device_add(). This makes the device the parent of the cdev, so the cdev holds a device reference until the last file is closed.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved: rapidio: mport_cdev: fix use-after-free in mport_mm_close() A use-after-free vulnerability was identified in mport_mm_close() in drivers/rapidio/devices/rio_mport_cdev.c, identical to the pattern previously addressed in dma_req_free(). This is observable from userspace when an application creates an mmap mapping via the RapidIO character device and subsequently unmaps it (or terminates, triggering exit_mmap()). During munmap, mport_mm_close() is invoked and drops the mapping reference via kref_put(). If kref_put() drops the last reference, mport_release_mapping() is called, which frees the underlying rio_mport_mapping structure. The subsequent mutex_unlock() then dereferences map->md to unlock buf_mutex, leading to a use-after-free: mport_mm_close() -> mutex_lock(&map->md->buf_mutex); ... -> kref_put(&map->ref, mport_release_mapping); /* map is freed */ -> mutex_unlock(&map->md->buf_mutex); /* UAF: map used */ Fix this by caching map->md before kref_put() and using the cached pointer for mutex unlocking, ensuring that freed memory is not accessed.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved: RDMA/irdma: avoid use-after-free in icrdma_remove icrdma_remove() dereferences iwdev after calling irdma_ib_unregister_device(): irdma_ib_unregister_device(iwdev) -> ib_unregister_device(&iwdev->ibdev) -> __ib_unregister_device() -> ib_dealloc_device() irdma registers irdma_ib_dealloc_device() as the dealloc_driver callback in its ib_device_ops. The RDMA core explicitly documents ib_unregister_device() that when ops.dealloc_driver is used, ib_dev will be freed upon return from the function. The ib_device is embedded in struct irdma_device and iwdev itself was allocated by ib_alloc_device(irdma_device, ibdev). Consequently, once irdma_ib_unregister_device() returns, iwdev must no longer be dereferenced. However, icrdma_remove() currently accesses iwdev->rf afterwards when deinitializing interrupts, destroying ah_tbl_lock, and freeing rf. Although the final ib_device storage is released with kfree_rcu(), the object lifetime has already ended and callers must not rely on the RCU grace period to continue dereferencing iwdev. Save iwdev->rf before unregistering the RDMA device and use the saved pointer for the remaining cleanup. This issue was found by manual code inspection.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved: RDMA/uverbs: Fix DMABUF use-after-free during ufile cleanup The DMABUF release can race with ufile cleanup. When the cleanup holds hw_destroy_rwsem for write, uverbs_uobject_release() fails its trylock and leaves the uobject on the ufile list, but the dma_buf is freed as soon as the release returns. The cleanup then destroys the uobject and uses the freed dma_buf: BUG: KASAN: slab-use-after-free in uverbs_dmabuf_fd_destroy_uobj+0x46/0x200 Read of size 8 at addr ff11000109cf14b0 by task repro/435 Call Trace: uverbs_dmabuf_fd_destroy_uobj+0x46/0x200 destroy_hw_fd_uobject+0x3f/0x50 uverbs_destroy_uobject+0xc5/0x380 __uverbs_cleanup_ufile+0x1a8/0x260 uverbs_destroy_ufile_hw+0x54/0x160 ib_uverbs_close+0x34/0x110 Allocated by task 435: dma_buf_export+0x1b5/0x530 ib_uverbs_handler_UVERBS_METHOD_DMABUF_ALLOC+0x223/0x3f0 Freed by task 436: kfree+0x301/0x530 dentry_kill+0x14c/0x560 __fput+0x23a/0x4a0 rdma_user_mmap_entry_remove() dereferences the same pointer. Protect the stored dma_buf pointer with a mutex and clear it before release returns. Use a shared revoke helper so uobject destruction and mmap entry removal both skip a cleared pointer. Hold a temporary uobject reference across uverbs_uobject_release() and the pointer update. Use a separate mutex because uobject destruction can free the mmap entry before release finishes. Map and unmap use attachment->dmabuf directly, so they do not need to take the new mutex while holding the reservation lock.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved: sched_ext: Fix use-after-free of a local reenq node left on an inactive cpu A local DSQ reenq is queued on the rq through a per-sched node and run from deferred work. When the reenq is requested from dispatch, the work is a balance callback queued once dispatch is done. A cpu going down installs balance push early in its teardown, and queue_balance_callback() refuses new callbacks from then on. ops.dispatch() keeps running on that cpu until the rq goes offline after an RCU grace period, so a reenq it requests in that window may never run. The IMMED handling in dispatch_one() requests one the same way. A reenq requested from elsewhere for a cpu that is already offline goes through irq_work_queue_on(), which warns, and its work doesn't run until the cpu comes back. Either way the node stays on the rq's list. When the scheduler is freed, scx_sched_free_rcu_work() warns and frees the pcpu with the node still linked, and the list is walked again once the cpu comes back. An inactive cpu's local DSQ holds only tasks that are bound to it or are being moved off, so the reenq is pointless. Ignore reenqs of an inactive cpu's local DSQ. The test is lockless. The hotplug thread of a cpu going down runs on that cpu, and it marks the cpu inactive before it installs balance push. A dispatch on the cpu runs to completion before that thread can run there, so a dispatch that saw the cpu active has queued its callback by then. Requests from outside dispatch run from the wakeup path or through irq_work, which balance push doesn't affect. The grace period after the cpu goes inactive waits for any requester that saw it active, so that irq_work is queued while the cpu is online.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved: smb: client: fix use-after-free in cifs_ses_add_channel() The error path of cifs_ses_add_channel() calls cifs_put_tcp_session() before cifs_chan_clear_need_reconnect(). The latter reaches cifs_ses_get_chan_index(), which dereferences server->terminate; if the put was the final reference, TCP_Server_Info is already freed and this is a use-after-free. Same put-then-use pattern as the recently fixed sibling in commit 717e0a25036b ("cifs: Fix server use-after-free in cifs_chan_skip_or_disable()"). Move the put last, but do not read chan->server after dropping chan_lock: chan points into ses->chans[], and once chan_count is decremented a concurrent add_channel can reuse the slot and overwrite the pointer, so the put would act on the new channel's server. Cache the pointer under chan_lock, clear the reconnect bit and decrement chan_count while still holding the reference, and release it after the unlock. This issue was discovered by Tencent CodeBuddy Security.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved: smb: client: fix use-after-free infoleak via the readdir resume name CIFSFindNext() copies the resume name that cifs_save_resume_key() recorded from the last entry of the previous response into its request; psrch_inf->presume_name points into the response buffer that entry came from, and nothing ever clears it. find_cifs_entry() records a new name only from a response with a usable last entry, and cifs_readdir() only from an entry it walks to, so a response that carries no entries and leaves last_entry NULL, because CIFSFindFirst() or CIFSFindNext() rejected LastNameOffset, refreshes neither and presume_name keeps pointing into the previous response. That buffer has already been released: by CIFSFindNext() before it installs the new response, or by find_cifs_entry() when it rewinds the search, which does not drop the name either and can then fail in initiate_cifs_search() before a new response replaces it. The next CIFSFindNext() then copies up to PATH_MAX - 1 bytes of the resume name out of the released buffer into its request and sends them to the server: a use-after-free read that leaks kernel memory to a malicious or compromised server, which can provoke it with a single FindNext response that carries no entries and a LastNameOffset above CIFSMaxBufSize, which is all the existing check rejects. With KASAN enabled, a server that answers a listing that way gives: CIFS: VFS: ignoring corrupt resume name ================================================================== BUG: KASAN: slab-use-after-free in CIFSFindNext+0x8ca/0x14c0 Read of size 4080 at addr ffff88807c823f98 by task ls/83 CPU: 0 UID: 0 PID: 83 Comm: ls Tainted: G B 7.3.0-rc4-00457-gf14572c203d5 #69 PREEMPT(lazy) Tainted: [B]=BAD_PAGE Call Trace: <TASK> kasan_report+0xdf/0x1a0 kasan_check_range+0x10f/0x1e0 __asan_memcpy+0x23/0x60 CIFSFindNext+0x8ca/0x14c0 cifs_readdir+0xf51/0x29c0 iterate_dir+0x1c0/0x570 __x64_sys_getdents64+0x133/0x270 do_syscall_64+0x109/0x5d0 entry_SYSCALL_64_after_hwframe+0x77/0x7f </TASK> Allocated by task 83 on cpu 1 at 13.497119s: cifs_buf_get+0x36/0x90 smb_init+0x4f/0x110 CIFSFindNext+0xf7/0x14c0 cifs_readdir+0xf51/0x29c0 Freed by task 83 on cpu 0 at 13.584018s: cifs_buf_release+0x41/0x80 CIFSFindNext+0xfce/0x14c0 cifs_readdir+0xf51/0x29c0 The buggy address is located 16280 bytes inside of freed 16588-byte region [ffff88807c820000, ffff88807c8240cc) ================================================================== The same memcpy() first reads past the end of that object while it is still live, a slab-out-of-bounds read that the following patches bound; that is the taint the report above carries. SMB1 is not negotiated by default; reaching this code requires an explicit vers=1.0 mount. Clear presume_name and resume_name_len whenever a new response is installed and when the rewind path releases the search buffer, so that the name never outlives the buffer it points into, and reset resume_key with them, since it was taken from the same entry and would otherwise be sent with an empty name. A response without a usable last entry then continues the search with an empty resume name rather than a stale one; CIFSFindNext() skips the copy of a zero-length name so that it never runs on the NULL pointer. The next patch in the series leaves last_entry NULL for a response that carries no entries, and bounds LastNameOffset against the received response rather than against CIFSMaxBufSize. Responses that are given a last entry today then take the path fixed here, so that patch must not be applied without this one.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved: spmi: Fix potential use-after-free by grabbing of_node reference As noticed by Sashiko during a review run of an unrelated patch, in of_spmi_register_devices(), for_each_available_child_of_node() is used to loop through children, and to also assign a node to a newly created SPMI child device. Problem is that the refcount is dropped at every iteration so, in the specific case of DT overlays, a use-after-free may occur when an overlay is dynamically unloaded! To resolve this, increase the of_node refcount when assigning (in function of_spmi_register_devices) and release the reference in spmi_device_remove().

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved: SUNRPC: fix netns use-after-free in write_gssp() While fuzzing with a customized syzkaller, I hit a refcount warning in xprt_alloc(), reached from a write to /proc/net/rpc/use-gss-proxy: refcount_t: addition on 0; use-after-free. WARNING: lib/refcount.c:25 at refcount_warn_saturate+0xf8/0x120 CPU: 0 PID: 10404 Comm: syz.0.17 Not tainted 7.3.0-rc1-00096-gcfebfd3db73d Call Trace: <TASK> xprt_alloc+0x83f/0x9d0 xs_setup_xprt+0xaf/0x3c0 xs_setup_local+0x47/0x7f0 xprt_create_transport+0x16c/0x730 rpc_create+0x38e/0x7f0 gssp_rpc_create+0xe2/0x180 set_gssp_clnt+0xba/0x1b0 write_gssp+0x200/0x310 proc_reg_write+0x240/0x330 vfs_write+0x2aa/0x1050 ksys_write+0x12a/0x250 do_syscall_64+0x117/0x750 entry_SYSCALL_64_after_hwframe+0x77/0x7f </TASK> create_use_gss_proxy_proc_entry() stores the struct net pointer as the proc entry's private data without taking a reference on it, and an open file descriptor does not pin the namespace either, as procfs only pins the proc_dir_entry. write_gssp() reads that pointer back with pde_data() and hands it to set_gssp_clnt(), which reaches xprt_init(): xprt->xprt_net = get_net_track(net, &xprt->ns_tracker, GFP_KERNEL); get_net_track() -> get_net() -> refcount_inc() is unconditional, so rpc_create() assumes its caller holds a reference on args.net. write_gssp() does not. Dropping the last ns.count reference does not make the file go away. __put_net() only queues cleanup_net() on a workqueue, and the remove_proc_entry() that fences off further writes runs from the rpcsec_gss pernet .exit method, that is, from inside cleanup_net(). A write landing between those two points increments a refcount that is already zero. cleanup_net() does not re-read ns.count, so the namespace is freed anyway and the rpc_xprt -- along with the AF_LOCAL socket opened for it -- is left pointing at freed memory. The resurrected count is visible to the rest of that teardown too: with CONFIG_IPV6_MROUTE the same cleanup_net() worker then trips !mr_can_free_table() in ip6mr_free_table(), which tests check_net() on the namespace it is freeing. It reduces to opening /proc/net/rpc/use-gss-proxy inside a new network namespace, calling setns() back to the original one to drop the last reference, and then writing "1" to the still-open descriptor. Take the reference in write_gssp() itself and refuse the write when the namespace is already gone. This is what procfs does for every other /proc/net file: get_proc_net() is maybe_get_net(PDE_NET(PDE(inode))) and seq_open_net() returns -ENXIO when it fails. PDE_NET() cannot be reused here because the parent directory /proc/net/rpc carries no namespace pointer. Adding a .pre_exit to rpcsec_gss_net_ops so the entry is removed earlier would only narrow the window, since pre_exit also runs from cleanup_net(). Live namespaces are unaffected: a write still returns the error from set_gssp_clnt(), a write of "2" still returns -EINVAL, and reads are untouched.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved: wifi: b43: fix use-after-free in b43_bcma_remove() b43_one_core_detach() frees the struct b43_wldev it is given the bus device of. b43_bcma_remove() then reads wldev->dev again to free the bus device, which is a read of freed memory. b43_ssb_remove() does not have the problem: it takes a copy of wldev->dev at the start. Do the same here.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved: cgroup: serialize migrations of newly forked processes With favordynmods enabled, a cgroup.procs migration takes the target threadgroup's cgroup_threadgroup_rwsem for writing. A process fork holds the forking threadgroup's semaphore for reading. These are different semaphores when fork creates a new process. copy_process() publishes the child's PID before cgroup_post_fork() links the child to its css_set. A writer can find the child in that interval, take its uncontended semaphore, and migrate it while child->cgroups still points to init_css_set and child->cg_list is empty. Migration links the node into init_css_set.mg_tasks. cgroup_post_fork() then adds the same node to the intended css_set as though it were unlinked, corrupting both task lists and their css_set ownership. This regresses the fork/migration race fixed by commit b12b533fa523 ("cgroups: add lock for child->cgroups in cgroup_post_fork()") and restored again in 2012 after the lock had been removed. The old task_lock protection was later superseded by global css_set and cgroup threadgroup locking. The change identified by the Fixes tag narrowed only the migration side back to a per-threadgroup lock, recreating the different-process exclusion failure. Take the new threadgroup's semaphore for reading before the child becomes visible and hold it through cgroup_post_fork(). Use a nested lock subclass because fork already holds the parent's semaphore. CLONE_THREAD children share the parent's signal_struct and remain covered by the existing lock. Migrations of unrelated, fully initialized threadgroups remain concurrent. An AI coding assistant was used to identify and reproduce the regression and to develop and test this fix.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved: ksmbd: verify transform SessionId matches the decrypted header When an encrypted request comes in, the decryption key is picked by the SessionId in the transform header, but the request is then authorized under whatever session the decrypted inner header names. Nothing ever compares the two, so on a connection with more than one session a client can get a request decrypted with one session's key and run it as another session. Encrypted requests are exempt from signing too, so a valid AEAD tag is the only proof of session identity, and it is checked against the wrong session. MS-SMB2 says the server must check that the transform SessionId matches the one in the decrypted SMB2 header and treat a mismatch as a protocol error. Add that check in __handle_ksmbd_work() after decryption, before dispatching: the message has to be at least one fixed SMB2 header, the first operation must not set SMB2_FLAGS_RELATED_OPERATIONS and its SessionId must match the transform SessionId, and every following non-related operation in a compound chain must carry the same SessionId. NextCommand offsets must be 8-byte aligned and stay inside the message; the bounds check is done by subtraction so it cannot wrap. When the decrypted payload is a compression transform, the existing decompression step runs first and the decompressed SMB2 message is checked instead, since a compression transform header carries no SessionId.

desc: In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved: ksmbd: validate security descriptor offsets before pointer arithmetic parse_sec_desc() constructs SID and DACL pointers by adding untrusted 32-bit offsets to the security descriptor before checking their bounds. The existing checks reject offsets into the descriptor header, but do not reject offsets beyond the descriptor's length. On a 32-bit kernel, a large offset can wrap the pointer before the descriptor. The end-only checks in parse_sid() and parse_dacl() can then accept it, allowing an authenticated SMB2 SET_INFO request to access memory outside the security descriptor and fault the kernel. Check each nonzero offset against acl_len before constructing its pointer. Initialize the optional owner and group SID pointers to NULL so an omitted SID remains absent when parsing the DACL.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved: ksmbd: validate AppInstanceId takeover target AppInstanceId lookup currently selects the first open with the matching identifier. CREATE for an unrelated share or path can therefore force-close another session's open before authorization of the new target. Matching only the base path also conflates alternate data streams with the unnamed stream. MS-SMB2 requires the old open to match the share and path, belong to a different ClientGuid, and be closed only when the requester has GENERIC_READ access. Search all opens with the ID and match share, resolved path, stream, and the current connection's client GUID. Retain a share configuration reference in ksmbd_file and reuse its name instead of allocating a name for every open. This keeps matching safe during tree connection teardown and preserves name-based matching across configuration updates. Refresh the share reference on durable reconnect and restore the old reference if reopening fails. Serialize connection and share comparisons with durable disconnect/reconnect, and recheck the target before closing it. Keep the original ClientGuid for durable replay and lease checks. Check AppInstanceVersion before querying access, even when GENERIC_READ is absent, and before disconnected delete-on-close cleanup. Rejected CREATE must leave other durable opens untouched. Calculate maximal access on the matched open's referenced path so a rename cannot substitute another file's authorization. Require read access with the effective VFS credentials as well as the NT DACL before takeover. Access denial only skips takeover and leaves CREATE to its normal access checks. Restore filesystem credentials before returning a takeover error. Handle takeover before checking FILE_CREATE collisions, and re-resolve the path after closing the old open. This lets delete-on-close remove the old file before a new one is created. Include SYNCHRONIZE in the baseline maximal-access mask so read-only files report GENERIC_READ correctly.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved: ksmbd: prevent stale data from being written by SMB2 WRITE requests Initialize the compatibility byte in request buffers without zeroing the entire allocation. Keep the one-byte compatibility exception for SMB2 messages so valid zero-length WRITE requests remain compatible, and validate the data range in the WRITE handlers against the current compound request before accessing it. This prevents stale request-buffer data from being written to files or sent to IPC pipes.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved: ksmbd: prevent share root removal through empty paths A FileLinkInformation request can supply "/" as the new link name. smb2_get_name() strips the trailing slash and passes an empty string to ksmbd_vfs_kern_path_start_removing(). ksmbd_vfs_path_lookup() resolves an empty pathname as the configured share path, without LOOKUP_BENEATH. With ReplaceIfExists set, smb2_create_link() can therefore remove the share root from its parent before link creation fails. An authenticated client with a writable share and DELETE access to a file can trigger this if the share root is empty and the mapped user has write and search permission on its parent directory. Return -EINVAL for empty pathnames when for_remove is set, before resolving the share path or acquiring removal resources. Ordinary lookups continue to accept empty pathnames for opening the share root.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved: ksmbd: prevent session binding in compound requests A failed multichannel binding can retain its target session on the work item so that the error response can be signed. Subsequent compound commands can then use that session together with a tree connection left over from an earlier command. Limit binding SESSION_SETUP requests to standalone messages during message validation, before smb2_sess_setup() can replace work->sess. Check both NextCommand and the current request offset to cover binding in the first, middle and last positions of a compound. The existing validation error path returns STATUS_INVALID_PARAMETER and stops processing the remaining commands. This intentionally limits support for compounded binding. It is not a protocol requirement that binding be standalone. Standalone binding and non-binding compounds retain their existing behavior, without changing session, tree or response encryption handling.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved: ksmbd: preserve unreadable named streams on open A write-only client can open an existing named stream with FILE_OPEN_IF without permission to read the underlying file. The case-insensitive lookup finds the xattr name, but querying its value length then fails with -EACCES. smb2_set_stream_name_xattr() treats every negative result as a missing stream and replaces the existing xattr with an empty value. A failed xattr list is not proof that the stream is absent either: for example, -ENOMEM can lead to the same empty replacement. Preserve listing errors and create a stream only for -ENOENT or -ENODATA. The latter can occur if the xattr is removed between listing its name and querying its value. Return other lookup errors without changing the stream. A write-only FILE_OPEN now reports access denied instead of name not found. FILE_OVERWRITE_IF and FILE_SUPERSEDE on an unreadable stream also fail instead of appearing to replace it. Stream writes and EOF changes already need to read the old value, so such handles cannot update the stream after opening either.

desc: In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved: ksmbd: ignore network devices of other namespaces With no interface list configured, ksmbd binds every interface that comes up. ksmbd_netdev_event() does not look at the device's namespace, and create_socket() opens the listener in the namespace of the task raising NETDEV_UP. A container with its own address on a bridge brings up its interface and finds port 445 in its namespace already taken by ksmbd, so an SMB server running inside the container fails with "Address already in use". Interfaces are also matched by name only, so a container's eth0 going down would stop the listener on the host's eth0. Only handle netdev events for devices in init_net.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved: ksmbd: fix session reference leak on compounded SESSION_SETUP A compound request can place SESSION_SETUP after another command. That earlier command leaves a reference to its session in work->sess. smb2_sess_setup() then overwrites work->sess with the session it looks up or creates, and the dispatcher later puts work->sess only once. The inherited reference is never dropped. That leaks the session, together with its setup connection and socket, and every repeat of the compound leaks another. unreferenced object (size 512): __kmalloc_cache_noprof+0x32c/0x3a0 ksmbd_smb2_session_create+0xf6/0x9c0 [ksmbd] smb2_sess_setup+0xda4/0x6280 [ksmbd] handle_ksmbd_work+0x88c/0x1cb0 [ksmbd] Save the inherited session on entry. After the request has been processed, release it once, but only when smb2_sess_setup() has replaced work->sess with its own session or cleared it. Do this after ksmbd_conn_unlock() so the put does not run under srv_mutex. An error path may instead leave the inherited session in work->sess. Keep it there, so the dispatcher still puts it and the error response is still signed or encrypted with it as before.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved: ksmbd: fix parent dentry lifetime in directory enumeration ksmbd_populate_dot_dotdot_entries() builds the ".." entry from the open directory's d_parent and passes that pointer to ksmbd_vfs_fill_dentry_attrs() without taking a reference. That pointer is only valid while the directory stays under this parent. If a concurrent rename moves the directory elsewhere, the old parent loses its last reference; a following rmdir then turns it into a negative dentry with d_inode cleared, and after the RCU grace period the dentry itself is freed. The worker still holds the raw pointer and dereferences d_inode through vfs_getattr() and vfs_getxattr(). A remote SMB client, authenticated or guest, triggers this by listing a directory while that directory is moved under a new parent and the old parent is deleted. It can be done by the client itself with write access or by other concurrent writers, triggering null-ptr-deref and slab-use-after-free on a KASAN build. KASAN: null-ptr-deref in range [0x0000000000000000-0x0000000000000007] Workqueue: ksmbd-io handle_ksmbd_work RIP: 0010:xattr_permission+0x9d/0x160 Call Trace: vfs_getxattr+0x9c/0x1b0 ksmbd_vfs_getxattr+0x82/0x100 ksmbd_vfs_get_dos_attrib_xattr+0x7f/0x130 ksmbd_vfs_fill_dentry_attrs+0x435/0x650 ksmbd_populate_dot_dotdot_entries+0x25e/0x630 smb2_query_dir+0xcf9/0x1a20 handle_ksmbd_work+0x5f1/0x1c80 process_one_work+0x90b/0x19d0 Fix by using the dentry reference counting APIs: take the parent with dget_parent(), take a matching dget() on ".", and dput() the dentry once ksmbd_vfs_fill_dentry_attrs() has returned or the pattern does not match.

desc: In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved: ksmbd: fix OOB read and cross-share confusion in ksmbd_validate_name_reconnect() ksmbd_validate_name_reconnect() indexes ab_pathname[share->path_sz + 1] without checking that the path is longer than share->path_sz + 1 (d_path() fills the buffer from the end). A durable fp is not bound to its original share, so a client can preserve a file from a short-path share and reconnect it on a long-path share, making strcmp() read past the PATH_MAX buffer - with a long enough share path this oopses the kernel, and on a mapped page it also gives a byte-equality oracle on adjacent heap (the reconnect succeeds exactly when the out-of-bounds string equals the requested name). A same-share variant with the durable fp at the share root reads 1 byte past the buffer (strlen(ab_pathname) == share->path_sz). Check before comparing: the path must be longer than share->path_sz, it must start with share->path, and the next character must be '/'. The share root itself is accepted only for an empty name.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved: ksmbd: deny access for an empty DACL instead of granting the request smb_check_perm_dacl() returns the access mask it computes to the SMB2 CREATE handler, which uses it as the granted access for the open. For a security descriptor whose DACL is present but contains no ACEs, the function is supposed to deny access: an empty (non-NULL) DACL grants no access to anyone except the object owner's implicit READ_CONTROL and WRITE_DAC (MS-DTYP 2.4.5). The empty-DACL branch only denies when both - the DACL has no trailing bytes (pdacl_size == sizeof(struct smb_acl)), and - the request contains bits beyond READ_CONTROL / WRITE_DAC. In every other case it takes the shared "goto err_out" with rc still 0, which returns success without modifying *pdaccess, so the caller grants the full requested access. Three problems follow: - The READ_CONTROL / WRITE_DAC carve-out models the owner's implicit rights, but the check runs before is_owner is computed, so those rights are handed to *every* caller, not just the owner. For READ_CONTROL the SMB2 CREATE path does not fall back to inode_permission(), so any user can read the security descriptor of an object whose empty DACL is meant to deny them. - A request of exactly READ_CONTROL and/or WRITE_DAC is granted to any caller. WRITE_DAC lets the handle rewrite the DACL. - A DACL that declares zero ACEs but carries trailing bytes (pdacl_size > sizeof(struct smb_acl)) skips the deny entirely and is granted whatever was requested. On shares where the NT ACL is the authoritative access control -- e.g. "force user" shares, where every client maps to one POSIX identity so POSIX cannot distinguish users -- this is an access-control bypass. Compute is_owner before the empty-DACL branch and deny access from an empty DACL unless the caller is the owner requesting no more than READ_CONTROL / WRITE_DAC.

desc: In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved: backlight: qcom-wled: Fix NULL pointer dereference in wled_remove() wled_probe() doesn't set the driver data for the platform device. As a result, platform_get_drvdata() in wled_remove() will return NULL, and the first dereference of it crashes on unbind. Set the platform device driver data in wled_probe().

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved: Drivers: hv: vmbus: Bounds check the shared ring buffer indices In a CoCo VM the host is untrusted. Since the VMBus ring buffer read and write indices live in shared memory, the guest has to treat both as potentially malicious. hv_ringbuffer_write() copies into the ring at write_index with no bounds checking, so the host can make the guest write packet data at any offset up to 4 GiB past the start of the ring buffer. read_index matters too: the available space derived from both indices is the only bound on how much is copied, and an out-of-range index can make it far larger than the ring. The fix is to validate both indices before use and to use the validated snapshot instead of re-accessing. For invalid indices, hv_ringbuffer_write() logs and returns -EIO. One re-read of write_index is left unchecked in this patch: hv_get_ring_bufferindices() fetches it again for the prev_indices trailer. The value is only returned to the host and is not used as an offset or length for indexing. Since this is not a security issue, it is addressed later in the series. Open-coding the bytes available arithmetic keeps the fix free of prerequisites; a later patch refactors it into a helper function.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved: driver core: take parent lock on deferred probe USB interfaces should be probed with the parent USB device lock held, but this is not honoured when probe is deferred. Add a new bus_probe_device_deferred() helper to handle deferred probe where the parent device lock is not held.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved: net/sched: cls_flower: avoid stale mask references after delete Flower releases a mask reference when a filter is removed from the classifier. The filter object can remain alive while dump, walk, or hardware reoffload paths hold a reference to it. Those paths can then dereference f->mask after the mask has already been released. Keep the mask reference until the filter reference count reaches zero. Release the mask synchronously from the final __fl_put() while the caller still holds the tcf_proto reference, and leave the existing RCU work to free the mask. This keeps the mask available to every reader that still holds the filter. The filter is still removed from the classifier indexes immediately. Therefore, a deleted filter can temporarily retain an otherwise empty mask; fl_delete() uses the handle IDR, rather than the mask list, to determine whether the classifier has become empty. Failed mask assignment can leave fnew->mask as an error or borrowed pointer without an owned mask reference. Clear it before the common failure path so the final put cannot release an unowned reference. This fix does not add fields, snapshots, or per-filter memory.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved: thunderbolt: Do not RPM complete unrelated subtrees on unplug When a Thunderbolt device is unplugged, that switch and every switch subsequent to it on the bus device list is `complete()`d, not just its child devices. In the case of multiple domains, it may cause, eg, an attempt to `complete()` the uninitialized domain 1 root switch RPM completion on unplug of a switch from domain 0 (though ordering is not guaranteed numerically sorted). I initially noticed this issue on a Dell XPS9720 when the system would seem to sporadically not wake after unplugging a Thunderbolt dock. I tried multiple kernel versions including v7.2.7 and v7.3-rc4 to see if that resolved the issue, but the issue persisted. Eventually I found that I could consistently generate a kernel Oops reporting a page fault at 0xffff_ffff_ffff_fff8 on unplug from one side of the laptop and went bug hunting. I became suspicious of the `bus_for_each_dev()` walk that I ultimately ended up changing. To confirm this issue, I did an eBPF trace of `bus_for_each_dev()`, `complete_rpm()`, and `complete()` while unplugging in a variety of situations and found that an unplug from domain 0 tries to `complete_rpm()` domain 1's switch, whose RPM completion is not initialized and thus is holding a null wait-list pointer, triggering the page fault. Here are the key sections of that eBPF trace. Note that HEAD denotes the completion's own wait-list HEAD: ``` RESCAN_ENTER domain=0 COMPLETE rescan_domain=0 target=0-1 target_domain=0 route=0x1 parent=0-0 unplugged=1 COMPLETION done=0 head=HEAD next=HEAD prev=HEAD BUS_WALK domain=0 start=0-1 callback=complete_rpm CALLBACK_ENTER rescan_domain=0 dev=1-0 parent=domain1 is_switch=1 COMPLETE rescan_domain=0 target=1-0 target_domain=1 route=0x0 parent=domain1 unplugged=0 COMPLETION done=0 head=HEAD next=0 prev=0 complete+5 complete_rpm+43 bus_for_each_dev+133 icm_free_unplugged_children+250 icm_rescan_work+42 ``` This patch gates the `complete()` on an additional condition - that the Thunderbolt domain matches the domain of the device that was unplugged. I only have a single system with multiple Thunderbolt domains - the Dell XPS9720. I am consistently able to reproduce the Oops on that system. Since running with this patch, I have not seen the Oops reoccur. I have also tested it on a Thinkpad X1-Gen12, and that system boots and runs well with it, but it only has a single Thunderbolt domain, so it does not exercise the multi-domain failure case.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved: smb: client: fix early procfs exposure race Currently, init_cifs() calls cifs_proc_init() near the beginning of the function, before INIT_LIST_HEAD, leading to a momentarily uninitialized, but exposed, procfs. If a userspace process reads this empty procfs, iterating over a zeroed list_head leads to a NULL pointer dereference and a kernel oops/panic. For example, if a delay is added between cifs_proc_init() and INIT_LIST_HEAD, and a userspace process is polling /proc/fs/cifs/DebugData, the following oops occurs: BUG: kernel NULL pointer dereference, address: 0000000000000608 Oops: Oops: 0000 [#1] SMP PTI CPU: 0 UID: 0 PID: 3477 Comm: cat Not tainted 7.3.0-02212-g4df4d2a577db-dirty #6 PREEMPT(lazy) RIP: 0010:cifs_debug_data_proc_show+0x103/0xd80 [cifs] Call Trace: <TASK> ? seq_read_iter+0x86/0x400 ? seq_read_iter+0x86/0x400 seq_read_iter+0x183/0x400 proc_reg_read_iter+0x62/0x90 copy_splice_read+0x215/0x310 splice_file_to_pipe+0xec/0x1c0 do_splice+0x4b8/0x780 __se_sys_splice+0x18f/0x250 do_syscall_64+0x109/0x330 entry_SYSCALL_64_after_hwframe+0x77/0x7f </TASK> Fix this by moving cifs_proc_init() down in init_cifs(), ensuring it runs only after all internal lists, locks, counters, and workqueues are fully ready, but before registering the filesystem. Update the error cleanup ladder and exit_cifs() to maintain proper LIFO order.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved: smb: client: do not pass a NULL buf to is_oplock_break() receive_encrypted_read() sets *num_mids = 1 and never writes the caller's bufs[]. Offload returns -1 with *num_mids = 0, so the demultiplex thread skips the frame. The inline decrypt path returns 0 even when smb2_find_mid() fails. cifs_demultiplex_thread() then treats mids[i] == NULL as an oplock break and calls is_oplock_break(bufs[i], server) with bufs[i] still NULL. smb2_is_valid_oplock_break() reads hdr.Command at offset 12 and oopses. A large encrypted READ whose MessageId does not match is enough to panic cifsd. Oops: general protection fault, probably for non-canonical address 0xdffffc0000000001: 0000 [#1] SMP KASAN PTI KASAN: null-ptr-deref in range [0x0000000000000008-0x000000000000000f] CPU: 0 PID: 100 Comm: cifsd RIP: smb2_is_valid_oplock_break+0xc8/0x2270 [cifs] cifs_demultiplex_thread Kernel panic - not syncing: Fatal exception Return -1 when inline decrypt finds no mid, and skip is_oplock_break() plus the unknown-frame dump when bufs[i] is NULL. receive_encrypted_standard() already assigns bufs[*num_mids].

desc: In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved: ocfs2: pin owning modules for open debugfs files The OCFS2 debugfs file operation tables do not set owner. The full debugfs proxy obtains real_fops with fops_get() at open and keeps it until final release. Without an owner, this does not acquire a reference to the module containing the table and its callbacks. Removing the debugfs entries does not drain retained open files. An open connected_nodes file can therefore outlive ocfs2_nodemanager and make full_proxy_release() read real_fops->release from freed module memory. Heming also reproduced the issue with fs_state and asked for the other OCFS2 debugfs operation tables to be checked. Set owner to THIS_MODULE in all eleven explicit debugfs operation tables: five in ocfs2_nodemanager, four in ocfs2_dlm, and two in ocfs2. The existing debugfs get/put pair then holds the appropriate module until final release. Leave the open, read and release callbacks unchanged. The blockcheck table already sets owner through DEFINE_DEBUGFS_ATTRIBUTE(), so it needs no change. The original controlled test used an unloadable OCFS2 module and case-local probe filters without changing the candidate open, unload or release logic. Closing a retained connected_nodes file after normal unload produced: BUG: unable to handle page fault for address: fffffbfff804cfef Oops: Oops: 0000 [#1] SMP KASAN NOPTI RIP: 0010:full_proxy_release+0xbf/0x190 Call Trace: <TASK> __fput+0x39a/0xa60 fput_close_sync+0xff/0x200 __x64_sys_close+0x8c/0xf0 do_syscall_64+0x114/0x620 entry_SYSCALL_64_after_hwframe+0x77/0x7f </TASK> Modules linked in: [last unloaded: ocfs2_nodemanager]

desc: In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved: ocfs2: drain quorum work before removing the cluster The configured cluster must remain available until an in-flight quorum decision has finished using its fencing method. o2quo_make_decision() drops qs_lock before calling o2quo_fence_self(), which marks heartbeat regions for unclean stop and then reads o2nm_single_cluster->cl_fence_method. Cluster removal clears the singleton without waiting for this independent system-workqueue item. When a failed-quorum decision overlaps removal of the heartbeat regions, nodes and cluster through configfs, the worker can be preempted after marking the regions and resume after the singleton has been cleared: Quorum worker Configfs removal select fence; drop qs_lock o2hb_stop_all_regions() remove regions; join heartbeat threads remove nodes; stop o2net clear singleton; release cluster read cl_fence_method The resumed read dereferences NULL instead of applying the configured fencing method. The heartbeat thread's dependency protects the local node only until the thread exits, and draining o2net does not wait for qs_work. Add o2quo_flush_work() to drain pending or running quorum decisions before clearing the singleton in o2nm_cluster_group_drop_item(). By this point the heartbeat regions and nodes have been removed, so their work publishers are stopped. The worker can finish while the cluster and its configured fencing method remain available. It does not acquire the configfs mutex held by the removal path. Keep o2quo_exit() as the counterpart of o2quo_init() for module teardown and initialization failure, and have it call the same drain helper. Cluster removal uses only the explicitly named drain operation. KASAN report as below: Oops: general protection fault, probably for non-canonical address 0xdffffc000000011b: 0000 [#1] SMP KASAN NOPTI KASAN: null-ptr-deref in range [0x00000000000008d8-0x00000000000008df] CPU: 0 UID: 0 PID: 72 Comm: kworker/0:2 Not tainted 7.3.0-rc4-next-20260921-pmb-ocfs2-functional-v1+ #1 PREEMPT(lazy) Hardware name: QEMU Ubuntu 24.04 PC v2 (i440FX + PIIX, arch_caps fix, 1996), BIOS 1.16.3-debian-1.16.3-2 04/01/2014 Workqueue: events o2quo_make_decision RIP: 0010:o2quo_fence_self+0x65/0x200 Register dump omitted. desc: In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved: ocfs2/dlm: drain join handlers before releasing module text The code for a registered DLM handler must remain resident until its last invocation finishes. dlm_unregister_net_handlers() only removes dlm_join_handlers from the o2net registry. o2net_handler_get() takes a kref on the wrapper, but that reference does not pin ocfs2_dlm text. o2net_process_message() calls nh_func after dropping o2net_handler_lock. With CONFIG_OCFS2_FS_O2CB=m, ocfs2_dlm can be loaded independently of ocfs2_stack_o2cb while nodemanager continues handling messages from a configured, heartbeating peer. If no dependent module or module reference prevents normal unload, the following ordering is possible: Receive worker Module unload -------------- ------------- o2net_handler_get() take wrapper kref drop handler lock <preempted> dlm_exit() unregister handlers release DLM module text call saved nh_func in released module text Use o2net_unregister_and_flush_handler_list() in the shared DLM unregister helper. It first prevents new lookups, then waits for the ordered o2net workqueue to drain, including a concurrent destruction of that queue. The acquired invocation therefore finishes before dlm_exit() returns and the loader releases the callback code. The same helper covers partial registration and dlm_init() error unwind before module memory is released. Skip the drain when the private join-handler list is empty. Early dlm_init() failures can reach this helper before any handler has been published. Partial-registration failure also reaches it a second time after the first call has already unregistered and drained the list. Neither case needs to take o2net_wq_mutex or drain unrelated work. The list is changed only by serialized module init/exit paths; a nonempty list still uses the full unregister-and-flush helper. desc: In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved: nfsd: fix race between client_info_show() and free_client() client_info_show() renders /proc/fs/nfsd/clients/<id>/info and walks clp->cl_sessions under clp->cl_lock to print each session's slot counts. free_client() tears down the same list without taking cl_lock, and is the only unlocked mutator of cl_sessions. A reader can observe a client mid-teardown because get_nfsdfs_clp() pins the nfs4_client but not its sessions: free_client() frees every session before calling nfsd_client_rmdir(), so an in-flight seq_file reader can follow a list_del()'d node whose ->next now holds LIST_POISON1 and take a general protection fault: Oops: general protection fault, probably for non-canonical address 0xdead00000000014c CPU: 1 UID: 0 PID: 132488 Comm: cat RIP: 0010:client_info_show+0x2bf/0x3d0 RAX: dead000000000100 Call Trace: seq_read_iter+0x12a/0x4b0 seq_read+0xf1/0x130 vfs_read+0xbf/0x350 ksys_read+0x6f/0xf0 do_syscall_64+0x8b/0xcb0 entry_SYSCALL_64_after_hwframe+0x76/0x7e Kernel panic - not syncing: Fatal exception Detach cl_sessions onto a local reaplist under cl_lock, then free the sessions after dropping the lock. Removing entries from cl_sessions under cl_lock matches unhash_session(), and the detach-then-reap shape matches how __destroy_client() reaps cl_delegations. The sessions cannot be freed while cl_lock is held, since free_session() calls nfsd4_del_conns(), which re-acquires it.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved: net: usb: pegasus: do not advance rx_skb->data on dropped frames For the 0x8513 chip, read_bulk_callback() skips the 2-byte receive header by advancing pegasus->rx_skb->data in place. This is done before the pkt_len > PEGASUS_MTU check, and when that check drops the frame the good path resubmits the same skb with the advanced rx_skb->data as the transfer buffer, still PEGASUS_MTU bytes long. Every frame with an oversized length field therefore moves the receive buffer two more bytes towards the end of the skb data area. A device that keeps sending such frames makes the host controller write received data over skb_shared_info and past the end of the allocation, and the corrupted skb_shared_info is used when the skb is eventually freed. With an emulated device sending frames filled with 0x5a on a KASAN kernel: BUG: KASAN: slab-out-of-bounds in dummy_timer+0xade/0x3f00 [dummy_hcd] Write of size 1536 at addr ffff888105821202 by task swapper/1/0 ... Oops: general protection fault, probably for non-canonical address 0xeb4b474b4b4b4b4c: 0000 [#1] PREEMPT SMP KASAN NOPTI KASAN: maybe wild-memory-access in range [0x5a5a5a5a5a5a5a60-0x5a5a5a5a5a5a5a67] RIP: 0010:skb_release_data+0x36f/0x800 Only skip the header with skb_reserve() once the frame is going to be passed up, so the receive buffer always starts at the beginning of the skb data area. Unlike the old pointer adjustment, skb_reserve() also moves skb->tail, so the two header bytes now count against the buffer size: lower the length limit for the 0x8513 accordingly, otherwise a pkt_len of PEGASUS_MTU - 1 or PEGASUS_MTU would trip skb_over_panic(). Found by code review with LLM assistance and reproduced with an emulated USB device (raw-gadget + dummy_hcd).

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved: media: usbtv: fix null-pointer dereference on disconnect A null-pointer dereference can occur in usb_make_path() when called from usbtv_querycap() (and other ioctl handlers) during device disconnection. Oops: general protection fault, probably for non-canonical address 0xdffffc000000000a: 0000 [#1] SMP KASAN NOPTI KASAN: null-ptr-deref in range [0x0000000000000050-0x0000000000000057] RIP: 0010:usb_make_path include/linux/usb.h:985 [inline] RIP: 0010:usbtv_querycap+0x9c/0x100 drivers/media/usb/usbtv/usbtv-video.c:612 ... Call Trace: <TASK> v4l_querycap+0x236/0x470 drivers/media/v4l2-core/v4l2-ioctl.c:1106 __video_do_ioctl+0x8af/0xc70 drivers/media/v4l2-core/v4l2-ioctl.c:3133 video_usercopy+0x860/0x1430 drivers/media/v4l2-core/v4l2-ioctl.c:3475 v4l2_ioctl+0x18d/0x1e0 drivers/media/v4l2-core/v4l2-dev.c:366 vfs_ioctl fs/ioctl.c:51 [inline] __do_sys_ioctl fs/ioctl.c:597 [inline] __se_sys_ioctl+0xfc/0x170 fs/ioctl.c:583 do_syscall_x64 arch/x86/entry/syscall_64.c:63 [inline] do_syscall_64+0x174/0x580 arch/x86/entry/syscall_64.c:94 This happens due to a race condition between the USB device disconnect routine (usbtv_disconnect()) and V4L2 ioctls. When the device is disconnected, usbtv_disconnect() sets usbtv->udev = NULL without holding the usbtv->v4l2_lock mutex. Concurrently, an ioctl handler like usbtv_querycap() can be executing under the v4l2_lock and attempt to use usbtv->udev, leading to a crash. To fix this, move the usbtv->udev = NULL assignment into usbtv_video_free() and protect it with mutex_lock(&usbtv->v4l2_lock). This ensures that no non-queue ioctl handler can run concurrently with the pointer being nullified. If an ioctl is already running, the mutex will block the disconnect path until the ioctl finishes. If an ioctl is blocked waiting for the lock, it will acquire it after the disconnect routine releases it, but will then check video_is_registered() (which was cleared by vb2_video_unregister_device()) and safely return -ENODEV. Acquiring v4l2_lock after vb2_video_unregister_device() avoids reintroducing a historical deadlock issue, and usbtv_audio_free() remains safe as it is called before usbtv_video_free().

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved: ksmbd: serialize directory emptiness checks with readdir SMB2 QUERY_DIRECTORY holds fp->readdir_lock while it calls iterate_dir() on fp->filp. An SMB2 SET_INFO request with FILE_DISPOSITION_INFORMATION can resolve the same FileId and call ksmbd_vfs_empty_dir() on the same filp without that lock. iterate_dir()'s inode read lock permits concurrent readers and does not serialize per-file iterator state. ext4 stores its dx readdir cursor and fname RB tree in file->private_data. Concurrent reset or refill can therefore free a fname node while the other worker still traverses it or retains its RB-tree link, resulting in use-after-free accesses. An authenticated SMB client with list and delete rights on a directory in a writable KSMBD share backed by ext4 can trigger this when the directory takes the dx readdir path. The client overlaps an SMB2 QUERY_DIRECTORY request with an SMB2 SET_INFO request carrying FILE_DISPOSITION_INFORMATION on one live FileId. In one x86_64 SMP KASAN multi-shot guest using ksmbd-for-next at 171df27077fb, the unmodified kernel reported a cross-worker use-after-free before a panic. The first report's access and free stacks show the two request paths directly (trimmed): BUG: KASAN: slab-use-after-free in ext4_htree_store_dirent+0x488/0x550 Read of size 8 by task kworker/2:0/29 Workqueue: ksmbd-io handle_ksmbd_work Call Trace: ext4_htree_store_dirent+0x488/0x550 htree_dirblock_to_tree+0x535/0x990 ext4_htree_fill_tree+0x319/0xba0 ext4_readdir+0x175a/0x2f40 iterate_dir+0x1b6/0x630 smb2_query_dir+0x1003/0x1cc0 Freed by task 279: free_rb_tree_fname+0x67/0xc0 ext4_readdir+0x13a9/0x2f40 iterate_dir+0x1b6/0x630 ksmbd_vfs_empty_dir+0xa2/0x100 smb2_set_info+0x2ffa/0x45d0 Take fp->readdir_lock across the entire emptiness check. This places both iterators over that handle's filp in the same lock domain while preserving the disposition status handling. The exact code change completed a warning-free x86_64 KASAN bzImage build. Tracing three request pairs showed that the two iterate_dir() calls no longer overlapped and the expected statuses were preserved. A further 1,600 reproducer iterations completed with expected statuses and no KASAN report, Oops, or panic. The reproducer and complete guest configuration are available privately to maintainers on request.

desc: In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved: ceph: fail readdir when the MDS reply carries no dirfrag A ceph mount oopses in ceph_readdir() when the MDS answers a READDIR request with a reply whose extra blob is empty. parse_reply_info() skips reply blobs whose length is zero, so parse_reply_info_readdir() never runs, r_reply_info.dir_dir stays NULL, and the reply still parses as successful. ceph_mdsc_do_request() returns 0 and ceph_readdir() then reads rinfo->dir_dir->frag with no NULL check: /* extra */ ceph_decode_32_safe(&p, end, len, bad); if (len > 0) { ... err = parse_reply_info_extra(&p, p + len, req, features, s); ... } The oops on v7.3.0-rc4-00537-ga3ff15db6820, one getdents64(2) on the mount root after an ms_mode=legacy mount, trimmed: BUG: KASAN: null-ptr-deref in range [0x0000000000000000-0x0000000000000007] Oops: general protection fault, probably for non-canonical address 0xdffffc0000000000: 0000 [#1] SMP KASAN NOPTI CPU: 1 UID: 0 PID: 266 Comm: ls Tainted: G N 7.3.0-rc4-00537-ga3ff15db6820 #1 PREEMPT(lazy) RIP: 0010:ceph_readdir+0xbff/0x3ea0 Call Trace: <TASK> ? __pfx_ceph_readdir+0x10/0x10 wrap_directory_iterator+0xa2/0xe0 iterate_dir+0x1da/0x5d0 __x64_sys_getdents64+0x13b/0x2a0 do_syscall_64+0xdd/0x4a0 entry_SYSCALL_64_after_hwframe+0x77/0x7f </TASK> The unconditional frag read came in with 81c6aea5275ea ("ceph: handle frag mismatch between readdir request and reply"), so the bug is old. Treat a reply with no dirfrag as a protocol violation: warn once, drop the request and return -EIO, the same way ceph_readdir() already handles the two malformed-reply cases later in the function. Tested on v7.3.0-rc4-00537-ga3ff15db6820 (KASAN). Unpatched, the getdents64(2) above takes the machine down (oops=panic) on the first READDIR reply. With the patch it warns once and getdents64(2) returns -EIO, no oops, no hang. A conformant reply for an empty directory — dirfrag present, zero entries, FRAG_END|FRAG_COMPLETE — still lists "." and ".." and returns EOF on both kernels, so normal readdir behavior is unchanged. The oops is still present in v7.3-rc5 (72d3fcf802c45).

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved: blk-crypto: fix NULL deref and UAF in __blk_crypto_evict_key() Sashiko reported a possible NULL pointer dereference, triggered by the following flow: dm-inlinecrypt ctor # first use of the fallback ├─ blk_crypto_init_key() # succeeds, ctx->key.size != 0 ├─ blk_crypto_start_using_key() │ ├─ hw-wrapped key: -EOPNOTSUPP │ │ # profile never allocated (NULL) │ └─ raw key: fallback_start_using_mode() │ └─ blk_crypto_fallback_init() fails │ └─ kfree(profile) # not NULLed ├─ goto bad └─ inlinecrypt_dtr() # evicts whenever key.size is set └─ blk_crypto_evict_key() └─ blk_crypto_config_supported_natively() = false └─ blk_crypto_fallback_evict_key() └─ __blk_crypto_evict_key(blk_crypto_fallback_profile) └─ profile->num_slots # BOOM!!! This issue can be reproduced using the following commands: dd if=/dev/zero of=/tmp/backing bs=1M count=64 LOOP=$(losetup -f --show /tmp/backing) SZ=$(blockdev --getsz $LOOP) KEY=$(head -c 64 /dev/urandom | od -An -tx1 | tr -d ' \n') dmsetup create ic --table "0 $SZ inlinecrypt aes-xts-plain64 \ $KEY 0 $LOOP 0 1 keytype:hw-wrapped" And the following oops is triggered: ================================================================== blk-crypto: loop0: no support for wrapped keys Oops: general protection fault, probably for non-canonical address 0xdffffc000000000b: 0000 [#1] SMP KASAN PTI KASAN: null-ptr-deref in range [0x0000000000000058-0x000000000000005f] CPU: 5 UID: 0 PID: 901 Comm: dmsetup 7.3.0-rc3 #1 PREEMPT(lazy) RIP: 0010:__blk_crypto_evict_key+0x2e/0x3b0 Call Trace: blk_crypto_evict_key+0x24c/0x320 inlinecrypt_dtr+0xf6/0x160 inlinecrypt_ctr+0x2d3/0xbd0 dm_table_add_target+0x661/0xf40 table_load+0x1c4/0x490 ctl_ioctl+0x32f/0x5f0 dm_ctl_ioctl+0xe/0x20 ================================================================== dm-inlinecrypt is the only caller that can evict a key that was never started, as fscrypt frees such a key without evicting it. Fix this by returning early from blk_crypto_fallback_evict_key() when tfms_inited[] is not set for the key's mode. tfms_inited[] is only set after blk_crypto_fallback_init() has successfully initialized the profile, so the crash above is no longer reachable. The bug has been latent since commit c984ff1423ae ("blk-crypto: dynamically allocate fallback profile") was merged in v6.5, and only became actually triggerable when commit e7f57d2c47e2 ("dm-inlinecrypt: add target for inline block device encryption") was merged in v7.2.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved: ARM: 9524/1: mm: align hugetlb mappings to the huge page size mmap(MAP_HUGETLB) on 32-bit Arm can return an address which is not aligned to the huge page size. In a QEMU virt guest, unmapping the VMA then hits the alignment check in __unmap_hugepage_range(): kernel BUG at mm/hugetlb.c:5213! Internal error: Oops - BUG: 0 [#1] SMP ARM PC is at __unmap_hugepage_range+0x540/0x584 LR is at __zap_vma_range+0x13a0/0x1410 Commit 7bd3f1e1a9ae ("mm: make hugetlb mappings go through mm_get_unmapped_area_vmflags") made hugetlb mappings use the architecture's arch_get_unmapped_area(). The generic implementations handle hugetlb alignment, but the Arm implementations only account for the optional SHMLBA cache-colouring constraint. A 4 KiB-page kernel can therefore align the mapping to 4 KiB or 16 KiB instead of the required 2 MiB. Set the alignment mask from the file's hstate for hugetlb mappings in both Arm implementations. Huge-page alignment also satisfies the SHMLBA constraint.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved: wifi: mt76: mt7925: fix reset panic caused by the WM2 rx irq mask mt7925_irq_map sets wm2_complete_mask, but mt7925_dma_layout has no tx done ring, so the MT_RXQ_MCU_WA queue and its NAPI are never set up. On a chip reset, mt7925e_mac_reset() calls napi_disable() on that NAPI and crashes: BUG: kernel NULL pointer dereference, address: 0000000000000a40 Workqueue: mt76 mt7925_mac_reset_work [mt7925_common] RIP: 0010:mutex_lock+0x1c/0x50 Call Trace: napi_disable+0x1d/0x50 mt7925e_mac_reset+0x327/0x420 [mt7925e] mt7925_mac_reset_work+0x9a/0x1a0 [mt7925_common] Remove the WM2 mask from mt7925_irq_map and from MT7925_INT_RX_DONE_ALL.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved: fork: don't create io threads once PF_POSTCOREDUMP is set zap_process() skips every thread that already has PF_POSTCOREDUMP set. Such a thread is past synchronize_group_exit(), so a coredump can't catch it anymore. It isn't counted in core_state->threads_remaining and it isn't sent SIGKILL. do_exit() sets PF_POSTCOREDUMP in synchronize_group_exit() and calls io_uring_files_cancel() right after that. The cancellation runs task work and a create_worker_cb() that io-wq queued before the exit creates a new io-wq worker from there. If another thread started a coredump in the meantime that worker joins a thread-group which is already being dumped. zap_process() never saw it so it was never counted. But when it exits it sees signal->core_state in synchronize_group_exit() and decrements threads_remaining like any other thread. So the count reaches zero one thread early and the dumper leaves coredump_wait_inactive() while a thread it counted is still running. The task has no fatal signal pending because zap_process() deliberately didn't send it one, and it never went through get_signal() so it doesn't have PF_SIGNALED either. Refuse to create an io thread when the creator has PF_POSTCOREDUMP. That costs nothing. io_uring_files_cancel() raises IO_WQ_BIT_EXIT before it runs any task work, so a worker created from there only ever gets to exit again, and io_should_retry_thread() doesn't retry -EINTR. Clearing PF_POSTCOREDUMP for the new thread in copy_process() was the other option. It makes the worker a thread like any other, but it only helps while the dump hasn't started. A worker born after zap_process() has run is invisible to it whatever its flags say and still decrements threads_remaining on the way out. Refusing to create it covers both, and then no task is ever born with the flag, so there is nothing to clear. Moving io_uring_files_cancel() ahead of synchronize_group_exit() closes the same window. It runs the cancellation, and whatever that can block on, before the thread announces itself to the dumper. A thread that blocks there never reaches coredump_task_exit() at all, so the dumper ends up waiting for a thread that never parks. Refusing the creation leaves the cancellation where it is. But it's very ugly to run io_uring work even before we did all the generic exit work.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved: ksmbd: reject FSCTL_SET_ZERO_DATA on a directory handle An authenticated client with a writable tree connection can open a directory with FILE_WRITE_DATA and send FSCTL_SET_ZERO_DATA on that handle. The handler only checks fp->daccess & FILE_WRITE_DATA_LE, but on a directory FILE_WRITE_DATA is the legitimate add-file right, so the check passes. ksmbd_vfs_zero_data() then calls kernel_write() on the directory file, which has no FMODE_WRITE, and __kernel_write_iter() hits WARN_ON_ONCE(!(file->f_mode & FMODE_WRITE)), panicking a panic_on_warn kernel. Before commit 25e414db7033 ("ksmbd: report holes in allocated range queries") the dense-file path used vfs_fallocate(), which rejects directories with -EISDIR. The kernel_write() loop that replaced it has no such check. Reject a directory handle in ksmbd_vfs_zero_data() before writing, as ksmbd_vfs_write() already does for SMB2_WRITE. WARNING: fs/read_write.c:608 at __kernel_write_iter+0x74b/0x8c0 Workqueue: ksmbd-io handle_ksmbd_work Call Trace: kernel_write+0x1ef/0x4d0 ksmbd_vfs_zero_data+0x413/0x590 smb2_ioctl+0x21fa/0x66a0 handle_ksmbd_work+0x61b/0x1ff0

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved: smb: smbdirect: release failed pending sockets of a listener A child of a listener only left the listen.pending or listen.ready list via smbdirect_socket_accept() or when the listener was destroyed. So every connection that failed before it was accepted (negotiate timeout, peer disconnect, invalid negotiate request, ...) stayed on the list and counted against the backlog until the listener was destroyed. After about backlog (10 for ksmbd) such connections smbdirect_listen_connect_request() rejected every new connection with -EBUSY, so an unauthenticated peer was able to permanently stop ksmbd from accepting SMB-Direct connections. Now a failed child moves itself to a new listen.orphaned list at the end of smbdirect_socket_cleanup_work(), after the disconnect was started, and queues listen.purge_orphaned_work, which releases it with smbdirect_socket_release(), without holding the listener's rdma_lock_handler() lock, in the same way smbdirect_socket_destroy() does for the remaining children. Orphaned sockets still count against the backlog until they are released. sc->accept.listener is now only changed under listener->listen.lock and whoever clears it is responsible for releasing the socket: smbdirect_socket_accept(), purge_orphaned_work or the destroy of the listener. In order to make that work: - a struct smbdirect_socket that is a listener is now freed via kfree_rcu(), so that a child can dereference sc->accept.listener under rcu_read_lock(), even if the listener is released concurrently. - smbdirect_listen_connect_request() adds nsc to the listen.pending list and sets nsc->accept.listener before it calls smbdirect_accept_connect_request(), and always returns 0 so the rdma_cm core keeps the connection id and nsc owns it. On a non-zero return it schedules nsc's teardown with smbdirect_socket_schedule_cleanup(), which orphans it off the listener so that purge_orphaned_work releases it; nsc destroys its own connection id with rdma_destroy_id() in that teardown. The teardown has to be deferred because the rdma_cm core holds nsc's id_priv->handler_mutex across the handler, so nsc->rdma.cm_id must not be destroyed synchronously from here. That same handler_mutex (and the listener's) also guarantees nsc can't go away under us, so setting the listener before the call is safe and lets a failure orphan nsc. - smbdirect_accept_negotiate_recv_work() no longer moves a socket to the ready list if it already failed or no longer belongs to the listener. Every accepting socket has a listener, so if sc->accept.listener is already cleared, it no longer sends a negotiate response, as the socket is about to be released. - smbdirect_socket_destroy() of the listener disables purge_orphaned_work and also releases the orphaned sockets.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved: smb: smbdirect: don't wait for RDMA_CM_EVENT_DISCONNECTED in smbdirect_socket_destroy_sync() smbdirect_socket_destroy_sync() waited for RDMA_CM_EVENT_DISCONNECTED after smbdirect_socket_cleanup_work() called rdma_disconnect(). That can take very long, e.g. if the peer just disappeared, until the rdma cm gives up, or forever if the event already happened, but the status was overwritten afterwards. This is not needed: smbdirect_socket_destroy() drains the qp under rdma_lock_handler(), destroys it and calls rdma_destroy_id(), which only waits for a currently running event handler and makes sure no further events are delivered. The rest of the disconnect protocol (DREQ/DREP and timewait for IB, abrupt close for iWarp) is handled by the rdma core asynchronously. drivers/nvme/host/rdma.c also just calls rdma_disconnect() and ib_drain_qp() before rdma_destroy_id(). So smbdirect_socket_destroy() now also accepts SMBDIRECT_SOCKET_DISCONNECTING and changes the status to SMBDIRECT_SOCKET_DISCONNECTED itself under rdma_lock_handler(). We could still get RDMA_CM_EVENT_DISCONNECTED in the small windows between rdma_unlock_handler() and rdma_destroy_id(), but in that case smbdirect_connection_rdma_event_handler() is basically a no-op.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved: ksmbd: wait for negotiation before receiving another PDU The receive thread queues a request and can read the next PDU before the negotiation worker finishes. While need_neg is set, the next PDU can cause ksmbd_init_smb_server() to replace conn->ops. A pipelined SMB2 request can therefore make the worker handle an earlier, shorter SMB1 request with SMB2 operations and read beyond its buffer. An SMB1 multi-protocol negotiate may be followed by an SMB2 NEGOTIATE that changes conn->ops again. Wait for work queued while the connection is new or needs negotiation to complete before reading another PDU. This keeps the operations stable for both stages of negotiation without changing when need_neg is cleared.

United Chargers Grizzl-E Smart 40A OCPP GetConfiguration Stack-based Buffer Overflow Remote Code Execution Vulnerability. This vulnerability allows network-adjacent attackers to execute arbitrary code on affected installations of United Chargers Grizzl-E Smart 40A EV chargers. Authentication is not required to exploit this vulnerability. The specific flaw exists within the handling of OCPP messages. When parsing GetConfiguration requests, the process does not properly validate the length of user-supplied data prior to copying it to a fixed-length stack-based buffer. An attacker can leverage this in conjunction with other vulnerabilities to execute code in the context of the device. Was ZDI-CAN-28968.

Authentication is not required to exploit this vulnerability. The specific flaw exists within the handling of Wi-Fi configuration requests. The issue results from the lack of authentication prior to allowing access to functionality. An attacker can leverage this in conjunction with other vulnerabilities to execute arbitrary code in the context of the device. Was ZDI-CAN-29068.
