In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved: assoc_array: keep gc's cleanup out of the live tree on allocation failure assoc_array_gc() builds a copy of the tree. Where the copy reaches a shortcut, it allocates the copy of the shortcut with kmalloc_flex(), fills it with memcpy(), links it into the new tree, and only then allocates the copy of the node after it. The memcpy() leaves the new shortcut's next_node pointing at the old tree's node, so if that second allocation fails, the cleanup, assoc_array_destroy_subtree() on the new tree, follows the new shortcut into the old tree, and the BUG_ON() on the old node's back pointer fires. Allocate the node first, and the shortcut once the node exists, freeing the node again if the shortcut cannot be allocated. A copied shortcut is then only linked into the new tree when the copy of its node is there to follow it. Nothing else changes: with no allocation failing, the trees gc builds are the same as before. Found by a userspace test that makes each allocation of each operation fail in turn.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved: assoc_array: don't chain a new shortcut onto an existing one When a full node's leaves and the new key all share the node's segment, assoc_array_insert_into_terminal_node() replaces the node with a shortcut to a pair of new nodes. If the node is itself the target of a shortcut, the new shortcut is installed as that shortcut's next node, and a shortcut leading to a shortcut is something nothing expects: assoc_array_walk() indexes the second one as a node, and assoc_array_apply_edit() hits the BUG_ON() in the loop that adjusts nr_leaves_on_branch, on that same insertion. Deletion gets a node there. When the subtree below a shortcut shrinks enough, assoc_array_delete() collapses it into one node below the shortcut, and the leaves it collects can all share that node's segment. The next key that shares it too takes this path. Eighteen insertions and a deletion are enough: sixteen keys that agree on bits 0-11, one that leaves them at bit 8 and is deleted again, and one more that agrees with the sixteen. Have the new shortcut replace the one in front of the node as well. assoc_array_insert_shortcut() gives it that shortcut's back pointer and parent slot, so the caller installs it where that one was, and excises the old shortcut along with the node, which takes a second entry in excised_meta[]. The new shortcut's index key comes from the new key up to the new skip level, so it covers what the old one did. Found by a userspace test doing random insertions and deletions on keys that share long prefixes; a targeted case builds a shortcut, deletes down to the collapse and inserts one more key.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved: iommufd/iova_bitmap: Ensure that iova_bitmap_set() handles the full IOVA Generally userspace is going to step the dirty bitmap through the IOVA space. However if the bitmap ends in the middle of a large PTE this is problematic. The first step will clear the dirty bit and report dirty to the end of its bitmap while the second step will see the clear'd dirty and report clean for the start of the bitmap. If it happens this ends up losing dirties. Further this function is missing bounds checking so if this does happen ther is a good chance it will write memory beyond what the userspace was expecting. Return an error code if this illegal condition happens.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved: f2fs: release a removed xattr node in roll-forward recovery When xattrs shrink enough to fit in the inline xattr area, write_all_xattrs() truncates the xattr node and clears i_xattr_nid. If the file is then fsynced without a checkpoint, only the inode block is written, with i_xattr_nid of 0. Roll-forward recovery starts from the checkpointed inode, whose i_xattr_nid still points to the old xattr node. f2fs_recover_inline_xattr() copies only the inline xattr area, and f2fs_update_inode() writes the old i_xattr_nid back. So the inode keeps the stale xattr node: - The node block is never released, and fsck reports "nonzero bytes in xattr space after end of list". - If the inline xattr list ends exactly at the end of the inline area, its terminator is read from the stale node, and the removed xattrs come back after recovery. When the fsynced inode has no xattr node but the checkpointed one has, release the old xattr node as truncate_node() does: check its block address, invalidate the block and drop its node cache, which may still be dirty.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved: f2fs: fix to invalidate curseg if change_curseg() fails Our consistency stress test (fsstress + fio + atomic write workers + "f2fs_io shutdown 1") triggers below kernel BUG: F2FS-fs (vdd): Stopped filesystem due to reason: 0 ------------[ cut here ]------------ kernel BUG at fs/f2fs/segment.c:3989! Oops: invalid opcode: 0000 [#1] SMP KASAN PTI Workqueue: writeback wb_workfn (flush-253:48) RIP: 0010:f2fs_allocate_data_block+0x257a/0x38e0 Call Trace: <TASK> do_write_block+0x155/0xc10 f2fs_outplace_write_data+0x192/0x340 f2fs_do_write_data_page+0xc57/0x1880 f2fs_write_single_data_page+0xda9/0x15a0 f2fs_write_cache_pages+0x973/0x1f20 __f2fs_write_data_pages+0x6c4/0x1890 do_writepages+0x21e/0x560 __writeback_single_inode+0x119/0x11b0 writeback_sb_inodes+0x67d/0x17a0 wb_writeback+0x207/0x820 wb_workfn+0x128/0xc30 process_one_work+0x925/0x1600 worker_thread+0x60a/0xff0 kthread+0x35f/0x460 ret_from_fork+0x474/0x7e0 ret_from_fork_asm+0x1a/0x30 </TASK> The BUG is f2fs_bug_on(sbi, curseg->next_blkoff >= BLKS_PER_SEG(sbi)) in f2fs_allocate_data_block(), next_blkoff was 512. The root cause is a race in between atomic write commit and shutdown as below: Thread A (commit atomic write) Thread B (shutdown) Thread C (writeback) - f2fs_ioc_commit_atomic_write - f2fs_commit_atomic_write - __f2fs_commit_atomic_write - __replace_atomic_write_block - f2fs_replace_block - __f2fs_replace_block - f2fs_ioc_shutdown - f2fs_do_shutdown : F2FS_GOING_DOWN_METASYNC - f2fs_sync_fs - f2fs_write_single_data_page : pass f2fs_cp_error() check - f2fs_stop_checkpoint : set CP_ERROR_FLAG - change_curseg - reset_curseg : curseg->segno = new_segno : curseg->alloc_type = SSR : curseg->next_blkoff = __next_free_blkoff() which is BLKS_PER_SEG if there is no free slot in new_segno - f2fs_get_sum_cache : return -EIO due to f2fs_cp_error() : return error w/o restoring curseg : goto out_unlock, skip restoring old segno, blkoff and alloc_type - f2fs_do_write_data_page - f2fs_outplace_write_data - do_write_block - f2fs_allocate_data_block : curseg->segno is valid : f2fs_bug_on(next_blkoff >= BLKS_PER_SEG) Since commit 86f33603f8c5 ("f2fs: handle errors of f2fs_get_meta_page_nofail"), change_curseg() can fail after the curseg has already been switched to the new segment, then the curseg is left in an inconsistent state: it points to a segment which may have no free slot, its summary block is zeroed, and the caller can not restore it. Subsequent block allocation on the curseg will trigger the BUG. Moreover, the writeback thread dies with curseg_lock, curseg_mutex and sentry_lock held, so the commit, shutdown and other I/O threads hang in D state. Since change_curseg() only fails once CP_ERROR_FLAG is set, no checkpoint will be committed afterward, let's invalidate the curseg via reset_curseg_fields() on failure, as new_curseg() does for -ENOSPC, then f2fs_allocate_data_block() will fail with -ENOSPC on the curseg instead of triggering BUG, and do_write_block() can handle the error since CP_ERROR_FLA ---truncated---
family: Périmétrique (VPN, pare-feu, passerelle); Système d'exploitation; Réseau (routeurs, commutateurs, Wi-Fi)

desc: In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved: nvme-tcp: Validate the queue state under the queue lock in the address attribute Reading the "address" sysfs attribute calls kernel_getsockname() on the admin queue socket, which can race with the queue teardown during connection error recovery: a reader can observe NVME_TCP_Q_LIVE set, then block on the queue lock while nvme_tcp_free_queue() releases the socket and clears queue->sock without holding the lock. Once the reader acquires the lock it dereferences the NULL socket pointer. Commit 76d54bf20cdc ("nvme-tcp: don't access released socket during error recovery") had the queue liveness check inside the lock. Commit 782373ba2766 ("nvme: tcp: avoid race between queue_lock lock and destroy") moved it back out because the lock itself is destroyed in nvme_tcp_free_queue(), so a reader arriving late trips mutex_destroy(). Check the queue liveness inside the queue lock, and clear queue->sock under the same lock. The teardown clears NVME_TCP_Q_LIVE under the lock well before the socket is released, so a reader either sees the bit cleared or a socket that cannot be released while it holds the lock. To also close the lock lifetime race, the queue locks are now owned by the controller: they are initialized with the queue array and only destroyed when the controller is freed, which cannot happen while a sysfs attribute read is still in progress. The queue count is computed by the NVME_TCP_OPT_NR_QUEUES() macro from the original connect options for both initialization and destruction, as reconnects may shrink ctrl->queue_count.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved: f2fs: fix to avoid potential reference count leak in do_garbage_collect() In do_garbage_collect(), we have reserved reference counts on summary cache of all segments, once gc_thread encounter freezing, we need to release all reference counts.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved: KVM: arm64: vgic: Stop the target vcpu when disabling LPIs Disabling LPIs is pretty nasty, as it directly messes with the AP list of the affected CPU, which could be running... This has the potential to lead to really bad behaviours, and we should not be doing that. Take example on the way the Active state is handled and simply pause the the vcpu so that we are sure it is in a quiescent state, and the state be safely manipulated. Nobody has any expectation of performance for this anyway.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved: f2fs: bound the SIT/NAT bitmaps by the checkpoint pack sit_ver_bitmap_bytesize and nat_ver_bitmap_bytesize are used as memcpy lengths into and out of sbi->ckpt, which is sized from cp_payload alone, and nothing compares either length against that allocation. sanity_check_ckpt() has checked these two fields since c77ec61ca0a4, which added them after a crafted image overran build_sit_info(). That check ties each length to a segment count; it never compares either against the allocation, which is the half this adds. Mounting over-reads in build_sit_info() and build_node_manager(), and the first checkpoint writes the same lengths back through the same pointers, so the over-read's contents reach the on-disk checkpoint. An unmount is enough; the filesystem does not have to be used. Bound both ends the way __bitmap_ptr() lays them out. The three branches differ, so a single sum of the two lengths would still admit a small overflow when cp_payload is non-zero.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved: f2fs: return -EIO for a lost inode block after cp_error After cp_error, dirty node caches are dropped without being written. If such an inode was never written, its NAT entry is still NEW_ADDR, and reading its inode block returns -ENOENT. f2fs_get_dnode_of_data() passes that -ENOENT up, and callers take it as a hole. Since the inode block is missing, the next offset can only advance one block, so fiemap walks block by block up to maxbytes, about 2^30 blocks, while holding the inode lock. It took hours in a power-off recovery test after shutdown and blocked unlink and umount on the file. Return -EIO instead of -ENOENT when the inode block itself is missing after cp_error or shutdown. A missing direct or indirect node is still reported as -ENOENT.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved: f2fs: zone: fix to avoid bio split on sequential zone In the block layer, bio_split_to_limits() splits a bio if it exceeds any underlying queue limits: 1. queue_max_sectors: Splits bios larger than the transfer limit. This limit is set by the device driver/DMA controller (max_hw_sectors) and device-mapper targets. When flushing dirty pages (governed by VFS writeback_chunk_size() and f2fs nr_pages_to_skip()), f2fs merges contiguous pages into bios up to 512KB (1024 sectors) or more without checking queue_max_sectors, which will be split if the device or DM target enforces a smaller limit. 2. queue_max_segments: Splits bios exceeding scatter-gather segment limits. f2fs allocates bios with up to 256 pages, exceeding the 128-segment limit of DM targets (dm-default-key/dm-crypt) if pages are discontiguous. 3. chunk_sectors: Splits bios crossing chunk/zone boundaries. In f2fs, section_size strictly matches zone_size, and block allocation never spans across section boundaries, so bios never cross chunk_sectors. Crucially, when bio_split_to_limits() splits a bio, bio_submit_split() submits the tail half via submit_bio_noacct() before returning the head half to the caller. On a sequential zoned device, this causes the tail bio to arrive at the zone write plug before the head: dm-3: zone 7: prepare_bio wp mismatch: bio sector 30720 offset 2048 != wp_offset 248, len 248 The write plug rejects the out-of-order tail with BLK_STS_IOERR, causing f2fs_stop_checkpoint() and remounting the filesystem read-only: 2026-09-30T22:09:23.725678+08:00 localhost kernel: CPU: 9 UID: 0 PID: 243 Comm: kworker/9:1H Not tainted 6.12.81-gb3ef518fb26d #5 2026-09-30T22:09:23.725750+08:00 localhost kernel: Hardware name: QEMU Standard PC (i440FX + PIIX, 1996), BIOS 1.17.0-debian-1.17.0-1 04/01/2014 2026-09-30T22:09:23.725753+08:00 localhost kernel: Workqueue: dm-3_zwplugs blk_zone_wplug_bio_work 2026-09-30T22:09:23.725756+08:00 localhost kernel: Call Trace: 2026-09-30T22:09:23.725758+08:00 localhost kernel: <TASK> 2026-09-30T22:09:23.725758+08:00 localhost kernel: dump_stack_lvl+0x4d/0x70 2026-09-30T22:09:23.725759+08:00 localhost kernel: f2fs_stop_checkpoint+0x1df/0x5d0 2026-09-30T22:09:23.725759+08:00 localhost kernel: ? blk_zone_wplug_bio_work+0x4eb/0x740 2026-09-30T22:09:23.725760+08:00 localhost kernel: f2fs_cache_write_end_io+0x545/0x6e0 2026-09-30T22:09:23.725761+08:00 localhost kernel: blk_zone_wplug_bio_work+0x4eb/0x740 2026-09-30T22:09:23.725762+08:00 localhost kernel: process_one_work+0x5c6/0xde0 2026-09-30T22:09:23.725764+08:00 localhost kernel: ? assign_work+0x124/0x4e0 2026-09-30T22:09:23.725765+08:00 localhost kernel: worker_thread+0x403/0xb70 2026-09-30T22:09:23.725765+08:00 localhost kernel: ? __kthread_parkme+0x82/0x140 2026-09-30T22:09:23.725766+08:00 localhost kernel: ? __pfx_worker_thread+0x10/0x10 2026-09-30T22:09:23.725766+08:00 localhost kernel: kthread+0x235/0x2e0 2026-09-30T22:09:23.725767+08:00 localhost kernel: ? recalc_sigpending+0x128/0x1d0 2026-09-30T22:09:23.725767+08:00 localhost kernel: ? __pfx_kthread+0x10/0x10 2026-09-30T22:09:23.725769+08:00 localhost kernel: ret_from_fork+0x2f/0x70 2026-09-30T22:09:23.725769+08:00 localhost kernel: ? __pfx_kthread+0x10/0x10 2026-09-30T22:09:23.725770+08:00 localhost kernel: ret_from_fork_asm+0x1a/0x30 2026-09-30T22:09:23.725771+08:00 localhost kernel: </TASK> 2026-09-30T22:09:23.725771+08:00 localhost kernel: F2FS-fs (dm-0): Stopped filesystem due to reason: 3 To prevent write bios destined for sequential zones from being split: 1. In __bio_alloc(), bound npages to bdev_max_segments(bdev) for writes to sequential zone areas. 2. In page_is_mergeable(), check queue_max_segments() and queue_max_sectors() for sequential zone areas, so f2fs will not merge beyond the queue limits.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved: wifi: rtw88: usb: bound what the driver feeds the after-DTIM queue Frames routed to the high queue are transmitted right after DTIM beacons only, inside the ATIM window, while they wait in the shared TX page pool. The driver puts no limit on how many it hands over, so as long as one station dozes, any sustained broadcast or multicast traffic outruns the drain and empties the pool: measured on an RTL8822BU AP with a single client in power save and ~40 frames/s of mDNS chatter, the free page count at 0x240 goes from 1803 to 16 in about 100 seconds and stays there for as long as the traffic lasts. From that point every other transmit queues behind the backlog, authentication responses arrive too late for anyone to join, and the reserved page download fails ("error beacon valid"). The AP keeps beaconing and only a reboot recovers. Feed the high queue through a small budget that refills below the measured drain rate (about 3 frames per DTIM, ~15/s at dtim_period 2 on the default 2 TU ATIM window); whatever exceeds the budget leaves on its access category queue right away. The high queue backlog is now bounded by the burst size under any load, so the page pool cannot run dry, at the price that a dozing station may miss part of a broadcast storm.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved: wifi: rtw88: usb: route bmc frames via the high queue only for DTIM delivery In AP mode every broadcast and multicast data frame is routed to TX_DESC_QSEL_HIGH, the after-DTIM queue, whether or not anybody is asleep. The firmware drains that queue at beacon pace, a dozen or so frames per second measured on RTL8822BU, while one associated client's mDNS/SSDP chatter alone exceeds that. The excess accumulates inside the chip until the shared TX page pool is exhausted (measured: 14 of 1803 pages left). From that point every host-sourced frame queues behind the backlog: authentication responses reach the air seconds after the client has given up, so no station can associate anymore, and the beacon reserved-page download fails the BCN_VALID poll ("error beacon valid") because it needs pages from the same pool. The AP keeps beaconing, so the failure looks like a silent RX stall and only a reboot recovers. mac80211 already decides when after-DTIM delivery is needed: it sets IEEE80211_TX_CTL_SEND_AFTER_DTIM on bmc frames only while at least one station is actually dozing. Honor that instead of routing unconditionally: flagged frames keep going through the high queue with the MORE_DATA and HGQMD handling introduced by commit 076f786a0ae1 ("wifi: rtw88: Fix AP mode incorrect DTIM behavior"), everything else leaves at line rate through the AC queues. This partially reverts the usb.c hunk of that commit, whose unconditional routing is what lets the backlog build up. On a bench AP (USB2, 20 MHz, WPA2, hostapd, a Windows client driven through disconnect/reconnect cycles): reconnects fail 0/5 on RTL8822BU and 0/3 on RTL8821CU before this change, and pass 10/10 and 5/5 with it, with the page pool staying healthy and no beacon errors logged.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved: mm/shmem: honour F_SEAL_EXEC when an ACL is set The owner of a memfd sealed with F_SEAL_EXEC can still change its execute bits by setting a POSIX access ACL. With CONFIG_TMPFS_POSIX_ACL, this lets an unprivileged owner make a non-executable memfd executable, bypassing vm.memfd_noexec=2. simple_set_acl() updates i_mode directly, bypassing the seal check in shmem_setattr(). Add shmem_set_acl() to check the resulting mode. Share the F_SEAL_EXEC check with shmem_setattr() using memfd_check_seals_mode() in include/linux/memfd.h. Fix generated by an LLM and sent by Chris Mason in private. [ david: use common helper; simplify description ]

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved: mm/userfaultfd: only allocate anon_vma in CoW mappings find_vma_and_prepare_anon() can end up allocating an anon_vma in VMAs that are not CoW mappings, which is wrong. If we have a MAP_SHARED R/O file mapped, we lack VM_SHARED (but do have VM_MAYSHARE) and lack VM_MAYWRITE. While uffd later rejects such mappings (uffd registration requires VM_MAYWRITE, see comment in validate_dst_vma) find_vma_and_prepare_anon() still wrongly allocates an anon vma before it validates the vma. This in turn later confuses copy_page_range()->vma_needs_copy() such that we end up calling copy_hugetlb_page_range() with ranges that actually do not contain *any* per-pagetable information that would require copying, which is the basis for PMD-table sharing in the first place. copy_hugetlb_page_range() should not have to worry about shared PMD tables at all: it doesn't make any sense to copy page tables that are shared, as they can be fully recreated later. Ending up in the function with shareable page tables is the real issue. If a destination PMD table is shared in copy_hugetlb_page_range(), it might get concurrently unshared as we are not holding relevant locks, resulting in us using a page table that is no longer mapped and possibly freed after calling: dst_pte = huge_pte_alloc(dst, dst_vma, addr, sz); To fix it, do not allocate an anon_vma in non-CoW mappings and add a safety guard to copy_hugetlb_page_range(), making sure that we never end up messing with shared PMD tables in there. Before commit 867a43a34ff8a ("userfaultfd: use per-vma locks in userfaultfd operations") we would always validate the VMA before allocating an anon_vma, and consequently never wrongly allocate an anon_vma. As uffd_lock_vma() is part of the same lookup machinery and also contains a misleading VM_SHARED check, change that one as well directly for consistency. A follow-up cleanup will stop taking the hugetlb_vma_lock_read(src_vma) lock in copy_hugetlb_page_range() entirely. Further, the usage of VM_SHARED in userfaultfd code should be cleaned up later to focus on CoW vs. non-CoW mappings.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved: platform/chrome: cros_usbpd_notify: Only use drvdata when parent is GOOG0004 cros_usbpd_notify_probe_acpi() takes the EC device pointer from dev_get_drvdata(dev->parent) and assumes it is a struct cros_ec_device. That only holds when GOOG0003 is a child of GOOG0004. On older devices without that hierarchy, such as Google Nami, GOOG0003 and GOOG0004 are siblings under the ACPI EC (PNP0C09): PNP0C09:00 (acpi-ec) |-- GOOG0003:00 (cros-usbpd-notify-acpi) `-- GOOG0004:00 (cros_ec_lpcs) Before commit db65a06d10b3 ("ACPI: EC: Convert the driver to a platform one") the parent platform device had no driver data, so the driver warned and continued without an EC pointer, as intended for these devices. Since that commit the ACPI EC driver stores its struct acpi_ec there, so the driver treats a struct acpi_ec as a struct cros_ec_device and calls cros_ec_cmd() on it for every USB-C PD host event. Plugging or unplugging a charger then intermittently oopses, followed by soft lockups and a hung system: BUG: unable to handle page fault for address: ffffffff9cf03220 #PF: supervisor write access in kernel mode Hardware name: Google Nami/Nami, BIOS 09/19/2019 Workqueue: kacpi_notify acpi_os_execute_deferred RIP: 0010:native_queued_spin_lock_slowpath+0x29d/0x330 Call Trace: _raw_spin_lock_irqsave+0x59/0x80 __mutex_lock.constprop.0+0x129/0x930 cros_ec_cmd_xfer+0x2a/0xf0 [cros_ec_proto] cros_ec_cmd_xfer_status+0x1a/0x90 [cros_ec_proto] cros_ec_cmd+0xb7/0x140 [cros_ec_proto] cros_usbpd_get_event_and_notify+0x42/0xc0 [cros_usbpd_notify] acpi_ev_notify_dispatch+0x4e/0x70 acpi_os_execute_deferred+0x1a/0x30 Only read the parent's driver data when the parent's ACPI node is GOOG0004, and otherwise continue without an EC pointer. While at it, drop the reference taken by fwnode_get_parent().

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved: sctp: re-point retained control chunks on association migration sctp_sock_migrate() transfers DATA chunk ownership but leaves retained control chunks pointing at the old socket. A later retransmission can therefore access the socket after it has been freed. Extend the migration walk to cover retained control chunks and use sctp_control_set_owner_w() to assign their new owner. Reuse the DATA ownership check so each chunk is processed once per pass, even when it is reachable through multiple lists or retained pointers. Preserve a control chunk's existing authentication key across migration so its final release can still generate SCTP_AUTH_FREE_KEY when needed.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved: sctp: hold shkey across socket migration sctp_sock_migrate() transfers queued DATA skbs from the old socket to the new one. skb_orphan() invokes sctp_wfree() during that transfer and drops the skb-owned shared-key reference. If userspace has removed that key from the association, this can be the final reference. The following sctp_set_owner_w() then dereferences the freed chunk->shkey while trying to take the new owner reference. Take a temporary shared-key reference before orphaning the skb and release it after the new owner has taken its reference. This preserves the selected authentication key throughout the ownership transfer. Bug found and triaged by OpenAI Security Research and validated by Trail of Bits.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved: f2fs: fix to avoid folio->mapping dereference in is_{meta, node}_folio() Otherwise, it may cause NULL pointer dereference in race condition: Thread A Thread B - f2fs_setattr - f2fs_truncate - f2fs_truncate_blocks - f2fs_do_truncate_blocks - f2fs_truncate_inode_blocks - truncate_dnode - truncate_node - invalidate_mapping_pages - folio->mapping = NULL - folio_lock - is_node_folio - F2FS_F_SB(folio): dereference on folio->mapping

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved: KVM: arm64: Use kvm_s2_fault_vma_info in gmem_abort() gmem_abort() maps at s2fd->fault_ipa, which HPFAR_EL2 holds at 4K granularity whatever the page size. The generic page-table code aligns it, but pkvm_pgtable_stage2_map() looks up existing mappings over [addr, addr + size), so on a pKVM host with pages larger than 4K a guest_memfd-backed guest that faults past the first 4K of a page can find its neighbour's mapping, get -EAGAIN and take the same fault forever. The memory fault exit reports s2fd->fault_ipa too, which for a nested guest's fault is the nested IPA rather than the canonical one kvm_gmem_get_pfn() failed on. Take the addresses from kvm_s2_fault_vma_info instead, as user_mem_abort() does, and report the canonical gfn in the memory fault exit. kvm_s2_fault_get_vma_info() itself isn't called: a guest_memfd memslot's userspace_addr doesn't need to be backed by a VMA.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved: iommu/arm-smmu-v3: Handle ARM erratum for CONT under invalidation with SVA The erratum (MMU-700: #3777127, S3: #3673557) deals with under invalidation of a CONT PTE grouping in the SMMU. The recommended work around is to use a range invalidation that spans the entire CONT. The only user of CONT in the kernel right now is through SVA sharing a CPU page table that contains a CONT created by the mm. Previously it was thought that this errata was dealt with because the driver always uses range invalidation. However, there is a subtle detail in the errata that the invalidation range must fully enclose the entire CONT for it to work. It seems that two sequential range invalidations, with a split point falling inside a CONT grouping, will not prevent the errata. The SMMU's range invalidation generation algorithm does not produce a single invalidation for a single SVA invalidation request, nor does the mm carefully align the SVA invalidation ranges to accommodate the splitting of the invalidation into several ranges. Thus, when processing a SVA invalidation, the range invalidation splitting routine can generate a range invalidation that is split in the middle of the CONT and risk under invalidation from this errata. This condition could be triggered by a malicious userspace manipulating the TLB gathers via mmap/mprotect/munmap. Update the errata list to the include the S3 variation, detect the IOMMUs that have it, and then have SVA invalidations use a simplified version of the over invalidation algorithm from the tlbi rework series. This ensures that a single range invalidation is issued for a single MMU notifier callback and now the range invalidation is guarenteed to cover any posible CONT. Future work to add CONT to iommu_domain page tables should either use this one-invalidate/one-range invalidation algorithm or disable CONT support in the iommu_domain.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved: ata: libata-scsi: reject data-in commands with a data-out buffer SG_IO can submit a data-in SCSI command with DMA_TO_DEVICE. The scatterlist can then contain pages pinned without write access. ata_scsi_rbuf_fill() writes simulated replies to that scatterlist; in the reported case, the copy tried to write the shared zero page and faulted in the kernel. The same mismatch can affect SG_IO commands translated by libata. ZBC IN and GET PHYSICAL ELEMENT STATUS completion handlers can modify the receive buffer even if the drive aborts the command. For ATAPI, the successful INQUIRY completion also rewrites the buffer in atapi_fixup_inquiry(). Reject these mismatched commands before the buffer is written or the command is issued. Report ABORTED COMMAND / DATA IN BUFFER ERROR because the CDB itself can be valid; the supplied transfer direction is wrong.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved: batman-adv: tt: only update flags for TT events In the first implementation of the translation table events, it was only possible to announce: * ADD: new locally detected client * DEL: disappeared local client If an ADD event was queued and then a DEL event was queued in the same timeslot, it is valid to destroy both events because nothing actually changed for remode nodes But with commit 3c4f7ab60cc2 ("batman-adv: improve the TT component to support runtime flag changes") and subsequent changes, it could also happen that there are extra ADD events: * ADD: _NEW_ locally detected client * ADD: already existing client with new flags * DEL: disappeared local client The first and the last type of event could in theory still be removed together from the (to be announced) events queue. But if the "update flags" ADD is dropped together with the DEL, it would still leave global translation table of a remote node in the incorrect state - believing that the client didn't disappear. If a detected client was previously announced, a DEL event must only overwrite the "update flags" ADD but the DEL itself must still continue to exist in the (to be anounced) events queue. For now, adjustment of the announced flags is used for everything instead of dropping already queued up events completely. Similarly, a DEL followed by an ADD caused both entries to be deleted. But the new ADD could announce flags changes which were not yet present for the client before it was marked for DELetion. The new ADD must therefore only overwrite the DEL - but still be kept.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved: batman-adv: tt: clear ROAM flag when re-adding a pending local client When a ROAMING_ADV is received for an announced local client, batadv_tt_local_mark_removed() sets BATADV_TT_CLIENT_ROAM, queues a DEL|ROAM change and marks the entry as BATADV_TT_CLIENT_PENDING. If the client sends a frame again before the next TTVN commit, batadv_tt_local_add_existing() only clears the PENDING flag and returns early. The ADD cancels the queued DEL, but the entry keeps the ROAM flag: * batadv_is_my_client() reports the client as not served by this node * batadv_tt_local_client_is_roaming() reroutes unicast frames for it to the node which sent the ROAMING_ADV The ROAM flag is only removed with the next frame of the client. Since BATADV_TT_CLIENT_ROAM is set together with BATADV_TT_CLIENT_PENDING, it has to be cleared also at the same time with BATADV_TT_CLIENT_PENDING when the client roamed back.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved: ceph: clamp the inline data length in ceph_fill_inline_data() The MDS decides how much inline data to attach to a reply, and the client parses inline_len without any upper bound: ceph_decode_need() only verifies that the message actually carries that many bytes. ceph_fill_inline_data() then copies the data into a single folio with no length check, so a malicious or buggy MDS returning more inline data than the folio can hold writes past its end. Clamp the length to folio_size() so both callers, handle_cap_grant() and fill_inode(), are covered.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved: iommu/amd: Force device table to maximum size IOMMU can perform out-of-bounds read of the device table entry (DTE) that is adjacent to the last DTE and falls outside the device table. For example, if the device table can hold 0 to N-1 entries, then the IOMMU can be made to fetch the Nth entry, which falls outside the device table. The device table is owned by the hypervisor (HV) and is assigned in 4KB pages that are contiguous in system physical address (SPA). If the out-of-bound DTE falls on a guest-owned page, then the guest can exploit this bug to setup malicious table walks to corrupt HV pages and/or bring down the system. Note that this bug does not manifest when the device table size is set to its maximum size of 2MB. Therefore, force the device table size to the maximum 2MB on affected processors. These are CPU family 0x17 (Zen1/Zen2) through family 0x1a (Zen5/BRH). This is a mitigation for CVE-2024-21963. kdump reuses the previous kernel's device table only when the size encoded in the IOMMU device-table register matches pci_seg->dev_table_size. A mixed rollout disagrees: the unpatched kernel uses the IVRS-derived size and the patched kernel uses 2MB, so __reuse_device_table() rejects the table. On SNP-capable IOMMUs that rejection panics the kdump kernel. Kernels that both have this patch agree on 2MB and reuse succeeds. Update the production kernel and the crash kernel together.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved: x86/mm: Fix global ASID handed out to two processes On AMD CPUs with INVLPGB, two live processes can get the same MAX_ASID_AVAILABLE global ASID value. The two then hit each other's TLB entries, so each can read or corrupt the other's memory. The global ASID space is managed lazily. When a global ASID is freed, its bit is set in the global_asid_freed bitmap. Once the free ASID search reaches the end of the global_asid_used bitmap, a global flush is done to really reclaim the lazily freed global ASIDs. However, the current code can assign the same global ASID to two different processes, if one process is assigned MAX_ASID_AVAILABLE - 1, another process MAX_ASID_AVAILABLE, and both stick around (keeping their global ASID numbers in use) until the search wraps around again. At that point a third process could also get assigned MAX_ASID_AVAILABLE. the highest ASID stays in use, so it is not handed out again last_global_asid stays below it, so no reset the clear bits run out find_next_zero_bit() returns MAX_ASID_AVAILABLE global_asid_available > 0, so the failure is not caught MAX_ASID_AVAILABLE is handed out as an ASID A search only looks at the bits below MAX_ASID_AVAILABLE, so it cannot see that this value is in use. The next failed search hands it out again, even if the first process still holds it. The fix used here is to reset the global ASID space after a failed search, and to search again. If that search fails too, no global ASID is handed out. The test for !global_asid_available is removed, because use_global_asid() only calls allocate_global_asid() if global_asid_available > 0. The remaining test is for a condition that should be impossible. [ riel: simplify code, massage changelog and comment ]

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved: arm64: sdei: Preserve the interrupted context's exception registers An SDEI event is dispatched by firmware regardless of PSTATE.DAIF, so it can interrupt the kernel where the exception registers are live: - exception entry, before kernel_entry has saved ELR_EL1/SPSR_EL1 and before the C handler has read ESR_EL1/FAR_EL1; - exception return, after kernel_exit has loaded ELR_EL1/SPSR_EL1 and before the ERET. An IRQ or pseudo-NMI cannot arrive there with PSTATE.I set. Firmware saves only x0-x17, PC and PSTATE around an SDEI event, so a synchronous exception taken by the handler overwrites the interrupted context's ELR, SPSR, ESR and FAR. do_sdei_event() only notices that ELR changed, and warns. The interrupted context then carries on with the handler's state. A task interrupted on its way into the kernel can be sent SIGILL for the handler's kernel data abort. A task interrupted on its way back to user space ERETs to EL1, at the handler's fixup address, with user registers loaded. With SDEI delivering NMI backtraces, this happens in normal operation. The handler runs show_regs(), which reads through possibly-NULL pointers with the _nofault() accessors. print_worker_info() faults this way for a kworker that is not running a work item, and a single sysrq-l warned once per such kworker. Save ELR, SPSR, ESR and FAR in __sdei_handler() before irqentry_nmi_enter(), which can take an exception too, and restore them after irqentry_nmi_exit(). Once they are restored, a nested exception is harmless if its handler is safe in NMI context. That holds for EL1 data aborts on translation, permission and access-flag faults, which never take the mmap lock in NMI context, and for BRK. Warn once, with the syndrome, about any other exception class.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved: arm64: kexec_file: Fix elf_headers memory leak in retry loop A retry allocates new elf headers and overwrites image->elf_headers, leaking the previous buffer. Free it before assigning. [catalin.marinas@arm.com: drop the redundant NULL check before vfree()]

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved: sched/fair: Clear throttle state when leaving the fair class Task-based CFS bandwidth throttling removes a task's fair sched_entity while the scheduler core still considers the task queued. p->throttled carries the fair-specific state across dequeue/enqueue operations. DEQUEUE_CLASS removes the task from cfs_rq->throttled_limbo_list but retains the bit. If the last finite CFS quota is disabled while the task runs in another class, it is absent from the unthrottle walk and the bit survives. Returning to fair while cfs_bandwidth_used() is false then performs a real fair enqueue with p->throttled still set. After bandwidth is re-enabled, a class-change dequeue treats the stale bit as limbo state and skips __dequeue_task(). p->se.on_rq therefore remains set, and put_prev_task_fair() places the entity in the EEVDF tree while the task moves to RT. On exit, the fair picker can select the TASK_DEAD task. __schedule() then returns to do_task_dead(), which hits BUG(). Keep p->throttled across migrations and group moves, but clear it on DEQUEUE_CLASS because fair-specific state must not outlive fair-class membership. A later return to fair uses the normal enqueue path. That path still respects a throttled cfs_rq. A KASAN, LOCKDEP and DEBUG_LIST v7.3 kernel reproduced the do_task_dead() BUG in 3/3 root and 3/3 delegated uid-1000 runs with CapPrm=CapEff=0 and RLIMIT_RTPRIO=1. The fix passed both matrices plus a 3/3 class-switch control with bandwidth continuously enabled, without a scheduler warning, KASAN report, lockdep splat or crash. An AI coding assistant analyzed the state mismatch and drafted the initial reproducer, fix candidate and this changelog. The source paths, trigger, controls and results were rechecked against the cited revisions.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved: nvme: wait for SRCU readers before splicing the namespace list Readers walk ctrl->namespaces under ctrl->srcu, and some of them sleep there, e.g. nvme_wait_freeze() waiting for I/O to drain. nvme_remove_namespaces() moves the list onto its on-stack ns_list with list_splice_init_rcu(), which only waits for RCU readers before relinking the entries. A reader still on the last namespace then follows its next pointer to ns_list instead of ctrl->namespaces and treats the stack as a namespace. Deleting a controller while a Format NVM passthrough waits for a delayed read on the last namespace gives: BUG: KASAN: stack-out-of-bounds in nvme_wait_freeze+0x102/0x120 Read of size 8 at addr ff110001d2f3fc38 by task nvme/4413 Call Trace: nvme_wait_freeze nvme_passthru_start nvme_submit_user_cmd nvme_user_cmd nvme_dev_ioctl BUG: unable to handle page fault for address: ffffffff8af04850 Use list_splice_init_srcu() instead, which waits for the SRCU readers. This also takes the RCU grace period out of every controller deletion. Deleting 64 tcp controllers with one namespace each, median of 3 runs on each of two boots per kernel: before after nvme disconnect-all (ms) 3491 / 3509 2996 / 3165 nvme_remove_namespaces() avg (ms) 39.0 / 40.5 31.9 / 34.7

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved: srcu: Add list_splice_init_srcu() list_splice_init_rcu() makes a list look empty to new readers, waits for the current ones with the given sync function, and only then links the entries into the new list. The sync function takes no argument, so it can wait for RCU readers but not for the readers of an srcu_struct. Passing synchronize_rcu() for a list read under SRCU still builds, but leaves SRCU readers on the entries while the last one's next pointer is moved onto the new list head. nvme_remove_namespaces() does this today. Add list_splice_init_srcu(), which waits for the readers of the given srcu_struct instead.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved: MIPS: sgi-ip32: Leave MACE PCI control alone in config accesses mace_pci_read_config() clears the master abort interrupt enable in the MACE PCI control register around each config read. A register read followed by two register writes can hang CRIME 1.1 under DMA load. Ack master aborts in the error register instead, and follow every write with a read so back-to-back accesses cannot form that sequence.

desc: In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved: udf: don't use eloc after the end of the unallocated space table When udf_next_aext() returns 0, its eloc, elen and etype outputs hold no defined value. Two walks of the unallocated space table still use eloc after the walk has reached the end of the table. udf_table_prealloc_blocks() looks for a free extent starting at first_block and decides whether it found one by comparing eloc with first_block after the walk. If the table's list ends in a continuation descriptor that leads to an empty allocation extent, eloc is then the block of that allocation extent, which is in use, and if that is first_block, the block is handed out as preallocation. Once udf_discard_prealloc() no longer frees the wrong block, this is what still makes fsx in generic/091 and generic/263 read back bad data on a table, in about one run in four. Only take the extent if the walk stopped at it. When udf_table_free_blocks() cannot merge the freed blocks into an existing extent, it appends a new one and sets only its block number, so the partition reference comes from whatever eloc held after the walk, and with long allocation descriptors it is written to disk. For a table without extents, eloc was never set. Take the partition reference from the freed blocks instead. Short allocation descriptors do not store the partition reference, which is why this half remains a latent long-descriptor fix rather than a reproduced failure.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved: udf: fix preallocation discarding before an empty allocation extent udf_discard_prealloc() finds the last extent of a file by peeking at the next one with udf_next_aext() and stopping when that returns 0. The peek reads into eloc and elen, and the code then uses them as the last extent. But when udf_next_aext() returns 0 they hold no defined value: if the extent list ends in a continuation descriptor that leads to an empty allocation extent, they describe that continuation, i.e. the block of the empty allocation extent, one block long. The kernel creates such lists itself: when udf_delete_aext() removes the only descriptor of the last allocation extent in a list, it leaves that allocation extent empty and the continuation to it in place. If the last extent is a preallocation, udf_discard_prealloc() deletes it with udf_delete_aext(), which finds the following allocation extent empty, so it also removes the continuation and frees that allocation extent's block. udf_discard_prealloc() then frees eloc and elen: that block a second time, instead of the preallocated blocks. On a space bitmap the preallocated blocks leak and the free block count drifts. On an unallocated space table the second free adds a second free extent for the same block, which is later handed out twice: fsx as run by generic/091 and generic/263 ends up with two parts of its test file in one block and reads back bad data. Peek into separate variables, so that eloc and elen keep the last extent that udf_next_aext() returned with 1.

desc: In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved: udf: check the unallocated space table when it is loaded udf_table_new_block() hands out the first block of the extent closest to its goal and trusts that the extent covers at least one whole block inside the partition. Nothing checks that. A zero-length extent makes it return the block the extent points at, which need not be free, and the subtraction of one block then underflows the length into the type bits, turning the entry into a bogus continuation. An extent running past the end of the partition makes it return blocks behind the partition. Such tables are not only found on crafted images: until the previous commit, udf_table_new_block() itself left zero-length extents behind in tables written by mkudffs, and then converted them into extents running past the partition. Check every extent once when the table is loaded, and refuse read-write access if one is empty, is not a whole number of blocks, or does not lie inside the partition, in the same way as for other allocation information the kernel cannot use. Check first that the table is an Unallocated Space Entry at all: the walk starts at the offset of the allocation descriptors in one, and for a file entry that offset lies before the inode's in-memory copy of the descriptors. Treat a chain of allocation extent descriptors that leads back to itself the same way: the walk would otherwise return the same extents forever, and the mount would never finish. Let a fatal signal interrupt the walk and fail the mount. Refusing read-write access to an empty extent is deliberate. It shows that an old kernel took the last block but left the entry behind. If consumed again, the entry returns an in-use block and turns into a huge bogus extent. Refusing the table before that happens avoids this second allocation; the filesystem can still be mounted read-only. The check cannot detect every overlap that may already exist in a damaged table. This patch should be backported together with the previous one: that patch stops creating new empty extents, and this one rejects existing ones before they are consumed again.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved: udf: don't let the extent type hide an exhausted free-space table extent udf_table_new_block() takes the first block of the free-space table extent closest to the goal. It keeps that extent's type and length together in goal_elen, subtracts one block, and deletes the extent only if goal_elen then reaches zero. UDF 2.60 section 2.3.7.1 requires the free-space extents of an Unallocated Space Entry to be of type 1 (allocated but not recorded), and mkudffs writes them that way. For such an extent the type bits keep goal_elen non-zero, so taking its last block leaves a type-1 extent of length zero behind, starting at the block after the extent, which is in use. The next allocation that picks this empty extent returns that in-use block. Subtracting a block from 0x40000000 then borrows from the type bits, and the extent becomes type 0 with a length of 2^30 - blocksize: about a gigabyte of "free" space overlapping live metadata, the other table extents and whatever lies behind the partition. From then on blocks are handed out twice, or past the end of the partition. Extents that udf_table_free_blocks() adds are type 0, where the check works, so only tables written by mkudffs or by another implementation are affected. Nothing more than filling such a filesystem is needed: on a fresh 1 MiB "mkudffs --space=unalloctable" image, creating empty files until the partition is full writes file entries over the reserve volume descriptor sequence and the backup anchor, and df then reports a negative amount of used space. On syzbot's images the same double allocation is what the two reports below trip over. In the first, ftruncate() extends a new file with enough hole extents to need a chain of allocation extent descriptors; one AED is placed on another inode's file entry, and a later one is placed on the block of the AED currently being filled, which udf_setup_indirect_aext() zeroes, so __udf_add_aext() finds lengthAllocDescs out of step with its cursor. In the second, an AED is placed past the end of the device, sb_getblk() fails, and the error path of udf_do_extend_file() calls udf_truncate_extents() on an extent list that no longer covers i_size. Keep the type separately from the length, as udf_table_prealloc_blocks() already does.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved: mptcp: pm: kernel: use RCU to free endpoint listeners mptcp_pm_nl_create_listen_socket() starts the TCP listener directly instead of going through mptcp_listen(). It consequently misses setting SOCK_RCU_FREE on the parent MPTCP socket. tcp_child_process() can invoke the listener's subflow_data_ready() callback without holding the MPTCP parent lock or a reference to the parent. An authenticated MP_JOIN racing with endpoint teardown can therefore access the parent after its last reference has been dropped. The ADD_ADDR error path can also close an already published listener. Set SOCK_RCU_FREE before __inet_listen_sk() publishes the TCP listener, matching mptcp_listen(). This protects the parent on every subsequent close path, including a failed endpoint addition.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved: drm/etnaviv: Flush the tile status cache through both the PE and BLT Since commit f232d9ec029c ("drm/etnaviv: fix TS cache flushing on GPUs with BLT engine"), jobs on GPUs with a BLT engine use a BLT command to flush the tile status cache instead of TS_FLUSH_CACHE, which is broken on most of these GPUs. GC7000 r6008/r6009 and GC8200 r6401 are the other way around: TS_FLUSH_CACHE works, but the BLT command does not flush the cache. The vendor driver handles these GPUs using TS_FLUSH_CACHE, but the etnaviv kernel driver has no way to identify them. As a result, dirty tile status cache lines survive the end of a job. They are written back by the next cache flush, using the page table of the job issuing it. If that job belongs to another process, the write goes to the wrong address space. On GC7000 r6009 this causes MMU faults and GPU recoveries blamed on an innocent process. I see around 1100 per run of a multisample depth/stencil test running alongside two other GPU clients. Emit both flushes at the end of every job on GPUs with a BLT engine. Whichever does not work on a given GPU is a no-op. Since dirty lines are only written back once, this costs one additional state load per job.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved: drm/etnaviv: Fix NULL dereference on unbind without PPU flop reset flop_reset_data_ppu is only allocated on GPUs that need the PPU flop reset. However, etnaviv_unbind(..) frees it unconditionally, and etnaviv_cmdbuf_free(..) dereferences cmdbuf->suballoc before checking whether cmdbuf is NULL. As a result, unloading the driver on GPUs that do not need the PPU flop reset causes a NULL pointer dereference at address 0.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved: net/smc: don't spin in smc_rx_recvmsg() while a pipe holds spliced data While bytes spliced off the RMB are still in a pipe, recvmsg() waits for the pipe to release them before it copies the data behind them. The path to that wait skips the timeout and signal checks, and smc_rx_wait() returns at once on RCV_SHUTDOWN. With a signal pending, after SHUT_RD, or once the peer closes or shuts down writing, recvmsg() spins on a CPU until the pipe is drained, and SIGKILL cannot stop it. MSG_DONTWAIT and an expired SO_RCVTIMEO wait there too instead of returning -EAGAIN. Check the timeout and signals before that wait, and end it when the pipe releases the data or the connection is killed, not on RCV_SHUTDOWN. A zero-length read returns 0 without waiting for the pipe; a non-blocking one returns -EAGAIN while poll() still reports the socket readable (splice() can still take those bytes). The wait sets SOCKWQ_ASYNC_WAITDATA like smc_rx_wait(), so a byte arriving behind the pipe raises no SIGIO on a reader already asleep for it, and a full barrier orders its wait queue entry before its read of splice_pending, so no wake is lost.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved: ext2: preserve IOMAP_F_DIRTY for extending direct writes ext2_iomap_begin() sets IOMAP_F_DIRTY for writes that may extend i_size, but clears the flag after ext2_get_blocks(). When the write uses an existing mapped block, iomap can then use FUA and skip generic_write_sync(), even though ext2_dio_write_end_io() updates the inode size. An O_DSYNC write can therefore return without persisting the new size. For example, on a FUA-capable device, a 512-byte O_DIRECT|O_DSYNC write at offset 512 into a fsynced one-byte file returns successfully and extends the in-memory size to 1024, while an immediate read of the on-disk inode still shows size 1. An explicit fsync persists the new size. Move setting of IOMAP_F_DIRTY after the initialization.

desc: In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved: ALSA: usx2y: Guard the playback copy usx2y_urb_play_prepare() sums the packet lengths of a whole URB, copies that many frames with a single wrap, and sizes each playback packet from the capture packet's actual_length. Three things are unchecked: that the URB fits in the ring buffer, that a packet fits in the playback endpoint's maxpacksize, from which tmpbuf is allocated, and that actual_length is a whole number of frames. The ISO descriptors take the raw actual_length while transfer_buffer_length and the copies take count * stride, so a packet that is not a multiple of the stride makes the descriptors add up to more than the buffer, by up to stride - 1 bytes per packet. Return -EPIPE, as the existing packet-size check does, when the URB is larger than the buffer or a packet is larger than maxpacksize, and size each descriptor from whole frames, so the descriptors add up to transfer_buffer_length and each stays within maxpacksize. The buffer case is prevented by the previous patch and this is the guard for it; the other two depend only on the device. The first case is reachable on the unpatched driver with ordinary packets: on 7.3-rc7, a USB/IP device presenting the US-122 interface layout and sending 48-frame packets, with a 100-frame playback buffer (two 50-frame periods, inside the stock constraints), KASAN reports: BUG: KASAN: out-of-bounds in i_usx2y_urb_complete+0x79b/0x1ac0 Read of size 18446744073709551280 at addr ffff88800e6b02e0 by task vhci_rx/80 With both patches, the same device and a 200-frame playback buffer is refused at hw_params with EINVAL, and a 400-frame buffer plays for 30 s with the position advancing inside the buffer, no KASAN report and neither guard message. The maxpacksize check is not exercised: the emulated device reports the same wMaxPacketSize on both endpoints. The descriptor case is visible with capture packets of 195 bytes at stride 4 (48 frames and 3 bytes): without this change the four descriptors add up to 780 bytes for 768 bytes of data, and USB/IP's completion check refuses the URB ("total length of iso packets 780 not equal to actual length of buffer 768", -EPROTO), after which the driver stops the streams. With this patch every descriptor is 192 bytes, the descriptors add up to the data in every URB for 30 s, the position advances inside the buffer and KASAN reports nothing. The 48-frame playback run above is unchanged.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved: ALSA: usx2y: Require a buffer of two URBs usx2y_urb_capt_retire() wraps the ring buffer once per packet and usx2y_urb_play_prepare() once per URB of nr_of_packs() packets of up to 50 frames. Both assume that the data fits in the buffer, and the hw constraints only require about two 1 ms periods, so a packet larger than the buffer on capture, or a URB larger than the buffer on playback, violates that assumption. Constrain SNDRV_PCM_HW_PARAM_BUFFER_SIZE in snd_usx2y_pcm_open() to at least two URBs, 2 * nr_of_packs() * 50 frames, for both directions. The bound is in frames and derived from the driver's own packet limit, so it does not read the endpoint, whose altsetting is only selected in prepare. Two URBs rather than one, because the position advances by a URB on playback and only moves when a URB is less than the whole buffer. Keep a guard in usx2y_urb_capt_retire() that drops a packet larger than the buffer, for the case the constraint makes unreachable. With nrpacks above about 163 (S16_LE) or 109 (S24_3LE) the bound exceeds the 64 KiB buffer the substream preallocates (twice that with the preallocation raised to its 128 KiB maximum), so hw_params fails for those module settings. That is intended: the driver cannot be safe with a URB larger than half the largest buffer. Reproduced on 7.3-rc7 with a USB/IP device presenting the US-122 interface layout and 1024-byte packets into a 512-byte capture buffer: BUG: KASAN: out-of-bounds in i_usx2y_urb_complete+0x1285/0x1ac0 Read of size 18446744073709551104 at addr ffff88800e448800 by task vhci_rx/83 Tested on 7.3-rc7 with the same device, S16_LE at 44100 Hz, nrpacks 4, so the bound is 400 frames. A 128-frame capture buffer and a 200-frame playback buffer are refused at hw_params with EINVAL. A 400-frame buffer streams for 30 s in each direction with the position advancing inside the buffer and no KASAN report; the capture guard did not fire. The same 400-frame capture buffer with S24_3LE, which selects altsetting 2 in prepare, streams for 30 s with the same result.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved: ALSA: caiaq: free the EP4 URB when input setup fails The three controllers that use the EP4 input URB allocate it before checking the endpoint type and before registering the input device. On failure they jump to exit_free_idev, which clears cdev->input_dev but leaves cdev->ep4_in_urb set. The card teardown then calls snd_usb_caiaq_input_free(), which returns early because input_dev is NULL, so the URB is never freed. Release the URB before dropping the input device on the error path.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved: ALSA: line6: Reject capture buffers smaller than two packets line6_capture_copy() splits the copy into the ALSA ring buffer once at the buffer end and wraps pos_done once, which is only correct when one packet holds at most buffer_size frames. The packet size comes from the device's endpoint, and the per-device hw structs allow 64-byte periods with periods_min 1, so a packet can be larger than the whole buffer. audio_in_callback() logs an oversized packet and then copies it anyway. The packet size is known at probe time, so constrain SNDRV_PCM_HW_PARAM_BUFFER_BYTES in snd_line6_capture_open() to at least twice the larger of the two endpoints' packet sizes. Two rather than one, because pos_done advances by the packet and wraps once, so a buffer of exactly one packet leaves the position unchanged after every packet. hw_params then rejects a buffer that cannot hold two packets, and the single wrap is valid for every configuration that gets through. Keep a guard in line6_capture_copy() that drops an oversized packet with a ratelimited error, for the case that should no longer be reachable. Reproduced on 7.3-rc7 with a USB/IP device presenting the GuitarPort interface layout and 1024-byte packets into a 128-byte buffer: ALSA logged "invalid position: pos = 224, buffer size = 32" and the driver logged "driver bug: len" on every following packet. With this patch a 1024-byte buffer is refused at hw_params, and a 2048-byte buffer streams for 30 s with no report and with the position moving inside the buffer.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved: ALSA: hda/tas2781: Only accept CRC-less V1 data if all entries are valid Commit 408249089c48 ("ALSA: hda/tas2781: Accept V1 calibration data without CRC") only checked the first device entry. On machines where the BIOS populates fewer entries than p->ndev, the remaining all-zero entries are applied and tas2781_cali_preproc() divides by zero on playback open. Accept CRC-less V1 data only if every expected entry is non-zero and self-consistent (R0 * 1/R0 close to 1.0), otherwise reject it as before.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved: ALSA: cs46xx: Handle SCB creation failures before dereferencing With CONFIG_PM_SLEEP enabled, cs46xx_dsp_create_scb() can return NULL if kmemdup() fails to allocate the SCB data saved for resume. cs46xx_dsp_scb_and_task_init() and _dsp_create_generic_scb() dereference the returned pointer without checking it, causing a NULL pointer dereference on allocation failure. Check both return values before accessing the SCB descriptors. Return -ENOMEM when creating the null SCB fails and propagate NULL from _dsp_create_generic_scb(). Found by Linux Verification Center (linuxtesting.org) with SVACE static analysis tool.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved: drm/nouveau/nvkm: clear use.enabled when subdev init fails On Kepler boards without the video decode falcon firmware installed (msvld/mspdec/msppp), every other VA-API decode attempt binds to an engine with no ucode loaded. The submitted work never completes, which leads to a context switch timeout, a channel recovery that cannot reset the engine, and eviction waits on fences that never signal. The process ends up stuck in D state, or killed by SIGBUS when it touches a buffer evicted after the wait times out: msvld: unable to load firmware data msvld: init failed, -19 fifo: SCHED_ERROR 0a [CTXSW_TIMEOUT] vo[5444]: channel 14 killed! WARNING: drivers/gpu/drm/nouveau/nvkm/engine/fifo/runl.c:117 at nvkm_runl_rc+0x2a4/0x3b0 [nouveau] [TTM] Buffer eviction failed WARNING: drivers/gpu/drm/nouveau/nouveau_bo.c:1092 at nouveau_bo_move_ntfy.part.0+0x9b/0x100 [nouveau] Tracing nvkm_subdev_ref() and nvkm_subdev_init_() shows the pattern: a reference taken with enabled=0 runs nvkm_falcon_init(), which returns -ENODEV; the next reference sees enabled=1 and succeeds without running it. Clear use.enabled when init() fails, so that every later reference retries init and fails cleanly. The other readers of use.enabled are fini() handlers that use it to skip teardown, which they now also do after a failed init(). On a GK107 (Quadro K1100M) without video firmware, playing H.264 with mpv --hwdec=auto: without this patch the GPU channel is killed within a minute and mpv hangs; with it, VA-API decoder creation fails, mpv falls back to software decoding, and no faults are logged.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved: l2tp: only return sessions of the given tunnel in l2tp_session_get() Commit 5f77c18ea556 ("l2tp: use IDR for all session lookups") made pppol2tp_connect() and the netlink session commands find sessions with l2tp_session_get(), passing the socket of the tunnel they name. L2TPv3 session IDs are unique per network namespace, except that sessions carried over UDP are only unique per UDP socket, the socket of their tunnel. However, l2tp_v3_session_get() only checks the socket when another session has the same session ID. Otherwise it returns the session, whichever tunnel it belongs to. As of now, a session command that names the wrong tunnel acts on a session of another tunnel, and a PPPoL2TP socket for a second L2TPv3 tunnel fails with EEXIST, because it finds session 0 of the first tunnel. The issue can be reproduced with: ip l2tp add tunnel tunnel_id 3 peer_tunnel_id 3 encap udp \ local 127.0.0.1 remote 127.0.0.1 udp_sport 5003 udp_dport 6003 ip l2tp add tunnel tunnel_id 4 peer_tunnel_id 4 encap udp \ local 127.0.0.1 remote 127.0.0.1 udp_sport 5004 udp_dport 6004 ip l2tp add session tunnel_id 3 session_id 7 peer_session_id 7 ip l2tp del session tunnel_id 4 session_id 7 ip l2tp show session Before that commit, the delete fails with "No such device", and session 7 of tunnel 3 is still listed. After that commit, the delete succeeds, and session 7 of tunnel 3 is gone. This patch will make l2tp_session_get() return NULL when the L2TPv3 session it finds does not belong to the given socket. The receive path calls l2tp_v3_session_get() directly and is not changed.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved: ovl: look up the index by the decoded origin A file opened by file handle on an overlay with nfs_export=on can show the stale lower data of a file that was copied up to the upper layer. While the file opened this way stays in the inode cache, a lookup of the copied up file by path fails with ESTALE for all users. The open can also succeed for a file that was removed, where it has to fail with ESTALE. This happens with a handle that has one byte changed. The handle comes from an NFS client, or from a process that calls open_by_handle_at() with CAP_DAC_READ_SEARCH in the initial user namespace. When a file in a lower layer is about to be modified, overlayfs first copies it to the upper layer (copy up). With nfs_export=on, each copy up also creates an entry in the index directory, a directory that overlayfs keeps for itself on the upper filesystem. The handle of an overlay file that comes from a lower layer wraps the handle of its lower inode. Overlayfs calls this lower inode the origin. The overlay handle stays valid after a copy up. To decode such a handle, ovl_lower_fh_to_d() first decodes the wrapped handle to the origin. If no overlay inode is cached for the origin, it looks in the index directory: - An index entry there leads to the upper file. - A whiteout, the marker that overlayfs uses for a removed file, means that the overlay file was removed. The name of an index entry is the handle that copy up encoded for the origin, as a hex string. ovl_lower_fh_to_d() builds the name for this lookup from the bytes that the caller passed in. But handles with different bytes can decode to the same inode: - Overlayfs ignores some flag bits of the handle. - A lower filesystem can accept a different fid type, extra bytes, or generation 0 for any generation. Such a handle decodes to the origin but misses the index entry or the whiteout. So the decode returns an overlay inode that has only the lower file. While that inode is cached, a path lookup of a copied up file fails with ESTALE, since the upper file that the lookup finds does not match the cached inode, which has none. Reproduced on tmpfs and on ext4 with open_by_handle_at(), after a copy up and a mount cycle. A handle in which one flag bit, the fid type, the length or the generation was changed read the old lower data, and path lookups returned ESTALE. Fix this by re-encoding the decoded origin and building the index name from that handle.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved: arm64: mm: validate /dev/mem mmap ranges without overflow An arm64 syzkaller reproducer creates a FUSE character device with major:minor 1:1, so opening it uses the /dev/mem file operations. It maps one page from offset 0xfffffffffffff000 at user address zero. The next openat() with a NULL pathname triggers a synchronous external abort (SEA, ESR 0x96000010) in strncpy_from_user() via do_getname(), panicking the kernel. valid_mmap_phys_addr_range() checks the exclusive end by adding the mapping size to the starting address. For this offset, the sum wraps to zero and passes the PHYS_MASK test, allowing an out-of-range PFN to reach remap_pfn_range(). The inclusive-end overflow check in mmap_mem_prepare() does not catch it because the end is ULONG_MAX. Reject starting PFNs outside PHYS_MASK and compare the inclusive length against the remaining physical range without overflowing. This also allows mappings that end exactly at PHYS_MASK, which the old check incorrectly rejects. [catalin.marinas@arm.com: changed the check to look more like __access_ok()]

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved: nvmet: don't return memory contents beyond valid data when reading ANA log page The host side does not know how much valid data will be returned by the target so it will typically provide a buffer larger than the amount of valid data in the ANA log page. The memory allocation used by the target does not guarantee that prior kernel memory contents will not be returned past the end of the valid page data. Fix this to ensure that the SGL is zeroed before copying the data.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved: drm/amdgpu: don't drop the gang dependency fence twice drm_sched_job_add_dependency() drops the fence reference when it fails, but amdgpu_cs_submit() drops it again, so the scheduled fence of a gang member loses a reference it still needs. A GFX+COMPUTE gang waiting for another context, with the xarray node allocation for the leader's dependency failed through failslab: WARNING: drivers/dma-buf/dma-fence.c:589 at dma_fence_release+0x34d/0x730, CPU#1: amd_uapi_regres/2993 drm_sched_job_cleanup+0x2c2/0x340 [gpu_sched] amdgpu_job_free+0xcb/0x3e0 [amdgpu] amdgpu_cs_parser_fini+0x435/0x710 [amdgpu] amdgpu_cs_ioctl+0xcd2/0x7a60 [amdgpu] Oops: general protection fault, probably for non-canonical address 0xdffffc0000000001: 0000 [#1] SMP KASAN NOPTI KASAN: null-ptr-deref in range [0x0000000000000008-0x000000000000000f] RIP: 0010:dma_fence_signal_timestamp_locked+0x1b8/0x610 (cherry picked from commit 5aa070a83c8378810b906cc8bfc650ce69822a7c)

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved: drm/amdgpu: don't walk the CS chunks when allocating them failed amdgpu_cs_pass1() sets p->nchunks before allocating p->chunks, and the allocation failure path skips resetting it. amdgpu_cs_parser_fini() then frees the kdata of nchunks chunks from a NULL array. On navi48 with the chunk array allocation failed through failslab: Oops: general protection fault, probably for non-canonical address 0xdffffc0000000001: 0000 [#1] SMP KASAN NOPTI KASAN: null-ptr-deref in range [0x0000000000000008-0x000000000000000f] RIP: 0010:amdgpu_cs_parser_fini+0x35d/0x710 [amdgpu] amdgpu_cs_ioctl+0xcae/0x7a20 [amdgpu] drm_ioctl_kernel+0x180/0x320 [drm] Set nchunks once the array exists. (cherry picked from commit 0c828445757b86aaa3ed2638832d76f450022bdf)

desc: In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved: drm/amdgpu: unlock the VM and BO when attaching a KFD BO fails kfd_mem_attach() locks the page directory and the BO with a drm_exec transaction on its stack, but leaves through the unwind label without drm_exec_fini() when locking fails, e.g. when MAP_MEMORY_TO_GPU gets a signal while the page directory or the BO is busy. Reservations already acquired then remain locked with their ww_acquire_ctx pointing into the expired stack frame. With one thread doing GEM_VA map/unmap on the KFD VM and another one mapping KFD BOs while getting SIGUSR1 every 20 us: BUG: KASAN: stack-out-of-bounds in __ww_mutex_lock.constprop.0+0x34f5/0x3da0 ww_mutex_lock_interruptible+0x2f/0x150 drm_exec_lock_obj+0x107/0x2d0 [drm_exec] kfd_mem_attach+0x4dd/0x1b60 [amdgpu] and the process ends up in D state. Finish the transaction before unwinding. (cherry picked from commit 7b885fa27e4b9fa5cbdc64e66fc35872aee296f5)

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved: drm/amdgpu: drop the dma-buf reference when a KFD import fails import_obj_create() takes a reference on the dma-buf for the new kgd_mem, but the error path after validating the BO doesn't drop it. Since the validation reserves the BO interruptibly, an import failing with -ERESTARTSYS leaks the exported BO with its memory, and keeps the module in use. Importing a 64 MiB VRAM BO in a loop while getting SIGUSR1 every 20 us and another thread changes the BO's mappings: INFO: 171821 imports, VRAM used before 65 MiB, after 129 MiB modprobe: FATAL: Module amdgpu is in use. Drop the reference, and free the sync object and the mutex of the kgd_mem as well. With that VRAM usage returns to 65 MiB after the same test. (cherry picked from commit b4d1eca2729840148ff2ea957724ce764ca5a94e)

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved: drm/amdgpu: Clamp the ATIF backlight curve to its 99 points amdgpu_atif_query_backlight_caps() stores the firmware's number_of_points as data_points but copies only the 99 points that luminance_data[] holds. number_of_points is a u8, so a firmware table that claims more makes the custom curve code in amdgpu_dm index past the array, and dm_query_extended_brightness_caps() copy past the end of the data_points[] buffer it fills Clamp the count to ATIF_QBTC_MAX_DATA_POINTS and warn, since a table that claims more is a firmware bug (cherry picked from commit af8a1c2b7d3de4960e10f94e8ba2fc0ccd168072)

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved: drm/amdgpu: Report MES ring wait timeouts. Return -ETIMEDOUT when the fence wait before submission expires instead of reporting success without submitting the packet. (cherry picked from commit 34341594a87b4a3f28be41e3e70a4787f02b3d9e)

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved: drm/amdgpu: Fix duplicate dependency fence releases drm_sched_job_add_dependency() consumes its fence reference on success and failure. Do not release the fence again if drm_sched_job_add_dependency() fails. (cherry picked from commit e04f3dfb2071451633e6440a3911a9bb65df9144)
